Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Brahmā suddenly descended and bathed the Bodhisattva with various fragrant waters; nine dragons above showered fragrant water to bathe the Holy Honored One, and having completed the bath, his body and mind were pure.

His dwelling and conduct were transcendent and complete; born into a great clan like a true and perfect jewel, endowed with marvelous marks and myriad excellences, he was fit to turn the Wheel of Dharma. Like a Wheel-Turning King, he dwelt within the triple world, covering the ten directions with the single canopy of the Way.
King Śuddhodana felt his heart become serene and experienced immeasurable joy.
At that time, five thousand maidservants each gave birth to a son; all were powerful youths who appeared before the king to serve him as attendants.
Eight hundred nurses also each gave birth to a son.
A hundred thousand elephants were born;
white mares gave birth to foals, their color like snow and their coats sleek and lustrous;
yellow rams gave birth to lambs, numbering twenty thousand.

When the precious chariot with its jeweled lattice canopy proceeds along the sacred path, one likewise bows one’s head in reverence. Now, as it travels, what deeds shall be performed? Its virtue surpasses that of all the devas; its great transformations are immeasurable, and its life-work is vast. For these reasons, its radiance shines everywhere.
Five thousand jade maidens, naturally perfumed with fragrant flowers, each holding scented oils, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother, their minds intent upon the Mahāyāna practice;

the various devas came to offer congratulations, wishing that she might not be weary, and five thousand jade maidens all came to attend her, each holding flowers and incense to congratulate the Bodhisattva’s mother, whose garments, bedding, and dwellings were as if they were in the heavens;
the young boys requested five hundred seats and approached the Bodhisattva’s mother, wishing that she might not be fatigued.
Furthermore, he adorned his body with necklaces; the Bodhisattva was fearless and would surely attain the Way of Buddhahood.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Bodhisattva was born, his mother remained peaceful and secure; she had no sores or scars, nor did she feel any pain or itching, but was restored to her former state.”

At that time, five thousand celestial maidens from before and behind brought celestial incense and oil-scented perfumes to present to the Bodhisattva’s mother; kneeling for a long time, they inquired after her well-being, asking if she was free from fatigue.

Five thousand jade maidens presented celestial medicines; five thousand jade maidens brought precious necklaces; five thousand jade maidens brought celestial garments; and five thousand jade maidens brought celestial music to serve the Bodhisattva’s mother, each inquiring after her well-being and saying:
"May you not be weary or fatigued."
"Now, these five-attainment sages of the world, soaring lightly through the void, have suddenly appeared before King Śuddhodana.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"When the Bodhisattva was born, for seven days and nights, with music and various offerings of a hundred kinds of food and drink, they attended upon the Bodhisattva’s mother beneath the Lumbinī tree; there they practiced giving, upheld the precepts, exercised patience, and applied diligence to perform meritorious deeds and establish virtuous foundations."

At that time, thirty-two thousand brahmins constantly brought whatever they lacked, providing daily supplies to satisfy all their needs. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and Brahmā, the King of Brahmās, transformed themselves into young scholars (*maṇava*), appearing most upright and handsome amidst the assembly of brahmins, and recited these verses of auspiciousness:
"May all evil realms be stilled, Bringing universal peace to sentient beings;
When sentient beings are harmonious and at ease, All shall be free from affliction."
Just as light dispels all darkness, and the radiance of the devas illuminates the impurities;
so too does the light of virtue penetrate all other splendors, causing them to be obscured and no longer appear.
When one no longer perceives the traces of past karma, one likewise hears nothing more of it.
Just as the Buddha’s light appeared, he became the Great Sage of the world.
Unaffected by the maladies of worldly toil, his compassionate heart took pity upon all beings;
hundreds of thousands of millions of Brahmā deities came to make offerings to him in measureless numbers.
Just as when a tree’s flowers are in full bloom, standing firm upon level ground,
all people go there to seek them and everyone gathers them;
so too in this world, from the muddy mire grows the lotus flower.
The World-Protector’s wisdom is thus, nourishing and sustaining all beings.
Like a soft garment perfumed with celestial incense,
he acts as the King of Physicians to heal those who are afflicted by disease.
Should there be one who has transcended desire, dwelling in the realm of form with harmonious voice,
and with palms joined in salutation, then for him he speaks of the Multitude of Blessings.
If gods and humans behold the gentleness of the celestial being;
Mutually honoring one another, they serve as guides for the multitude.
Like pure water, they cause all things to flourish;
because of this right view, their dwelling is always peaceful and secure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, seven days after the Bodhisattva was born, his mother passed away.
What do you think, bhikṣus?"
If he passes away after seven days, is it the fault of the Bodhisattva?
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
This is indeed as it ought to be according to his original destiny.

When the Bodhisattva observed that his mother’s life was nearing its end, he descended to be born. While she bore him in her womb, the devas made offerings to her until his birth; because he had partaken of celestial food, he found no pleasure in worldly nourishment—this is likewise as it ought to be according to his original merit.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present are all likewise; the mother passed away seven days after [the birth]. Why is this?

When the Bodhisattva was born, the mother’s physical faculties were complete and free from any impurity; she was destined to receive the merit and enjoyments of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and thus ascended to that heaven.

Just as he ascended to that heaven, before the Bodhisattva was born, the palaces, mansions, lecture halls, and residences provided by the various devas for his dwelling were prepared. Five thousand jars filled with fragrant water were offered for the Queen; five thousand celestial maidens each moved their couches and seats; five thousand celestial maidens held crowns and turbans in their hands, while others carried scented bathing water to sprinkle the ground before them.
Fifty thousand Brahmā devas each held precious vases and proclaimed "Ten Thousand Years" of longevity.

Twenty thousand nāgas adorned their bodies with precious necklaces; twenty thousand white elephants adorned their bodies with jewels and pearls; and twenty thousand chariots, equipped with banners and canopies, followed in a procession behind jeweled latticed carriages.
Forty thousand foot soldiers, valiant and preeminent, followed behind the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, in the void of space, countless billions of devas suddenly erected walls and barriers of purple gold to make offerings to the Bodhisattva’s mother.

On that night when the Bodhisattva descended as a spirit, within the infinitely adorned Great Hall of the Desire Realm, twenty thousand wives of Māra came to attend the Bodhisattva’s mother, each holding precious threads.

Furthermore, twenty thousand men had their bodies adorned with necklaces. At that time, during that night, two jade maidens heard [the news]; among them was one lady-in-waiting who was a non-human jade maiden, whose countenance would flourish upon seeing [the Bodhisattva].

At that time, through the power of the Bodhisattva’s virtue and majestic spiritual authority, within this great city of Kapilavastu, five hundred elders—all of whom were of the Śākya clan—each constructed five hundred residences. Upon entering the city of Kapilavastu, they opened the city gates for the Bodhisattva and, surrendering their very lives, addressed him, saying:

"O All-Artha-Śiva (Auspiciousness of All Meanings), we entreat you to deign to enter these abodes of the devas. This is a pure place; as the Universal Eye has descended here, there is a great palace named *Rakṣita-puṣpa* (Guarded Flower) where the Bodhisattva ought to dwell."

"Then the great brahmins and the noble Śākyas said: 'At that time, King Śuddhodana, for the sake of the Bodhisattva, humbled himself and entered their dwellings; having entered five hundred such dwellings, he brought peace and security through his meritorious deeds and practiced what is upright and true.'"
The five hundred Chandakas each spoke, saying:
"We shall serve and make offerings to the newly born Prince. Some said:
"The Prince is sagely and wise, and his virtuous governance and instruction are excellent; he is upright and extraordinary, such that none can equal him even in his youth.
Furthermore, as the Prince now grows ever older, who will be able to nurture and raise him to maturity?
They all deliberated together, saying:

"Only Mahāprajāpatī is able to nurture him with a compassionate heart; by pushing aside the dry bedding for herself and taking the damp for him, feeding him with milk and nourishing him, she alone can cause him to grow up.
Mahāprajāpatī was the Prince’s paternal aunt; she was pure and had no husband, and thus she was capable of constantly remaining by his side without being far away.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with the Śākya clansmen, went in unison to Mahāprajāpatī and spoke to her with this intention:
"The Prince’s mother has passed away; at that time, may your niece nurse and raise him."
Then Mahāprajāpatī agreed to this.
Later, when the king met the Śākya clan, he wished to test them by asking:
"Now, will the Prince become the lord of the kingdom?"
"If he were to leave the household life?
We wish to resolve this doubt.
The Śākyas then addressed him, saying:
"I have heard that on the Snowy Mountains there is a seer and brahmin named Āḷāra, who is aged, highly learned, and clearly understands the marks of physiognomy.

The king was greatly delighted; he therefore prepared his carriage and white elephant, intending to go to the practitioner, while the devas, nāgas, and spirits manifested countless transformations to lead, follow, and guard him.
At that time, Āyudha beheld these various divine transformations and knew that King Śuddhodana had given birth to a holy prince whose majestic spiritual radiance surpassed that of gods and men;
his heart filled with joy, he desired to go and pay his respects in person.
Thereupon the World-Honored One, for the sake of the assembled multitude, spoke in verse:
"The seer Brahmāyus saw a deity flying through the void;
His form was the color of purple gold, and beholding him, he was filled with great joy."
The celestial Cakravartin and the Golden-Winged Bird, the *kiṃnara* who is the Buddha— Hearing these essential phrases, they rejoice;
with the divine eye, they observe the ten directions.
Thus their names are manifold, yet their virtue is as lofty and steep as a mountain.
Like a tree with tender flowers and fruit, he dwells as the Honored One within the triple world.
The universal earth is level as the palm of a hand; like the heavens, one rejoices without delusion.
As the Sea King possesses jewels, so does the manifestation of the Path of Dharma appear thus.
As evil is extinguished, there is no suffering; like a deity wandering through the void, he hears the soft, celestial sounds, and auspicious jewels manifest throughout the three realms.
Āyiraka surveys the world below, observing King Śvetaka of the Kāśis.
Seeing the auspicious marks of one who generates merit, he went toward him with joyful delight.
Standing at the gate of the royal palace, he beheld countless billions of people;
seeing a servant girl, he asked her:
"Excellent! Where is the King?
We wish to go before him to pay our respects.
With joyful hearts they entered and made their announcement; the King commanded them to come forward.
He spread out his seat and hurriedly welcomed him.
With a heart filled with longing and emptiness, he asked where the Honored Sage was;
though his years had grown old, he did not appear often.
The King commanded him to take a seat and asked, "For what reason have you deigned to come? [He replied:
"I came because I saw the various transformations of the assembly.
My son is renowned as foremost; his physical marks number thirty-two."
"I have come here for this very reason, wishing to see the meaning of Puji.
'Welcome; I am delighted by your arrival, but at present I am resting in tranquil sleep.
Wait but a moment until I awaken, and you shall behold one as wondrous as the full moon.'"
Thereupon, Ārāḍa was struck with astonishment and replied to the king in verse:
“From incalculable eons past, You have accumulated merit through diligent practice;
Since your awakening has been so long ago, How could you ever sleep again?”
Throughout successive lifetimes you practiced giving, Compassionately pitying all who were in distress;
Having no attachment to what you possessed, How could you now sleep in peace?
You observed the pure precepts with reverence, Protecting the Dharma without transgression.
Desiring to compassionately rescue all beings, how could one sleep again?
Always patient, gentle, and harmonious, with no resentment in the heart;
holding the mind as firm as the earth, how could one sleep again?
With diligence like the waxing moon, never slackening before one's eyes;
traveling to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, how could one ever again succumb to sleep?
With single-mindedness always in meditative contemplation, never allowing for distracted thoughts.
With the mind as steady as a great mountain, how could one sleep again?
With wisdom that reaches all things, with holy brilliance surpassing the light of the sun, there is nothing it does not illuminate; how could one sleep again?
Constantly upholding the four immeasurable minds, practicing kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity;
like Brahmā, being free from negligence—how could one indulge in sleep again?
Following and cultivating the practice of the four debts of gratitude, practicing generosity and benevolence;
Benefiting others is equal to benefiting oneself; how can one then indulge in sleep?

Practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the strengths, the limbs of awakening, and the eightfold path—how can one then indulge in sleep?
Constantly practicing skillful means, he transforms beings according to the times;
going and returning, he delivers all—how could he ever again indulge in sleep?
His mind is ever tranquil, his concentration steadfast and free from negligence.
Having entered this profound samādhi, how could one sleep again?
Contemplating the beginning and end of self and others, and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions;
realizing that all are fundamentally non-existent, how could one sleep again?
Constantly practicing the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
with neither attachment to existence nor non-existence, how could one still indulge in sleep?
With great compassion and boundless pity, you navigate the triple world in the ship of the Dharma.
Having delivered all from birth and death, how could one sleep again?
With a virtue as vast as space, he humbles himself for the sake of the multitudes;
through these conditions, he transforms beings via the three vehicles—how could he sleep again?
The void may yet be measured, and one might know how many drops there are in the ocean;
all grasses and trees could be counted—how then can you sleep again?
I pray that Your Majesty will listen to my words: the virtue of your son is beyond all comparison.
His wisdom exceeds the number of all motes of dust; how could he sleep again?
Having descended his spirit into his mother’s womb, those whom he delivers are immeasurable;
this is not something attained by those of minor virtue—how could he sleep again?

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva arose from his sleep; Mahāprajāpatī wrapped him in a large white cotton cloth, carried him to the king’s presence, and the king presented the ascetic with one bag each of gold and silver, which the ascetic did not accept.
"Having donned the cotton robe, he examined the Prince and beheld the thirty-two marks: his body was golden in color; he had a fleshly protuberance upon the crown of his head;

his hair was deep blue-black; between his eyebrows was a tuft of white hair; from his neck issued a radiance like sunlight; the lashes of his eyes were deep blue; both upper and lower eyelids blinked simultaneously; he had forty teeth; his teeth were white, even, and level; his jawbones were square and broad; his tongue was long, measuring seven spans; his chest was full like that of a lion; his body was perfectly proportioned; his arms were long with elongated fingers; the heels of his feet were full, flat, and level; his hands and feet were webbed like a net; on his palms and soles were wheels with a thousand spokes; his male organ was concealed within a sheath; his calves were like those of a deer; his bones were linked like hooks; his body hair curled to the right; from each pore grew a single hair; his skin and hair were fine and soft, repelling dust and water; and upon his breast was the *svastika* symbol."
Upon seeing this, Āyu increased his sighs of lamentation; tears flowed as he was overcome with grief and unable to speak.
The King and Mahāprajāpatī, their hearts filled with trepidation, prostrated themselves and asked:
"Is there some inauspicious omen?"
"I pray you, tell me its meaning.
He raised his hand and replied,
"Auspiciousness without anything unfavorable."
"I venture to congratulate Your Majesty on the birth of this divine person!
That the heavens and earth shook so violently last night was precisely for this reason.

According to my method of physiognomy, it is said that when a king fathers a son who possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) while in his kingdom; he will naturally possess the seven treasures and a thousand sons, ruling over the four continents with the True Dharma."
"If I had abandoned my kingdom to leave the household life, I would have become a self-enlightened Buddha (*svayaṃbuddha*) to deliver sentient beings.

It grieves me that my years are already late and I am about to pass into the next world, such that I shall not behold the arising of a Buddha nor hear his sutras; for this reason, I lament for myself."
The king, deeply aware of his skill in physiognomy, built for him a palace with three seasonal halls, each in a separate location:
an autumn hall for the cool season, a cooling hall for the summer heat, and a warm hall for the cold and snow.

He selected five hundred female musicians, choosing those who were beautiful, neither too fat nor too thin, neither too tall nor too short, and neither too fair nor too dark; they were all exceptionally talented, each proficient in several arts, and adorned their bodies with necklaces of white pearls and famous jewels. A hundred women at a time took turns by rotation to guard and attend before his hall.

Between rows of trees bearing sweet fruits were bathing pools, within which bloomed extraordinary flowers and gathered birds of many hundreds of thousands of species, resplendent and magnificent, seeking to delight the Prince so as to prevent him from pursuing the Way;
the palace walls were solid and secure, and the sound of the gates opening and closing could be heard for forty *li*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Bodhisattva was born, the Great and Wondrous Devas announced to the Śuddhāvāsa deities:

‘The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has accumulated merit and virtue for countless billions of years, purifying his site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Through generosity and extensive learning, his observance of the precepts is pure and transparent; he diligently cultivates right practice, possessing great kindness and great compassion, thereby joyfully protecting all sentient beings and establishing them in great peace.’”

"The Bodhisattva’s diligence is firm and unyielding; he has donned the great armor of his solemn vow and planted the roots of great virtue under past Buddhas. His physical form is adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings, and his actions are peaceful and harmonious, surpassing all others.

His mind is clear and bright, governing itself without defilement; by means of these pure practices, he establishes the great banner of the infinite Dharma of Great Wisdom, naturally subduing all worldly powers.

As a great guide of the three thousandfold world, he is served by devas and humans; he establishes great shrines and leads others without obstruction. Valuing only the Way and its Virtue, he cuts off the source of birth and death, exalting and manifesting the Mahāyāna."

"Having been born at a most opportune time into the royal household, by this cause sentient beings are graced with his vast and noble resolve. You who have not yet awakened should go to him to prostrate, praise his meritorious virtues, and serve him with offerings."

For the sake of other devas and humans who do not understand the Dharma—those who are arrogant and conceited, failing to recognize the Ultimate Truth—he reveals the Great Way and its infinite, supreme deeds. Many bodhisattvas of majestic and holy transcendence all come to make offerings;

by hearing and seeing this, the king’s land and meritorious achievements are increased. Beholding his birth and the towering sublimity of his sacred wisdom, all who contemplate the True Reality resolve their minds [upon enlightenment]. As they go there and return, their deliverance is boundless.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"At the time of his birth, his virtue was like the ocean; The Great and Wondrous One has proclaimed this.
Hard to hear in countless kalpas, I have gone to serve the Honored One among Sages."
The Śuddhāvāsa devas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, their bodies adorned with brilliant pearls,
all proceeding with perfect dignity, threw themselves down to take refuge in the Most Honored One.
Protected by the devas throughout the long night, they abide in the pure gateway of manifold virtues.
Adorned with precious necklaces, his complexion is as beautiful as the full moon.
His radiance cannot be surpassed by the sages; his fame extends even a single step beyond.
None dare to transcend the triple world; within the triple world, none can withstand him.
The body emanates pure light, and speech is harmonious and beyond contradiction;
with deep consciousness one cultivates wholesome deeds, such that neither devas nor humans can surpass them.
Surpassing the merit of various sublime incenses, they are revered and supported with respect.
"I have never before seen a prince who serves the God among Gods.
Ārāḍa then addressed the King: "The physiognomist wishes to see him;
his deportment and virtue are divine and holy. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with supreme joy.
The gatekeeper announced the King’s arrival, and the Honored One among Men listened;
holding flowers with joyful hands, the Spirit entered the dwelling of the Sage.
As the King was ushered in, he immediately rose and joined his ten fingers in reverence.
"A bed with legs of purple-gold treasure— I invite you, O Benevolent One, to sit upon this couch.
He sat down and saw through all four directions; The King asked the reason for his coming.
"The son born possesses the virtues of the body; Because his conduct is true, he has come to see me."
The Sage’s brilliance and marks of excellence are complete, yet one knows not where he is headed;
for this reason, I troubled his bed and seat, merely to show him these majestic marks.
This multitude has come surrounding him, as the household joyfully brings forth the Crown Prince.
Receiving the celestial manifestation with reverence, he stepped out the gate and marveled at what he had never known before.
Seeing the Wondrous and Victorious Guide, whose majestic holiness was like purple-gold,
he immediately rose to behold his countenance and prostrated himself before the stainless radiance.
Throughout his entire life he was seen with joy; his majestic virtue was such that none could see the crown of his head.
With white hair, he stood amidst the heavens; having attained Buddhahood, he subdued the hosts of Māra.
Praising the virtues of the Ultimate Truth, he eliminated all worldly afflictions.
The Lion of Jewels appears; one should sever the defilements of birth and death.
The three poisons of the three periods of time blaze fiercely, arising from the filth of signs;
The rain of Dharma heals the trichiliocosm, and the nectar extinguishes worldly toil.
The Lamp of Compassion beholds the merit of his pity; his Brahma-voice is soft and supple.
He proclaims throughout the trichiliocosm, his mouth uttering the resonance of the Great Dharma.
He destroys the heterodox paths of outside teachings and the bonds of all manner of sins.
Through causes and conditions, one hears not of emptiness; the Dharma-hero transforms minor details.
Extinguishing the smoke of the great fire of delusion, he purifies the teachings of the Great Sage for the multitude;
seeing the world with the light of wisdom, he extinguishes the dark ignorance of the masses.
Devas and humans obtain great benefit, and behold the pure and true reality;
the celestial canopy of emptiness arises upon the divine path, and the Jewel among Men remains free from contention.
In Kapilavastu, devas rain down flowers, which they offer in worship and circumambulate to the right.
Praising the Buddha and praising the land, he ascended into the void and returned to heaven.
*The Puyao Jing*, Scroll Two;
*The Puyao Jing*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Entering the Temples of Devas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"At the very moment the Bodhisattva was born, twenty thousand wives of nobles, brahmins, and elders gave birth; their parents were filled with joy, and they all attended upon the Bodhisattva to serve him at his side."
"At that time, King Śuddhodana provided twenty thousand court ladies for the Bodhisattva to serve as attendants;
twenty thousand court ladies from his various kinsmen were presented to the Bodhisattva; and the ministers and officials likewise offered twenty thousand court ladies to the Bodhisattva.
The noble Śākyas all assembled together and came to the king’s presence, where they addressed him, saying:"
"Your Majesty should know that you ought to lead the Crown Prince to the celestial shrine.
The King agreed.

He then issued orders throughout the city to sweep the thoroughfares, the four main avenues, the various roads, and all the winding alleys, ensuring there was nothing impure or inauspicious—no shards, stones, ditches, pits, or unclean places.
Let there be no ill sounds from those who are sick, blind, or deaf; scatter flowers, burn incense, and select auspicious melodies. Hang banners and silk canopies, and adorn the gates.
After the King has returned to the inner palace, he shall inform Mahāprajāpatī that they will escort the Prince to the celestial shrine for protection.
As the Prince sat upon his seat, he immediately smiled, his countenance radiant with joy, and proclaimed these words:
"My body is at peace and well; for what reason do you wish to lead me to the celestial shrine?"
The Prince bathed and, laughing heartily once more, spoke this verse:

"Upon my first birth, I moved the three thousandfold world; Śakra, Brahmā, the Asuras, and the gods, The Sun, the Moon, and the Heavenly Kings, Came to prostrate themselves before me with their heads at my feet."
Is there any deity superior to this one who will lead me to his abode?
A transcendent god among gods, beyond all comparison, yet he manifests here in accordance with worldly custom;
appearing as an auspicious omen, he brings joy to humanity.
"Various kinds of offerings surpass even those of the holy gods and the God among Gods.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the elder and brahmin Śrīkara, together with the honored householders of various districts, counties, and towns; his wife, children, attendants, ministers, and vassal kings; the gatekeepers, officials, and kinsmen and acquaintances; scattering flowers and burning incense; and accompanied by elephants, horses, chariots, and the king’s courtiers, went together with the prince to enter the celestial shrine."

Just as he entered the celestial shrine, he took his stand above it; the various celestial images were devoid of thought or perception. The deities of the sun and moon, the Heavenly King Śikhin, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings each abandoned their original positions and descended immediately, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
A multitude of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans remained silent for a moment, then broke into loud cries of praise, exclaiming that such a thing had never been seen before;

they leaped for joy. Heaven and earth shook violently, and the heavens rained down myriad flowers; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. The celestial images manifested their true forms and, having paid homage at the Bodhisattva’s feet, stood before him, whereupon they spoke in verse:
"Comparing Mount Sumeru to a mustard seed, or surpassing the transformations of the Heavenly Dragon Kings—
is one paying homage to the sun and moon by bowing before a firefly?
How could one of wisdom and virtue pay such reverence?"
The three thousandfold world-system takes refuge;
a mustard seed is compared to Mount Sumeru, and a cow’s footprint to the great ocean. The Most Honored One is likened to the sun and moon.
If one can pay homage to this Honored One, the merit shall be beyond measure.
"May each and every one obtain peace and security, with abundant virtue beyond measure.
When the Bodhisattva entered the celestial shrine, thirty-two thousand devaputras, beholding his manifest majestic virtue, all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment;
for this reason, he was led by them as he proceeded into the celestial shrine.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Jyotiṣka; his father, surrounded by five hundred attendants, held a parasol made of the seven precious gems and offered it to King Śuddhodana, saying these words:
"This is to be offered to the Crown Prince."
The King accepted this immediately and summoned five hundred Śākyas. Five hundred necklaces were provided for their hands, feet, heads, and ears; they all wore these necklaces upon their arms.
At that moment, Puṣya arrived at the King’s residence and said to him, “You should have the Prince bathe and wash himself, and then adorn him with these necklaces to present him as an offering.”
The king replied to him, saying,
"I am making a necklace for the crown prince as well.
Once the prince has worn it for seventy-seven days, I shall then fulfill my obligation."

When that night had passed, on the first day of the month, there was a pleasure garden named Vimalaśuddha. The Bodhisattva went out to view it; Mahāprajāpatī took him in her arms and brought him out. Eighty thousand court ladies came to welcome the Bodhisattva and prostrated themselves in salutation.

Ten thousand Śākyas came forth to welcome the Bodhisattva, and five thousand brahmins likewise came to welcome him; those among the Śākya clan who had fashioned various necklaces to offer to the Bodhisattva caused him to put them on.
As soon as he put it on his body, it became instantly dark and dim; the majestic radiance of the Bodhisattva caused it to lose all luster, appearing like a mass of ink beside fine purple gold.
There was an elder named Vigatamala who stood before the Bodhisattva, wearing a most excellent and exquisite robe.
At that time, King Śuddhodana and the various members of the Śākya clan praised him with these verses:
“Even if the three thousandfold world system were adorned And covered everywhere with pure jewels,
And all were made of purple-gold, They would not equal this radiance.”
Though there be gold refined by purple fire, it is not equal to the luster of a single hair;
its brilliance eclipses all other lights, appearing like ink in the presence of the Sage.
Adorned with the majesty of the Way and its Virtue, even necklaces of jewels suddenly lose their splendor.
The radiance of the sun, moon, and great jewels, and even that of Śakra and Brahmā, cannot equal it.
Adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, how could the finest of gems surpass him?
No adornment is like the Buddha’s; all other ornaments fall short when compared to his transcendence.
"The Way is solemn, pure, peaceful, and luminous; it is born from a noble lineage of solemnity.
It radiates light so that all rejoice, and its canopy extends over the clan. Chapter Seven:
The Appearance of Writing The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance), Chapter Seven: The Appearance of Writing. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Prince was seven years of age. He manifested countless hundreds of thousands of auspicious signs. Ten thousand youths, ten thousand maidens, and ten thousand carriages carrying various kinds of delicacies and replete with all manner of jewels arrived at the kingdom of Kāśī and halted at the four crossroads. At the heads of every street and alley, they performed various musical entertainments;

among the trees, they adorned pavilions, galleries, eaves, windows, and doors, where the court ladies, decorated with ornate necklaces and jewelry, stood upon them scattering flowers and burning incense.
Eight thousand court ladies purified the roads to welcome the Bodhisattva."

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, each with their distinct forms, were in the void; scattering flowers, burning incense, and hanging down jeweled beads and silken banners, the entire assembly of Śākyas escorted King Śuddhodana from before and behind as they went together to welcome the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva, riding a sheep-drawn carriage, was about to go to the master of writing; having just entered the scriptorium wishing to see his teacher—the teacher’s name was Xuanyou—he beheld the majesty and radiant splendor of the Bodhisattva's divine power and, unable to endure it, immediately recoiled and fell to the ground.

In the Tuṣita Heaven, there was a devaputra named Viśuddha. He immediately stepped forward, took [the Bodhisattva] by the hand, and helped him rise from the ground. Placing him upon a seat before the great assembly, he spoke these verses:
“Born into the Śākya clan in the present world, While still a layman, you mastered the arts;
In calculation, writing, and scriptural commentaries, You have already reached perfection through countless kalpas.”
He appears for the sake of saving sentient beings, manifesting as a teacher who demonstrates entry through extensive learning;
he delivers countless youths, bestowing upon the multitude the entry into the nectar of immortality.
He transcends the world by understanding the Four Noble Truths and fully comprehending the causes and conditions of karmic retribution.
Whatever comes into being must inevitably perish; how much more so this present study hall?
He who is most enlightened regarding the three periods of time, the foremost honored one among devas and humans—through countless kalpas, he has studied here in various transformed study halls.
“The minds of sentient beings are full of discursive thoughts, while the True Sage alone knows the fundamental source;
this form is itself thoughtless, yet it manifests or transforms into forms of desire.

At that time, the Bodhisattva was dwelling together with the youths of the Śākya clan; the Bodhisattva held in his hand a golden pen and wrote in *li* script upon sandalwood, forming characters composed of various precious jewels and bright pearls, which an attendant brought to him.
He asked his teacher and chose a friend, saying:
"Master, what text are you teaching me now?
His teacher replied:
"It is merely that we teach one another using the Brahmī-Kharoṣṭhī script;
there are no other different scripts. The Bodhisattva replied, "There are sixty-four different scripts, yet now the Master possesses only two kinds of writing."
The Master asked:
"What are the names of those sixty-four scripts?
The Prince replied:
1. The *Brahmī* script;
2. The *Kharoṣṭhī* script;
3. The *Puṣkarasāri* script.
4. The Aṅka script; 5. The Maṅka script;
6. The Aṅgu script.
7. *Da Qin Shu* (Book of the Great Qin);
8. *Hu Zhong Shu* (Book on Protecting the Multitude);
9. *Qu Shu* (Book on Taking).
10. *Bāṣkalaśākhā*, 11. *Jaiminīyaśākhā*, 12.
*Śākalakaśākhā*, 13. *Taittirīyaśākhā*.
14. "Book on the Yi Di (Barbarians)";
15. "Book on Bestowal and Giving";
16. "Book on Kangju."
17. The *Uttara-lipi* (Supreme Script), 18.
The *Dhāra-lipi* (Dhāra Script), 19.
The *Kharoṣṭhī-lipi* (Kharoṣṭhī Script).
20. *Qin Shu* (Book of Qin);
21. *Hunnu Shu* (Book of the Xiongnu);
22. *Zhongjianzi Shu* (Book of Intermediate Characters).
23. The Vṛddha script; 24. The Puṣpaphala script;
25. The Devanāgarī script; 26. The Nāga script and the Yakṣa script.
27. The Gandharva script; 28. The Kinnara script; 29. The Mahoraga script; 30. The Asura script.
31. Kāruṇya Script; 32. Mṛgacakra Script; 33. Vākkuśala Script.
34. *Tianfu shu* (Book of Heavenly Belly);
35. *Feng shu* (Book of Wind);
36. *Jiangfu shu* (Book of Subjugation).
37. *Beifang Tianxia Shu* (Book on the Northern World) 38.
*Junaniti Tianxia Shu* (Book on the Junaniti World) 39.
*Dongfang Tianxia Shu* (Book on the Eastern World)
40. *Jushu* (Selected Letters), 41.
*Xiaoshu* (Letters to Subordinates), 42.
*Yaoshu* (Essential Letters)
43. *Dṛḍhalipi* (The Firm Script);
44. *Tālalipi* (The Palm Script);
45. *Divyalipi* (The Heavenly Script).
46. "Letter on Weariness and Exertion";
47. "Letter on Non-Participation"; 48.
"Letter on the Turning of Numbers"
49. *The Book on Turning the Eye*;
50. *The Book on Closing the Sentence*;
51. *The Book on the Petition*.
52. *The Letter on the Successive Approaches*; 53. *The Letter on Even the Writing*; 54.
*The Letter on Delivering One’s Kin*;
55. *The Letter on the Central Administration*.
56. *Sīmamocana-pustaka* (The Book on the Complete Extinction of Sounds) 57.
*Vidyut-loka-pustaka* (The Book on the World of Lightning) 58.
*Tvarita-pustaka* (The Book on the Swift Runner)
59. *The Book on the Ground of Excellent Tranquility*;
60. *The Book on Contemplating Emptiness*;
61. *The Book on All Medicines*.
62. *Susaṃvāha-lipi*, 63. *Saṃgraha-lipi*, 64.
*Sarvasvarā-lipi*. The Prince said to his teacher:
"Of these sixty-four scripts, which one do you wish to teach me?"
At that time, the teacher and his chosen friend were filled with joy and delight; casting aside their pride, they spoke these verses:
"The one who is difficult to approach, the Truly Pure Honored One, Arising in this world with great compassion;
Having mastered all the scriptures, He now manifests entry into the teachings of writing."
They all proclaim the names of various scriptures, yet I do not know their origins or conclusions;
they have mastered all these many books, and thus they again demonstrate how to enter into study.
I dare not look upon their crowns, for I see only people prostrating before them.
How could one cause the Great Sage to proclaim all the scriptures and various numerical categories?
He is the God among Gods, surpassing all gods; he is the most supreme among all deities;
he is the Most Honored One, without equal, for whom there can be no analogy in this world.
"By virtue of this majestic spiritual power, he purifies [the world] through skillful means;
who can equal his clarity and purity? He delivers all those in the worlds.

At that time, ten thousand youths, who were studying together with the Bodhisattva under their teacher, beheld the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue and the establishment of his great sagely wisdom. As he analyzed and explained the written characters, they proclaimed:
"Regarding the word 'non-existence' (asat):
it proclaims the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Regarding the word 'desire' (kāma):"
It produces sounds that eliminate lust, anger, and delusion,
as well as all cravings. "The word 'thorough' (jiu) produces sounds that are fundamentally and ultimately true and pure."
"The word 'his' refers to the sound of practicing the Way for incalculable kalpas.
The word 'not' refers to— "
The sound that emerges is one that does not follow the crowd and is detached from name-and-form.
As for the word "disorder," it is the sound that emerges from eliminating the turbid source of the abyss of birth and death.
"The word 'giving' issues forth the pure and correct sounds of generosity, ethical discipline,
and wisdom. The word 'bondage'..."
"Release from the prisons of punishment; examine and rectify conduct.
As for the word "burning," it issues forth the sound of incinerating the dust and toil of afflictions and desire.
"His words 'faith' produce the sounds of faith, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.
His words 'excellence'..."
It emits the sound of the transcendent, holy, and unsurpassed path.
As for the word "suchness" (tathatā):
it issues from the indestructible voice of the Tathāgata.
“‘That which is called “quiescence” (śānta) refers to the sound of the dharma that is tranquil and serene when emerging from contemplation.
‘That which is called “submergence” (nimagna) refers to— ”’
"It produces sounds that eliminate anger and weary of strife and litigation.
"As for those words: they produce sounds concerning the retribution of sins and merits received according to one's conduct."
"The term 'wise one' refers to the indestructible sound that gives rise to all wisdom.
The term 'Māra' refers to— "
The sound "Extinguish" issues forth the subduing of the power of Māra and his retinue.
The word "Harm" issues forth the sound of abandoning arrogance and false views.
"His speech regarding 'passing away' issues from the True Dharma as a sound free from confusion.
His speech regarding 'cessation'..."
They utter the sound of worldly powers and fearlessness.
As for the word "born," it utters the sound of transcending all sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"The meaning of his words is:
'His resolve is firm and resolute, and his voice walks alone through the three realms.
The meaning of his words regarding the Dharma is:"
"By means of the sounds of equal dharma, they govern, rescue, and circulate through the cycles of coming and going.
"As for the word 'praise' (stuti),
it produces all sounds that transform beings according to their respective aspirations."
"The word 'difficult' (duskarāḥ) signifies the utterance that eliminates the karmic retribution of the eight difficult conditions.
The word 'exhausted' (kṣayāḥ) signifies— "
"It issues from the sound of total extinction and non-arising.
"As for the word 'place' (sthāna):
it issues from the sound that eliminates the inversion of place."
"Regarding the word 'wisdom' (prajñā):
it issues forth the voice of holy wisdom that is free from all obstructions.
"Regarding the word 'this' (satya):"
"It issues forth the sounds of good and evil, calamity and fortune.
"The word 'existence' (bhava) issues forth the sounds of all that is practiced within the three realms of existence (trai-dhātuka)."
"The term 'abandoning' refers to abandoning all destinations, the notion of self,
and deceitful speech. The term 'self' refers to— "
"It issues forth the sounds of the wholesome and unwholesome karmas one has produced.
As for the word 'I,' it issues forth the sound of extinguishing the defilements of the body and craving."
"The term 'defilement' refers to the emergence of various forms of envy and so forth;
it is the sound of equality proclaimed by both virtuous and non-virtuous friends.
"The term 'number' refers to..."
It issues forth the sound of the discipline that transcends all reckonings and is free from ignorance.
As for the term "abode," it issues forth the sound of the limitlessness of abiding and non-abiding.
"The word 'if' refers to crossing over various perceptions,
the multitude of distractions, heedlessness, and the sound of silent aspiration.
"The word 'fruit' refers to:"
"The voice that realizes all fruits of fruition is the voice of non-abiding.
"The word 'removal' refers to the voice of emerging from greed for oneself and removing the five hindrances."
"The term 'erroneous' issues forth the sound that eliminates erroneous afflictions and removes distress.
The term 'wisdom'..."
He uttered the sound of wisdom born of generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning, a sound free from conceptual construction.

At that time, for the sake of the young boys, the Bodhisattva analyzed each letter according to its origin and its end, expounding such sounds of this Dharma-gate while gradually instructing and transforming them within the schoolhouse.
Thirty-two thousand boys were inspired to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; therefore, the Bodhisattva went to the schoolhouse to demonstrate following a teacher.

Chapter Eight: Sitting Beneath a Tree and Observing Plowing from the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance). At that time, the Prince had grown to adulthood. He requested permission from his father, the King, and together with his ministers, he traveled to a village.
There he observed those who were plowing; he saw that as the earth was freshly turned, insects emerged from the soil, and crows and birds immediately pecked at them.
The Bodhisattva, knowing this, asked again, questioning the plowman:
"What is this arrangement?
He replied:
"The King collects taxes from those who sow grain.

The Bodhisattva sighed in lamentation: "If even a single man causes the people such distress and turmoil—fearing the calamities of official flogging, caning, and punishment—their hearts are filled with dread and they are restless and uneasy. Human life is exceedingly short, yet its anxieties are immeasurably long. As the days and months pass by, one may not even wait for the next breath before departing for the afterlife;
from the beginning to the end of existence as a deva or human, the sufferings and afflictions of the three evil realms are beyond description."
The cycle of birth and death within the five destinies revolves without end; submerged therein, one remains unaware, and its poisonous pain is beyond comparison.
Only by entering the mountains to achieve the Way can one deliver others from the perilous afflictions of arising and ceasing throughout the ten directions and the three realms.

Having finished observing the plowman, he entered again for further contemplation. At that time, the Bodhisattva wandered alone without a companion, walking to and fro upon that ground. Seeing the shade of a Jambu tree, which was beautiful and lush, he sat beneath its cool shade, single-mindedly practicing dhyāna and samādhi with right concentration, regarding this as the foremost.

At that time, there were five hundred heterodox seers flying through the air from south to north; wishing to pass over the grove of trees, they were unable to do so and came to a halt, unable to proceed.

Seeing the Bodhisattva from afar, they together praised and extolled the meritorious achievements of his body; his virtue was so lofty and majestic that it was like Mount Sumeru or a great diamond mountain, and like a wondrous, bright pearl, securely established and immovable.
"Is he King Yama, a ghost, or a gandharva? they wondered.
"Now he sits beneath the tree with a mind like empty space; this must be his meditative sitting. What auspiciousness is there in this?
Might it cause us to lose our supernormal powers?
As they observed him, they perceived his great compassion, which was exceedingly radiant, brilliant, and dazzling; then they thought to themselves:
"Is this the deity Vaiśravaṇa, the Great Wealthy One; or is it a celestial being, the Lord of Gods Śakra; or the brilliance of the sun and moon; or a Wheel-Turning Sage King?"
Then the Ākāśadevatā spoke in verse:
“If he is the King of the Gods who excels in form, If he is the Deva Free from Enmity,
If he is the Immeasurable Vajra— This Honored One is the Great Man.”
Surpassing all the celestial deities, his radiance is like the full moon;
supreme in the world, he is beyond measure.
His virtue is immeasurable, serving as a refuge for devas and gandharvas.
His meritorious deeds shine with brilliant light, increasing his practice for billions of years.
Constantly returning to his divine power, he shall be the thousand-eyed one of this world;
the Heavenly King who protects the four quarters, the most honored among the Asuras and Brahmās.
"Yet he who upholds all auspiciousness is capable of this;
able to sit before him in such a manner, one beholds him as peerless.
At that time, having heard the hymn of praise uttered by the deva in the sky, the five hundred rishis immediately descended and took their places upon the ground.
Beholding the Bodhisattva’s divine mind settled in meditative concentration—his body unmoving and his mind free from deviant thoughts—he was filled with great joy.

He observed that the Bodhisattva’s merit was towering and immeasurable, its virtue so lofty and remote as to be beyond analogy; such a venerable one among gods and men had never before been seen or heard of, and it was only through the remaining blessings of his past lives that he beheld him now.
Filled with joy and celebration, he spoke these verses:
“The world is ablaze with the fires of worldly toil; One who attains the Way extinguishes all afflictions.
Abiding in the world like Mount Sumeru, Such a person is able to accomplish the Dharma.”
Having attained victory, he removes all forms; his noble conduct is as difficult to fathom as the ocean.
Having attained the Way, he is dyed with wisdom, such that there is none who does not receive his deliverance.
He has untied the fetters of the body and thereby reached the perfection of the Dharma.
"I shall deliver them all, so that they no longer see the realm of Māra.
At that time, the king’s ministers and the great multitude each ran about, seeking to know where the Prince was now.
From afar he saw the ministers pursuing him from behind; he then beheld [the Bodhisattva] beneath a Jambu tree, meditating with a concentrated mind.

At that time, the sun shone such that the tree bent over to cover the Bodhisattva’s body; all other trees likewise bowed toward the Jambu tree, prostrating themselves before the Bodhisattva without moving.
He went quickly to inform the king:
"The light and marks of that tree cannot be obscured; when the sun shines upon it, the tree inclines to shield the Prince’s body so as to protect those marks.
When the king heard this, he went to the tree and immediately beheld the Bodhisattva’s majestic power and auspiciousness, which were sublime and immeasurable. At that time, he spoke a verse:
“Like a fire atop a mountain peak, like the moon among the stars;
seeing him meditating beneath the tree, his majestic brilliance shines everywhere.”
Now once again I bow my head, paying homage at the feet of the Teacher;
at the time of his initial birth, his body sat in meditative concentration by itself.
The majestic spiritual radiance of his body was clear and penetrating, illuminating everywhere.
"Whoever beholds me cannot fail to rejoice; by this, they shall attain deliverance.
Thereupon, the Prince addressed the King:
"I had just been out for a short while on a stroll nearby; why have you come to pursue me?"
The king asked,
"For what reason do you act in this way?
He replied:

"The ministers desire to eliminate all dust and delusive thoughts; with luminous purity, they grasp the marks and signs, sitting in dhyāna-samādhi without wavering, subduing all māras and removing all obscurations."
The King said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"The auspicious omens manifested at his birth were not in vain; they have all now been fulfilled, and the ten directions have received deliverance.
Chapter Nine: The King Seeks a Consort for the Prince. The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance), Chapter Nine: The King Seeks a Consort for the Prince. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with his prince and the various members of the Śākya clan, resided there."
Then the Mallas, the Śākyas, and the elders addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:

"If Your Majesty would wish to know: these brahmins have not yet attained the ultimate goal; only if the Prince abandons his kingdom and renounces kingship to become a Tathāgata will they attain the ultimate goal.
Should he not go forth, he will become a Wheel-Turning King who governs by the True Dharma, and shall be known as a Dharma King."
Furthermore, there are seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure;

second, the deep-blue horse; third, the white elephant; fourth, the bright moon pearl; fifth, the jade-like queen; sixth, the minister in charge of the treasury; and seventh, the minister in charge of the military.
He also has a thousand sons who are handsome and excellent, fierce, brave, and extraordinary—each man capable of facing a thousand others and subduing enemies.
"If he becomes a Buddha, the lineage of the noble kings will be severed, and there will remain only scattered kings each bearing their own titles.
King Śuddhodana said,
"Let us observe for now which jade-like maiden is most suitable to be the Prince's consort."
The five hundred Śākyas each declared:
"I shall seek one to be the consort for the Crown Prince.
Then King Śuddhodana said to the Śākyas:
"Now the Prince's consort is most difficult to find; we do not know which maiden might suit his heart.
They all gathered together to deliberate on this matter and said to the Prince, "Now you must reflect upon it."
After seven days had passed, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"I have no craving for desire; it is not fitting that I remain at home. Having abandoned Tuṣita and come here to this human realm, my heart has no longing for anything. I shall enter the samādhi of tranquility and test myself through skillful means, diligently approaching the site of enlightenment to encourage and assist all with boundless compassion."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The royal lineage arises and pays homage; From fire, lotus flowers grow.
The Bodhisattva nurtures great power, Transforming billions with nectar for eons.”
Not abandoning the flavor of guiding others, their fearless virtue is truly perfected;
that which my heart yearns for and delights in is a resolve free from laxity and pure.
Though Bodhisattvas originally dwell in the realm of desire, they skillfully transform so that all perceive them as wives.
"Finding no delight in sensual desires, he abandons harm and trains in meritorious deeds.

At that time, the Bodhisattva had a master craftsman fashion a magnificent golden image upon which to inscribe these words: "If a woman’s virtue, conduct, physical form, and facial features were such as this, only then would I accept her."
I do not employ commoners; only one who accords with what I have described is worthy of marriage!

Her complexion and features shall be like purple-polished gold; her inner and outer selves shall correspond, and her body and speech shall not be at variance. Her mind shall be pure as space, serene and radiant; she shall not be dissolute, but shall speak sparingly yet with frequent accuracy. With a compassionate heart free from malice, she shall revere the Way and its principles;

she shall practice giving and uphold the precepts as a śramaṇa or brahmin, seeking this for my sake without envy or satiety. Her disposition shall be benevolent and virtuous, never missing the proper occasion; she shall be upright and without flattery, devotedly honoring her husband without harboring other thoughts, and shall always remain free from licentiousness.
She does not conceive in vain nor fail to carry her child to term; she renounces high status to serve her husband as a servant;

she does not indulge in wine, does not crave flavors, does not lust after sounds, and is not ignorant or deluded; she eradicates the root of ignorance and knows that dharmas abide in the ultimate truth;
she does not act rashly, possesses no heterodox arts, and always maintains a sense of shame and modesty.
He does not engage in harsh speech nor cast curses, but constantly practices and upholds the Dharma;
his body, speech, and mind are pure, and his words correspond to his deeds. His heart is like that of a lowly servant, cultivating much loving-kindness and compassion;

he does not boast of his own status, nor is he foolish or dull-witted. Free from resentment and anger, he remains composed even among the masses and is never deluded. All his actions are virtuous, and he honors his friends and kin as if they were the World-Honored One himself.
"One who regards her as herself, whose reputation spreads far and wide, who cultivates all virtues universally,
and who always serves with reverence and diligence—
only such a wife may be acceptable! At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard the Bodhisattva’s words, addressed the ancient Brahmin:
He entered the city of Kāśī and went from house to house, examining which virtuous young women possessed such qualities;
did any among the gentlemen, elders, artisans, or commoners have such corresponding merits?
"If it is possible for the Crown Prince, then he may indeed be welcomed. Why is this?
For the Crown Prince does not value noble lineage; he delights only in virtue."
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
“Whether one be of the noble Brahmin caste, A craftsman, or a commoner;
If they possess such virtues, Then they may be taken as a bride!”
"He does not take pleasure in noble lineage; the Prince finds wonder in the sublime.
Possessing the merit of supreme sincerity, his heart thus delights in such things.

At that time, having heard these verses of instruction, the brahmin traveled throughout every household in Kapilavastu, performing divinations for them. Upon entering a certain house, he beheld a jade-like maiden, exceptionally beautiful like a celestial nymph. Her countenance was foremost in purity, as immaculate as a lotus; neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark, neither stout nor thin, she possessed the perfect female form, resembling a *strī-ratna* (a precious jewel of a woman).
At that time, the daughter paid homage to the ancient brahmin and asked him,
"Brahmin, what do you seek?
The brahmin replied:

"When King Śuddhodana gives birth to a true prince, peerless in his upright and handsome appearance with the thirty-two marks, possessing merit and majestic spiritual power, and who can write verses with his own hand—only when such a youth, whose physical form and feminine grace are foremost among gods and men, is born, shall he take her as his bride!"
Then that woman spoke this verse:
“The verses proclaimed by the brahmin reveal the forms perceived by his mind;
if the brahmin wishes to know them, I possess all such qualities.”
"She should become my husband; his upright beauty is peerless.
Report this matter to the Prince: do not let him meet with one so unworthy.
When the brahmin heard this, he returned to the king's presence and reported it thus:
"Your Majesty, please consider this; it would not be fitting for her to become the Crown Prince's consort.
He asked, "Whose daughter is she?"
The brahmin replied,
"He was born into the Śākya clan of the Daṇḍapāṇi lineage.
The king thought to himself:
"The Prince’s appearance far surpasses that of the world; yet his facial complexion is so pure and serene that it may not please everyone's taste. Therefore, let him choose for himself.

They proceeded to the Hall of No Sorrow and gathered all the women there, instructing the Prince to examine them personally and for the Bodhisattva to look with favor toward whichever he found pleasing.

At that time, King Śuddhodana constructed a magnificent lecture hall adorned with various rare jewels and precious treasures; he then summoned all the most excellent and beautiful women of Rājagṛha to assemble in that hall.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva went to the lecture hall and sat upon the seat of benevolence and wisdom.
The king then dispatched a messenger:"
"Whosoever among the ladies whom the Bodhisattva gazes upon with a wondrous delight, let her come and inform me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gathered his court ladies. Then a maiden of the Śākya clan named Gopī, together with the other ladies, went to where the Bodhisattva was;
she stood to one side and gazed intently at the Bodhisattva, her eyes never blinking.
The Bodhisattva, observing her universally, immediately smiled with joy and took up a precious flower to bestow upon Kūyi.
Kūyi replied:
"I do not covet or long for various jewels or necklaces; rather, I shall adorn my body with merit."
The Prince returned to his chamber and marveled at what he had never before experienced, saying:
"Now this Gopī understands the impermanence of the world and does not crave worldly glory.
At that time, the king’s messenger went to the king's presence and reported these events from beginning to end.
"Previously, the Crown Prince set his heart upon the Śākya maiden Gopī.
Upon hearing these words, the King dispatched a brahmin to act as a matchmaker and seek this girl to be the Crown Prince's consort.
Then the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi said:
"It is our family custom to give our daughters in marriage only to those who possess artistic skills;

since the Prince possesses such skill—being clearly proficient in archery, charioteering, wrestling, writing, mathematics, and the six arts of ritual, music, and so forth—we shall indeed give him our daughter."
The brahmin immediately returned and reported this in detail to the king.
The king thought to himself and,
with these teachings, informed the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva addressed the king, saying:
"Cease for now using this as a means of seeking.
The king said:
"Why do you say 'cease'?
Is it because there is no skillful means?
Regarding the discussion of the True Dharma, let us for now cease."
The Prince replied,
"I am able to do whatever is required.
The King then questioned the Bodhisattva:
"What is this 'art'?
the Bodhisattva asked.
"Is there any extraordinary or marvelous artistry here that is equal to our own?"
"I shall come to see it later.
The king immediately smiled and said,
"Can you manifest such a feat?"
The Bodhisattva said, "I can!
I request that all the Śākya kinsmen be assembled, and we shall together display our arts."
The King commanded his attendants:
"Have bells and drums struck throughout the kingdom, and announce that seven days hence the Prince will display his skills;
let all those who possess artistic talents assemble there."

Within seven days, five hundred members of the Śākya clan gathered for an assembly; those who excelled in the arts were to be given the daughter of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi as a bride, while the one who was foremost in archery, marksmanship, and gambling was to win her hand. They all departed through the city gate.

Thereupon, Devadatta took hold of an elephant with his hands and led it into the city gate; seeing the Śākyas gathered there, he wished to display his magical powers. He immediately seized the elephant’s head with his right hand and its trunk with his left, crushing and killing it.
At that time, Nanda and his companions went out through the city gate and saw a great elephant lying dead across the road;
they asked, "Who killed it?"
He replied,
"Devadatta killed him. Immediately,
[the body] was dragged and moved to the side of the road.
At that time, the Bodhisattva went out through the city gate and, seeing this dead elephant, approached and asked,
"Who killed this elephant?
The attendant replied:
“Devadatta killed it.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
“Who then moved it and placed it by the side of the road?”
He replied,
"It is the virtuous Nanda.
He answered:
"Excellent! This elephant's body is so large that its putrid stench permeates the entire city.
He then took hold of it with his right hand and hurled it outside the city, casting it far beyond the moat.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans raised their voices in a great clamor, all exclaiming:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!
The devas in the void then offered this hymn of praise:
"Grasping a great white elephant, though already dead and its body exceedingly heavy,
he cast it away outside the city, at a vast distance from the moat."
"This one must surely be a supreme sage, an equanimous body detached from the mundane;
having attained all-encompassing wisdom, he shall abide forever by the power of his sanctity.
At that time, five hundred members of the Śākya clan all went to the city gate and gathered in a spacious place, intending to display their skills.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with his powerful kinsmen and the Śākyas, went to the place where the arts were being displayed;

meanwhile, an immeasurable multitude of attendants followed the Bodhisattva, desiring to witness his skills. When these Śākya kinsmen first saw the Bodhisattva in the writing hall praising and expounding upon the sixty-four kinds of scripts, their teachers and peers beheld him with great wonder, deeming it unprecedented. They said, "There is no such art in the heavens or the world; neither the various ghosts, spirits, nāgas, nor asuras can attain it. One who beholds such artistic mastery is truly a sage, possessing the Perfection of Deliverance."

He understood each character individually; as for its meaning and principle, from beginning to end, there was not a single point of doubt or obstruction. In his learning and insight, this virtue surpassed that of Śakra, Brahmā, the sun, the moon, and all the devas. We have witnessed with our own eyes such a mastery of the Way and its arts—who could possibly surpass him? The Śākya clan addressed the multitude, saying:
"Although the Bodhisattva has entered the schoolroom, he has fully mastered writing, calculation, accounting, and all various arts; those who have seen this are few."
"Now that this great assembly has gathered all at once, who among them is truly superior and capable of manifesting elegance? Let everyone observe and discern who is the most excellent.

Chapter Ten: The Trial of Skills from the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* "At that time, there was a great minister named Jyotīrasa, a high official among the Śākyas, who was foremost in calculation and arithmetic, and whose mastery was boundless.
The King appointed this man, saying: 'Observe now, which of the princes is the most excellent?'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva observed the Śākyas and the princes of the kingdom, numbering several hundred, each of whom failed to match the Bodhisattva in the game of discus-throwing.
The Bodhisattva replied, "Wait a moment; I shall throw it."
At that time, a prince came forward and joined them in the game of tossing, yet he too could not equal him;
even when five hundred men tried together, none could catch up to him.
Then, all those gathered raised their voices and sighed in admiration, saying:
"If even a single word he utters is so utterly marvelous, how much more so his countless arts? His extraordinary speech and discourses are inexhaustible.
Although the minister Jyotiṣprabha was skilled in calculation, he could not equal him in conversation or mathematics.

The number of trees, medicinal herbs, and various streams in Kapilavastu may each be known one by one; the arts of *chūpú* and *liùbó*, astronomy and geography, the diverse techniques of the eight directions, and even the phenomena of celestial collapses and terrestrial quakes—all such arts do not compare to those of the Bodhisattva.
His prior knowledge was infinite and his vision reached the ultimate; who could contain his six supernatural powers and three types of penetration?
"The devas, humans, and celestial deities of the void raised their voices in praise, saying:

'The thoughts within the minds of sentient beings in the three realms—all conceivable matters of good and evil, fortune and calamity, and all worldly or spiritual affairs—in the mere instant they arise, he knows them from beginning to end without a single obstruction; in song, dance, and music, there is nothing he does not master.'"

Through the power of patience, loving-kindness, and the Way, and with benevolence and harmony, they have rendered their actions light and effortless over hundreds of thousands of kalpas; wandering alone through the three periods of time like the sun revolving across the four quarters, the bodhisattva’s mind is thus free from the net of doubt.
In the midst of the void, the various devas again praised him, saying:
"This Great Man is the Ultimate and Most Holy One. Although you see him performing the deeds of a householder, listen now to my words:

in the mere instant of conceiving his resolve, he travels to and fro through countless billions of lands in the ten directions; all come to make offerings to him, and he likewise pays homage to the Teachers of the Ten Directions."
Although they manifest coming and going, there is no circumambulation; what do you think—how could such be the case with supernatural power?
Who is able to perceive or know this peerless one who walks alone and strides single-footed?
"For this reason, we all revere and honor the Bodhisattva as the most supreme.
The Śākyas replied,
"One who can understand this realizes that form and desire are both pure, and that all things are fundamentally non-existent."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, with single-minded focus, beheld its entirety from beginning to end.
At that time, all the members of the Śākya clan gathered together, wishing to test their skill in hand-to-hand combat.

While Devadatta was in the world, he was constantly arrogant and deemed himself worthy; he refused to humble himself and frequently contended with the Bodhisattva regarding their supernatural powers. All who came and beheld his extraordinary excellence would circumambulate him to the right, prostrate themselves, and pay homage to this Great Sage.

Devadatta and Nanda then intended to strike him with their fists; at that time, the Bodhisattva, remaining calm and composed out of compassion for them, lifted Devadatta’s body up into the air, where he whirled him around three times. With great loving-kindness and without causing him any harm, the Bodhisattva gently set him back down on the ground so that his body felt no pain.
"You all are arrogant and refuse to abandon your conceit; come together now and engage me in a contest of hand-to-hand combat at once. Let all those who possess skills and arts assemble here."

As soon as the Bodhisattva touched it with his hand by his own power, it naturally fell to the ground; at that time, countless billions of devas and humans, as well as the spirits of the void, raised their voices in a great sound and praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"The Bodhisattva is transcendent and beyond compare.
They rained down celestial flowers and, with one voice and in unison, praised him again, saying:
"Even if all sentient beings in the ten directions were to become mighty warriors and subdue him all at once, how much more so these [present] ones?"

The Bodhisattva’s patience is like Mount Sumeru; surpassing the Iron Ring Mountains, it cannot be shaken. Even if one were to take all the mountains of the ten directions in hand and crush them in an instant into dust and ashes, how much more so could one do this to ordinary beings?
Now, to manifest such power is not to be considered extraordinary; it is merely worldly power and is not yet the supreme, foremost power of the Way.

Having subdued all māras and their retinues, he shall certainly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One; thus manifesting these merits, this bodhisattva is most supreme.
When the Śākya youth Daṇḍapāṇi saw that the Bodhisattva possessed immeasurable great virtue and that his elephant-handled mace was peerless in the world, he wished to test his archery.
At that time, the king and the various Śākyas likewise desired to test his skill with the bow.
At that time, Devadatta drew his bow to a range of forty *li*, Nanda to sixty *li*, and the Bodhisattva to one hundred *li*.
Then, Devadatta shot and hit the drum at forty *li* but could not go beyond it;
Nanda shot to sixty *li*, yet likewise could not surpass it.
The Śākya clan of Daṇḍapāṇi also numbered forty *li*, yet none were able to pass [the test];
at that time, he took up a bow and presented it to the Bodhisattva, but as soon as the Bodhisattva drew the bow, it snapped in two.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
"In this city, is there perhaps another bow fit for my use?
The king then replied:
"It exists. Question:
"Where is it located?"

The king said, "In the past, my grandfather was named Siṃha. The bow he wielded was extraordinary and peerless; after his death, no one was able to use it, so it was enshrined in the celestial temple."
Then the Bodhisattva said,
"Bring it here. When it was brought and presented to him,
none among all the Śākyas of the Ikṣvāku clan were able to string it.

He presented it to the Bodhisattva; while seated, the Bodhisattva pressed down upon it with his hand and drew the bow. The sound of the twanging string was heard throughout the city, and hundreds of thousands of people from the kingdom and the devas in the sky raised their voices in praise, reciting this verse:
“Without rising from his seat, He has instantly drawn this bow;
Thus endowed with all vows, He will surely attain the state of a World-Honored One.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva took up his bow and fixed an arrow; he immediately released it, striking and piercing through the drum at a hundred *li* away.

The arrow sank into the earth, from which a spring of water gushed forth. The arrow then passed on and struck the Iron Encircling Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), causing the trichiliocosm to tremble in six ways. All the Śākyas marveled at this unprecedented event.
The devas in the void all sighed in admiration, saying:
"This is truly unprecedented! Such a wondrous art is pure and most true; among all bodhisattvas, it is the most extraordinary."
Thereupon, the Śākya clan member Daṇḍapāṇi escorted the maiden Gopī to the palace of King Śuddhodana to be the Bodhisattva’s consort;
he conformed to worldly customs and appeared to enjoy her company, among eighty-four thousand court ladies, of whom Gopī was the most honored.
At that time, Queen Gopī, her mind free from increase or decrease, remained constantly awake even while lying down and did not sleep at all; staying in her private chamber, she reflected in solitude:
"Will he perhaps abandon me?"
"His court ladies and attendants constantly surround him.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Thousands of people serve his person; He reflects that the Honored One does not exist."
With majestic virtue and utmost sincerity, he remains in the midst as if standing in fire;
constantly contemplating the protection of the sense faculties, his mind finds no pleasure in anything else.
Like the sun radiating its brilliance, he does not require countless questions.

"While the Bodhisattva was among the palace ladies, he instructed and transformed eighty-four thousand women, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and attain the stage of non-retrogression."

At that time, there was a son of heaven in Tuṣita named Pravrājaka (The One Who Should Go Forth), who had not regressed from his resolve for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. Surrounded by a retinue of thirty-two thousand devas, he went to the palace where the Bodhisattva resided; staying in mid-air, he spoke these verses:
"The Lion among Men has appeared; having descended from the realm of light, his fame is renowned throughout the world.
Following worldly custom, he dwells within the inner palace, yet while in the world, he brings great transformation through his teachings."
He has instructed countless devas and humans;
though he remains in the mundane world, today is precisely the right time for him to leave home and go forth.
As long as the various fetters have not been untied, one does not greedily seek the path seen by men.
One should investigate those who ought to be delivered, appearing as a path for the blind and ignorant.
Seeing that worldly people long for wives, children, wealth, honor, emolument, and all possessions,
one should observe the Noble One’s training and certainly go forth from the household life.
Having renounced the four continents and the seven treasures, and abandoned the pleasures of noble and exalted rank,
he beheld the practice of leaving the home life and wandered upon the lion throne.
Thus he knew that true peace lies in conduct, and took no delight in any sensual desires.
Having lived for a long time since birth, you have attained the Way as a celestial being.
I bow my head in refuge to you, who are like the waters of mountains and rivers;
it would be excellent to leave the household life and constantly perform sublime deeds.
Though your golden complexion is wondrous and beautiful, and your countenance is foremost in its perfection;
though you should bring forth light by renouncing the kingdom, it would be fitting to benefit all devas and humans.
One cannot attain such distinction by delighting in the five desires.
Noble wisdom can fulfill the noble deeds of those who transcend the world.
What your heart yearns for and delights in, O Śuddhodana, within the royal palace—
like a lotus shedding its water, you should contemplate renouncing it all.
When the afflictions are raging fiercely, one should leave behind strife within the prison;
with benevolent majesty as supreme, quickly establish the path of liberation.
Your realization of the realm of wisdom has long endured, and you behold the maladies of sentient beings.
Taking the Dharma as medicine, he establishes the security of Nirvana.
To eliminate the path of blind darkness, he unties the bonds of ignorance and the nets of evil;
he swiftly transforms all devas and humans, bestowing upon them the eye of the path of wisdom.
Manifesting in infinite numbers, devas, nāgas, asuras, and spirits—
who have already attained the path of Buddhahood— return to hear the unsurpassed Dharma.
Thus saving the kings of birds and beasts, its light shines upon their palaces.
Having subdued them, he prostrated; likewise, he caused the Four Heavenly Kings to universally submit and take refuge.
Desiring to offer the four bowls, he attained his wish upon becoming a Buddha, while Brahmā remained in tranquil conduct.
Contemplating great compassion and pity, he exhorts and assists those most honored among men;
rejoicing in the protection of all, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Having already attained the Way of the Buddha, he sits beneath the Bodhi tree.
