I have gained a sublime benefit in that I have beheld the Most Holy One. My mind was set upon worldly matters and I did not recognize the ultimate truth; therefore, I wished to invite one who is free from desire."
If I were to attain Buddhahood, may you look upon me with compassion alone; as the Lord of Dharma, may you deliver and liberate me.
Having encountered the One of Ten Powers, I am blessed by the remaining merit of my past lives to behold the Great Sage and cast myself down in refuge.
He prostrated before the Bodhisattva’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together with his ministers, prepared his carriage and returned to his kingdom.
*Puyao jing*, Scroll Four;

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 14: The Three Sections on Heterodox Teachings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva was dwelling among the mountains and went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River. Delighting in secluded residence, his mind was tranquil; with thoughts of loving-kindness directed toward the ten directions, he desired to benefit devas and humans.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“The Bodhisattva saw from afar that Udraka Rāmaputra was honored and revered by his disciples; he was a master of the most eminent among the multitude, proficient in prophetic charts, divination, mathematics, and the portents of heaven and earth.”
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Now these people, relying on their own persons, calculate and understand arithmetic, astrology, and portents; they act as teachers for the masses and are honored and served by them."

I went to where he was and inquired about his practice to discern its excellence; only then did I subdue him by lecturing on the existence and non-existence of dharmas. With a single-minded mind, he entered the gate of liberation through samādhi and right concentration, surpassing what he had previously studied.

Using skillful means, I observed the beginning and end of his practice; seeing that he was fit for the mundane concentrations, I then expounded for him the profound concentration of unconditioned samādhi, whereby he returned to the Great Way.
At that time, having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva went to where he was and asked:
"Venerable one!"
"Whom do you serve as your teacher?
Who has taught you the Dharma so that you have learned this practice?
Udraka Rāmaputra replied:
"I have no teacher; I have attained this spontaneously.
He was asked again:
"What have you obtained through this attainment?"
He replied,
"I have attained the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Bodhisattva said in response:
"Would it not be better to learn this concentration from another person?
He replied, "Excellent!"
"According to what his will delights in.
At that time, the Bodhisattva rose and sat cross-legged in a secluded place.

As soon as he was seated, his merit and virtue were extraordinary, his noble wisdom peerless, and his past deeds stood out with remarkable distinction; he entered into various meditative states and all samādhis.

Walking alone without companion, there is nothing he does not thoroughly master; the hundreds of thousands of meditative concentrations are all fully prepared within him. Like looking into a mirror, he attains mastery, free from all hindrance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva arose from samādhi and went again to where Udraka Rāmaputra was, asking once more:
"Is there any concentration superior to the state of non-perception?
Does it lead further toward the Way?"
He replied, "There is none.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Rāmaputra lacks faith, whereas I alone possess it;
Rāmaputra lacks diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, whereas I alone possess them."
Having reflected thus, he departed from there and went to where Kālāma was, asking him:
"Who is your teacher? From whom have you received the Dharma?"
He replied:
"I have no teacher; I have realized it spontaneously.
He asked again:
"What is gained by explaining it? He replied,
"One gains the samādhi of useless emptiness."
At that time, the Bodhisattva entered a samādhi that was most extraordinary.
He then spoke again, saying:
"This karma is excellent; it is where I am headed, and you, O virtuous one, shall also head there. Let us both dwell together here, becoming companions among this assembly."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"This present karma does not lead to extinction; it is not free from desire, nor does it reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it does not arrive at tranquility, there is no asceticism (*śramaṇa*) therein, it does not reach perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and it is not Nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva engaged in a series of debates with Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and this Kāla; realizing they were inferior to him, he abandoned them and departed.
Continuing further on his journey, he saw three brahmins:
the first was named Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, the second Nadi Kāśyapa, and the third Gayā Kāśyapa; these three brothers had a thousand disciples.
The Bodhisattva went to visit him and asked,
"What do you serve?
He replied:
"To serve water and fire, as well as the sun and moon, and to ascend as far as the Brahma Heaven.
The Bodhisattva replied: "These are not true or correct.

Water is not always full; fire does not remain hot for long; when the sun rises, it moves on; when the moon is full, it wanes. Even the Brahma Heaven is impermanent; though it lasts a long time, it must eventually end. Only the unconditioned (*asamskrta*)—which has no end and no beginning—is able to be infinite."
When his discourse was finished, he departed from there and returned to his original dwelling.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:”

"Now I dwell in an age of the five turbidities, encountering an inferior assembly where non-Buddhist scholars flourish. Each has fallen into one of the ninety-six heterodox paths or the sixty-two doubts; they are greedy for their bodies and attached to their lives, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. They are stained by and crave sensual desires, harboring hearts of malice; they do not accept instruction nor turn toward purity. Their wills are set on food and drink, and they are fondly attached to lands; they constantly practice what is unrighteous and do not aspire to the subtle and wondrous. They do not delight in wise giving but love wealth and harbor greed and envy; their minds do not dwell upon the meaning of these factors of the path, nor do they abide in non-obstruction, but instead indulge in emotional states. Dwelling in the ten evils and not leaving behind arrogance, they do not rescue others from calamity, being negligent and unstable—thus they are difficult to transform."
They kill living beings at will and drink alcohol without restraint, seeking only pleasure;
some serve fire, water, the sun, the moon, or Brahmā;
others serve mountain deities, shrine deities, celestial deities of the void, or deities of the ocean, springs, ponds, and trees.
Some consume fruits and gourds; some enter the mountains to practice asceticism, eating once every day, every two days, three days, or even up to seven days;
some take a single morsel every day, every two days, three days, or seven days;

some eat once every fifteen days or even once a month, purely cultivating the Brahma-conduct, the four dhyānas, and the four immeasurables, becoming superior immortals or Brahmās who do not pass through the cycle of birth and death.
Some go naked, while others wear deerskins;

some serve ghosts, rākṣasas, asuras, or spirits, yet they fail to escape the evil realms and cannot achieve the Way. Claiming that self-attainment is sufficient, they provide no standard for conduct and lack the means to transform the world or guide those of heterodox and deviant learning.

Now I should manifest pure conduct in order to attract those of external paths, revealing the true and correct practice so that they may abandon their delusions; regarding what ought to be practiced, those in the desire realm and the form realm who do not follow their own teachings shall come to enter the Buddha-way.
Chapter Fifteen: The Six Years of Austerities. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus: 'For six years, I shall manifest the practice of great austerity and diligent effort.'"
For what reason is it called "arduous practice"?
Because this matter is difficult to reach and beyond the capacity of ordinary people, it is therefore termed "arduous practice.

Among all sentient beings—whether gods or humans—none are able to cultivate or accomplish this karma; only a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood can perform it. Therefore, it is said to be difficult to accomplish.

Through this diligent ascetic practice, one manifests the dharma of the four *dhyānas*; by counting the inhalations and exhalations, one causes the mind to understand their meaning. Being without ideation, without thought, and without expectation, wherever one goes, one honors the mind with no dependence. One does not crave these four; their characteristics—from beginning to end—are what was studied in past lives, and they are the practice of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the *pratyekabuddhas*, and the *bodhisattvas*. This is called "pervading all of space."

Non-action is not action, yet there is nothing that is not done; this is called "universally protecting all. Because one practices the matters of meditative concentration with equanimity like space, it is also called "departing without going anywhere."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, wishing to manifest in the world to convert those of external paths, taught various categories of karma to instruct the devas and demonstrate their transgressions and blessings.
Regarding the heterodox arts of the outsiders, some reckoned that death was a total severance and that the spirit was not reborn;
others claimed there was permanence, asking how there could be transgression or blessing.

To explain in detail the retribution of his merits: manifesting in body, speech, and mind, he practiced purity; for six years, he performed arduous and difficult-to-attain ascetic practices, subsisting on only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day, thereby exhausting all karmic debts from past lives.

For six years, the Bodhisattva sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), his majestic deportment and ritual decorum never wavering. He constantly remained in the open air without any covering, avoiding neither wind nor rain, nor the affliction of dust and soil upon his head. He did not rise to move to the left or right for the purpose of defecating or urinating, nor did he produce snot or phlegm. He neither bent, stretched, bowed, nor looked up, nor did he lean or tilt; his body never leaned against anything nor did he lie down. Even when clouds gathered and great rains fell with lightning and thunderbolts, throughout spring, autumn, winter, and summer, the Bodhisattva sat in silence. Encountering these manifold hardships, he never once raised his hand to shield himself; his sense faculties remained undisturbed, and he gave rise to no fear.

Villages and hamlets with their men and women, young and old, herding horses, oxen, and sheep, or carrying firewood and grass, passed by raising clouds of dust, yet he did not mind them nor regard them as a trouble; they were neither a defilement nor an obstacle to him.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva was a marvel to all people, who envied his conduct; he took grasses and trees and placed them in his ears, yet his ears felt neither pain nor itch, and he placed them in his nose, yet his nose felt no irritation, nor did he cast them away."

The devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas personally beheld the Bodhisattva’s meritorious achievements and sublime virtue; they came to his side to make offerings and serve him, bowing their heads in prostration before the Bodhisattva.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva sat in meditation for six years, manifesting ascetic practices and teaching and transforming gods and humans for twelve years, establishing them in the Three Vehicles; it was for this reason that he sat for six years."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva previously left the household life; His meritorious achievements are truly authentic.
His mind is ever tranquil, Manifesting compassion for all sentient beings."
In this world of five turbidities, because of its inferior and mundane nature,
he was born here in Jambudvīpa to manifest both sin and merit to the world.
The study of false doctrines flourishes, along with the sixty-two views.
Therefore, he established this diligence, exhausting his body until his offenses were ended.
The bathing pools and various springs, the sun, moon, and all their radiance;
the trees, crags, and mountains—all the *yakṣas* and earth deities paid him homage.
Spontaneously practicing diligence, he establishes a conduct difficult to equal;
having cultivated and perfected arduous labors, he manifests this for the sake of the multitudes.
His physical strength is like a diamond, and his meditative contemplation is unshakable.
For various reasons, he likewise manifests as a Pratyekabuddha;
for those gods and humans who delight in the confused views of heterodox teachings,
he also transforms them by demonstrating the practice of diligent austerity.
He sat cross-legged upon the ground without any mat;
taking only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice daily, he manifested the act of consuming them.
He demonstrated the exhaling of breath without inhaling, nor was there any returning response of the breath.
For six years he was exceedingly steadfast, his meditative contemplation without flaw or omission.
Without thought and yet not without thought, he did not dwell on what should be practiced;
his mind was like empty space, and his meditative contemplation remained unshaken.
He does not cover his body, nor is there anything to obstruct him;
unmoving like a mountain, his meditative contemplation neither increases nor decreases.
He does not avoid the wind and rain, nor does he shield his head.
He did not lose his dignified deportment, and his meditative contemplation was without fluctuation.
The men and women of the village—tending oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep;
carrying firewood and burdened with grass—passed by his side, stirring up clouds of dust.
Impure filth covers his body, and he encounters various kinds of hardships;
yet, without thought, he is not deluded, and his meditative contemplation neither advances nor retreats.
The flesh of his body wastes away until only skin and bone remain.
Manifested on the front and back, inside and out, its form is like that of a *vīṇā* lute.
All those who perform celestial deeds— the *asuras*, *nāgas*, and *gandharvas*—
behold his total merit and all offer him worship.
Prostrating with the five limbs to receive the teaching, may they swiftly attain accomplishment;
may I likewise achieve this, as you hold compassion in your heart.
You wish to subdue those of external heterodox paths and the various deluded karmas of the ignorant and obscured.
Because of this, he manifested his offenses and blessings; his body sat still while his mouth spoke:
"This Buddha-way is difficult to attain; what way can there be for one with a shaven head?
Having practiced for incalculable kalpas, he completed his retribution in six years.
By means of this, he transformed devas and humans for a period of twelve years;
therefore, the Honored One among Men sat in meditation without advancing or retreating.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Bodhisattva had completed six years of practicing asceticism, he thought to himself:

'Although I possess the power of supernormal faculties, noble wisdom, and insight, if I were to go to the Bodhi tree now with this emaciated body, would there not be those in the borderlands of future generations who would mock me?'"
It is said that one attains the Way while starving.
My body must first consume soft and nourishing food to restore its health and regain its strength; only then shall I go beneath that tree and be able to achieve the Buddha-way.

At that time, there was a village named Śūrpāraka where there lived the daughter of an elder who daily provided food and drink for eight hundred brahmins; having learned that the Bodhisattva was engaged in diligent spiritual practice, she constantly aspired to offer him alms.
That night, the Great Sage Bodhisattva went and sat beneath the tree.

At that time, when the daughter of the elder was first being married off, she had made a vow that if she were to give birth to a son, she would surely prepare sweet and delicious delicacies to offer as a sacrifice to the mountain and tree spirits.

At that time, the daughter of the elder gave birth to a son and was filled with joy. She had a thousand cows suckle one another in succession and took their pure milk to prepare a milk gruel, intending to offer it as a sacrifice to the tree deity;
she then immediately sent a maidservant ahead to clear the area.

When the maidservant saw the Buddha sitting there, she did not recognize what deity it was. She returned and informed her mistress that she had finished sweeping; "Beneath the tree there is a deity, upright and exceptionally beautiful, such as has never been seen in this world."

When the woman heard this, she was delighted and went to take the milk-rice; however, the rice leaped out of the cauldron to a height of more than one zhang, so that it could not be taken. The woman found this very strange.
At that time, the master among the eight hundred brahmins saw this and said to the woman:
"This milk-rice is not something an ordinary person should consume; only when one is on the verge of attaining Buddhahood can one eat this food and digest it."
Then a deva spoke from the sky, saying:

"Today you wish to establish a great sacrificial feast; there is a Great Bodhisattva who has been dwelling in profound contemplation and diligently practicing asceticism, and he has now risen from his seat. You had a vow in the past that you should first provide him with food."

Once you have eaten and are fully satisfied, you shall then attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One; then you should speak of this intention so as not to violate your original vow.

At that time, having heard the words of the deva, the daughter of the elder took the milk-gruel and filled a golden bowl with it; holding the *piṇḍapātra* in her hand, she went together with eight hundred brahmins to the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

“The Bodhisattva, knowing this, used the power of his supernormal wisdom to return to the riverbank and cross over in an instant; yet, in accordance with local custom, he manifested entering the water to bathe himself.”

At that time, eighty thousand devaputras each grasped a tree branch to offer it to the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva pulled the branches out onto the bank, his body being light, agile, pure, and stainless.

Just as the Bodhisattva took his place, a son of the gods from Tuṣita named Vimalaprabha immediately took a celestial robe, a *saṃghāṭī*, and, manifesting the form of a śramaṇa, offered it to the Bodhisattva. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva accepted and donned it, remaining there in serene stillness.
At that time, the wife of a nāga from the waters of the Nairañjanā River emerged from the earth and offered a sublime couch to the Bodhisattva, upon which he sat.

Then, the daughter of a village elder from the village of Uruvilvā-Kauṇḍinya, together with various brahmins, brought exquisite milk-rice and approached the Bodhisattva. She prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, poured *piṅgala* water over the Bodhisattva’s hands, and presented the exquisite milk-rice to him as an offering.

Out of compassion for the woman, the Bodhisattva accepted her food; his physical strength was restored and his mind was free from attachment. He took the golden bowl and cast it into the river, where a thousand dragons immediately seized it to offer worship to the bowl. At that time, the dragon queen received it upon a bedstead, and she established a divine temple there to offer diligent and devoted worship.

The hundreds of thousands of billions of devas all took fragrant water mixed with mud to build temples; those who wished to make offerings to the Bodhisattva’s bowl each manifested their own palaces to serve it together.
At that time, the daughters of the village elders and others obtained the Buddha’s hair and nails and erected stupas to make offerings to them.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"As soon as the Bodhisattva consumed this milk gruel to fulfill his meritorious vows, his body became fully restored and his complexion shone with a brilliance surpassing that of the sun and moon."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, through profound contemplation, With a diligent mind, thought to himself:
'By the power of my physical supernormal faculties and wisdom, I shall go beneath the King of Trees.'"
Having perfected all wisdom and attained the various supernormal powers,
he then practiced universal compassion to finally rescue sentient beings;
"I should now take food so that my body may be fully nourished."
Having gone beneath the King of Trees, he attained the holy state of all-knowledge;
not by meager or thin merit can one achieve the peace of devas and humans.
Without attaining the clear eye, one cannot return to the nectar of physical strength.
When he spoke of his past merits, he resolved upon this sanctuary of peace.
With such thoughts in his mind, a deity heard him and announced to the village:
"A golden bowl filled with milk-rice; go to the banks of the river."
With a heart full of joy, he offered it up; he attained the nectar of the Way.
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, his conduct had been such that all his faculties were utterly tranquil and composed.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits approached as the Great Sage reached the riverbank.
Appropriately practicing the Perfection of Giving, he entered the water to bathe himself;
by washing away the defilements of the mind, he took pity on the mundane world.
A billion devas rejoiced, each bringing flowers, incense, and perfumes.
World-Pacifier has just entered the water, The Supreme among Men to bathe.
Knowing through mindfulness that this is a Bodhisattva, He establishes conduct free from stain;
As the Benevolent and Worthy One bathes, Hundreds of thousands of devas pay him homage.
His body was free from defilement, and the Son of Heaven offered him a *kāṣāya*;
he immediately donned the robe, and having finished dressing,
the Dragon’s wife was filled with joy and offered him an excellent seat.
With a mind in tranquil concentration, he sat down, becoming the Eye of the Path for the world.
The maiden Sujātā offered him food, a golden bowl filled with milk-gruel;
bowing her head in prostration at his feet, she presented it, and Mahāvīra immediately partook of it.
Having partaken of this, he attained fullness; he cast his alms-bowl into the water.
The devas, offering their sincere devotion, came to make offerings to the Buddha.
When the Tathāgata had just finished his meal, the milk-rice was exceedingly sweet and delicious.
His physical strength was full as he proceeded beneath the Bodhi tree;
having just arrived at the foot of the Bodhi tree, his gait remained unshaken.
His stride was as firm as that of Śakra, as he established the practice of a Bodhisattva.

Thereupon, having finished his meal and being fully satiated, the Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the ten directions and wishing to rescue those in peril and distress, desired to sit beneath a tree to manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way and deliver all sentient beings.

The Buddhas of the ten directions all manifested their majestic transformations and revealed their auspicious responses; five hundred transformed birds appeared spontaneously and approached him, circling the Bodhisattva’s body and uttering sounds of profound compassion. They extolled the immeasurable merit accumulated through his practices in past lives, explaining that he had manifested five hundred forms for the sake of all beings and to transform those in the five destinies. He causes them to leave behind the five aggregates (*skandha*), eliminate the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), uproot the conduct of the five paths, and attain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having transformed and removed these twenty-five matters—each consisting of five—he dwells in what is exceedingly difficult: abiding at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) while remaining in non-abiding, where from the beginning there is neither fixed wisdom nor fixed insight.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"From incalculable kalpas past, I have accumulated merit and practiced the six pāramitās;
With the four immeasurable minds and the four debts of gratitude, I am the protector of those within the three realms."
With great compassion and boundless pity, he seeks to liberate those who are deluded, deaf, and blind;
now he shall attain the Great Way, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Adapting to worldly conventions, he manifests his form and preaches suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
When one realizes that all things are fundamentally non-existent, one enters the Triple Gem of the Buddha.
Ordinary people are shrouded by transgressions and obstructed by the twelve links of dependent origination;
failing to reach the unsurpassed truth, they sink and perish within the cycle of birth and death.
If one understands that all things are empty, one does not transgress the conduct regarding the five aggregates;
once the decay of the aggregates has been extinguished, the mind is pure like the Dharma King.
This truly real, unsurpassed wisdom cannot be measured or limited.
His radiance surpasses that of the sun and moon, and those he delivers know no bounds.
One might weigh Mount Sumeru, or measure the void of space;
yet these cannot equal his great wisdom or the infinite conduct of the Great Sage.
"When this verse was recited, countless devas all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Bodhisattva had bathed by the side of the river and partaken of the milk gruel, knowing his strength was restored, he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree."

Beneath the King of Trees, the Buddha cultivated practices in accordance with the Dharma; all remained unmoved, as steadfast as mountains. His conduct was free from flattery and concealment; he established purity without coercion or shortness of spirit. His practice was unshakable and free from mutual conflict; because his nature was not stubborn and he was not impetuous, the high and low of his actions were naturally equal.
He manifested the radiant and brilliant King of Light, whose truly authentic and virtuous conduct eliminated defilements and humbled the mind.
He followed the pure and correct practices of the Buddhas of the past, reaching the Lion’s Throne with an indestructible nature of conduct.
He severs all evil destinies and contemplates eternal peace; he discards the power of Māra’s forces until they become powerless;
he delivers beings from wrong practices so they may undertake the karma of the True Dharma; he extinguishes the darkness, the dust of the trees, and the root of birth and death;
he causes them to have no factions, such that Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings have no place to exercise their influence.

With single-minded courage, he subdues enemies and difficulties; wandering alone, he attains all-knowledge. His mind is peerless, severing the growth of beginning and end; abandoning desire and all greed, he causes the four difficulties to cease. Being unconditioned and fearless, he crosses to the other shore.
For one who practices thus, the meritorious virtues and achievements of a bodhisattva are all perfected.

He proceeded to the banks of the Ganges and arrived beneath the Bodhi tree. Celestial beings and men transformed the road for his journey, making it vast and boundless. Furthermore, on both sides of this road were railings made of the seven treasures, all perfectly adorned and four zhang and two chi in height; above them were latticed pavilions and tiered galleries, likewise composed of various jewels, with celestial canopies, banners, and streamers decorating every part. The trees of the seven treasures were tall, grand, and exquisite, and between these precious trees, cords of rare gems were strung.
Between every pair of trees was a bathing pool, its bottom covered in golden sand from which grew blue lotuses and water lilies with green stalks and flowers.

The four sides of that tree were adorned with jeweled railings, interspersed with bright moon-gems and lapis lazuli; wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks sported within them. Eight thousand jade maidens sprinkled fragrant liquid upon the ground and swept the paths clean, while twenty thousand jade maidens draped various precious necklaces and scattered celestial flowers.

The ground between those trees was composed of the seven treasures; eighty thousand jade maidens each held offerings of famous incense, wood-honey, and various other rare and wonderful things, holding golden incense vases upon jeweled pedestals.
Upon each pedestal were five thousand jade maidens, playing celestial music.
The Buddha said: "It is so, bhikṣu!
When a bodhisattva wishes to proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree, he adorns and prepares the road with such sublime majesty."
Upon reaching the banks of the River Ganges, those who are resolved upon the Mahāyāna also enter this path.
On the night when the Bodhisattva was about to attain Buddhahood, a thousand Brahmā Kings addressed the assembly of Brahmās:

"His merit and virtue are radiant and pure; he has manifested all traces of the Path through compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, equanimity, meditative concentration, and supernormal powers. Having practiced the Great Way for a thousand kalpas, he now approaches the Bodhi tree. We should go together to make offerings to him, so that what he cultivates may be auspicious, enabling beings to take refuge, to be free from fear, to never have cause for dread, to be free from the calamities of the eight difficulties, and to be born among gods and humans before the Buddhas of the ten directions."

When the Brahmā in the Brahma-heaven palace heard this—that after six years of ascetic practice he was now approaching the Bodhi tree—all together, with virtuous minds, should harbor joy and provide offerings to the Bodhisattva, the Dharma Lord of the great trichiliocosm.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, Brahmā, and the Heavenly Kings of the Sun and Moon all went to the banks of the river to welcome him;

throughout billions of Buddha-lands, they all turned their minds toward him. Now, as he approaches the foot of the Bodhi tree to subdue Māra, none can see the crown of his head; reaching upward even to the Brahma Heaven, none can behold it.

Now the physical marks of the Honored One’s body are most wondrous, adorned with thirty-two characteristics; his speech is gentle, pure, and stainless, and his voice is elegant and sublime, surpassing that of Brahmā. As he now sits beneath the tree, we should together make offerings to him.

By the power of his forbearance, Śakra and Brahmā become aware of it and he suddenly attains peace; he completely severs all afflictions and fetters. If there are those who hear of this, they shall reach the state of the Deathless and accomplish the karma of a Pratyekabuddha;
if they attain the Way of the Buddha, sentient beings throughout the entire world will all come to make offerings to them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“There is a Brahmā deity named Trisahasra-vyūha (Establisher of the Three Thousand). Beholding this trichiliocosm buddha-field, he made it all equally illuminated, as level as the palm of a hand. He transformed this ground so that soft green grass grew upon it, appearing like celestial garments on its left and right. Such grass spread throughout the entire trichiliocosm buddha-field, yet it caused no harm to sentient beings, adorning this land.”
From the east, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings, along with incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas from all buddha-lands, all came to make offerings.

From the Buddha-lands of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, incalculable multitudes—Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Great Kings—with their magnificent offerings and ritual implements, all came to present their tributes.

The various adornments of each buddha-field, including the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains and all other mountains, suddenly vanished from those buddha-lands, and their locations could no longer be discerned. Only the bodies of all the bodhisattvas were seen pervading the entire buddha-fields, and among them were sixteen sons of gods who attended upon the bodhisattvas.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Parivarta-vikrama, Bodhisattva Anabhibhūta-vikrama, Bodhisattva Dāna-prada,
Bodhisattva Priya-darśana, Bodhisattva Parākrama, Bodhisattva Keśarin, Bodhisattva Suvihita, and Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī-dhara.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Mālādhara, the Bodhisattva Dharmakīrti, the Bodhisattva Bhayābhaya,
the Bodhisattva Anupahata-cakṣus, the Bodhisattva Mahāviśuddha, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhalaṃkāra, and the Bodhisattva Śīlaviśuddha, surrounded by their retinues—
these sons of gods have all attained non-retrogression and realized the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti).
He made offerings to the Bodhisattva by adorning the site of enlightenment; he leveled the ground for three thousand two hundred li,
surrounding it with seven tiers of beautiful railings, seven rows of trees, seven layers of jeweled nets,
and seven tiers of precious pavilions, all exquisitely decorated with various ornaments of gold and purple.
Various kinds of precious lotus flowers were spontaneously manifested, burning all manner of famous incenses;

above in the void of space, a single precious canopy was established, covering the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. Various precious trees grew forth, and for the devas and humans, the flowers and fruits of these trees all appeared within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
likewise, the myriad flowers of the waters and lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions all appeared within the site of enlightenment.
The bodhisattva assemblies in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions possess adornments that are immeasurable.
The pure karma of meritorious virtue and noble wisdom likewise manifests within these assemblies.
The Buddha-tree was likewise so; surrounded by the assembly of devaputras, they adorned the Buddha-tree until it was utterly pure.
All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others beheld from afar the various kinds of exquisite adornments of their palaces and dwellings, and they all exclaimed together:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"The merit and karmic reward of this response are inconceivable.

"The tree-spirit of that Buddha had four devas who together adorned the path and the tree: the first was named Footprint, the second Boundu, the third Good Intention, and the fourth Spread Essence; they adorned the Buddha-tree to make offerings to the Bodhisattva."

The roots, trunks, branches, nodes, leaves, flowers, and fruits of these trees were all lush and flourishing, surrounding the Buddha-tree to a width and length of eighty *li*, most exquisite and sublime. With immeasurable, towering railings and trees, and various canopies of interlaced nets, each sevenfold in layers, all composed of the seven treasures and encircling it completely; they were like the Pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, such that no one who beheld them could ever feel weary of the sight.
In three thousand lands, those lands were as firm and strong as vajra, indestructible; there, bodhisattvas spontaneously appeared sitting beneath trees, about to attain the path of Buddhahood.

The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “This bodhisattva’s body emanates a great radiance that universally blocks the evil realms and eliminates the eight difficulties. The sick are healed; those in terror find peace; the bound are released; the deaf, blind, mute, and infirm are all liberated; the poor become wealthy; those scorched by the heat of afflictions are all treated and cured; the hungry and thirsty are satiated; those who are pregnant give birth safely;
and the aged and decrepit regain vigor. At that time, there is no bondage of desire, nor lust, anger, or ignorance; there is no thought of weariness or aversion, and no disputes or litigation.”
At that time, all sentient beings looked upon one another as they would their own fathers, mothers, children, or their own bodies, and all harbored hearts of loving-kindness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"When one reaches the realm of no-selection, One appears within the hells;..."
All those who suffer distress shall attain peace and security;
animals will naturally become harmonious, each cherishing the others with affection;
all together harboring hearts of compassion, they shall reach a state of fearlessness.
As for those in the realm of hungry ghosts, who suffer from all manner of hunger, thirst, and destitution,
they all obtain food and drink through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
The eight difficulties are all closed off, and all evil destinies are extinguished.
All sentient beings are entirely at peace and secure, their happiness like that of the heavens.
Those who are deaf or blind, whose various faculties are incomplete,
all suddenly see and hear at that very moment, their bodies becoming fully restored.
The afflictions of lust, anger, and delusion cause sentient beings to suffer from burning distress;
when these defilements find rest, all shall mindfully dwell in the True and Right.
The poor shall obtain wealth, and all shall be born in the heavens.
The sick were all healed, and those in bondage attained liberation.
Free from weariness and anger, there were none who engaged in strife;
at that time, they all respected one another and together gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness.
Just as parents cherish their only child, with mutual and constant affection,
so too do all sentient beings love one another like father and son.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s radiance shone universally throughout the Buddha-lands.
Like the sands of the Ganges River, they pervade the realms of the four directions;
unimpeded by the Cakravāḍa mountains, they pass through the Kṛṣṇaparvata ranges;
all Buddha-fields appear as if they were a single land.
Beholding the arrayed jewels, as level and smooth as the palm of a hand;
adorning the buddha-fields to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
The sixteen sons of heaven surround the Buddha’s tree of enlightenment;
He adorns his site of enlightenment, extending three thousand two hundred li;
all that is worthy of adornment across inconceivable billions of lands,
through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, appears before that Buddha’s tree.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and kumbhāṇḍas;
each raised their palaces and beheld it all from afar.
Seeing this purity, the devas and humans were filled with joy.
Excellent is the retribution of merit; what was done is now fully seen.
Whatever the mouth and mind have practiced, that which was cultivated is impartial;
all beneficial aims are auspicious, and whatever the heart desires is immediately attained.
Just as he practiced in previous lives, all his vows were fully realized;
whatever retribution for sins or merits there was, what he obtained was likewise so.
He adorned the sublime site of enlightenment, with the four heavenly kings mutually embellishing it.
Just as when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven beneath the Pārijāta tree,
though constrained by causes and conditions, he fully expounded all his meritorious deeds;
so too are the pure karmas of the Bodhisattva, exactly as they were performed in the past.
16. The Chapter on the Kāliṅga Dragon King. Chapter Sixteen. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“The light from the Bodhisattva’s body illuminated the palace of the Kāliṅga Dragon King. Having received the Buddha’s light, the dragon’s body and mind were filled with joy; his afflictions were extinguished, he attained universal peace and security, and his countenance became radiant with delight.”
At that time, the Dragon King beheld this radiance, and his eyes were immediately opened. Together with his retinue, he came forward and praised it, saying:
"I have already seen the Buddha Krakucchanda in the distant past; I have also seen the Buddha Kanakamuni and Kāśyapa, illuminated by their radiance."

Beholding the stainless radiance of the King of All Dharmas, I know for certain that a Buddha must have appeared in the world—one endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, compassionate, and possessed of luminous wisdom—therefore he has illuminated my palace. This golden light shines with such brilliance that it does not flicker; its clarity surpasses that of the sun and moon, and cannot be matched by the flames of fire or the luster of bright jewels. The radiance of Śakra and Brahmā naturally recedes to the periphery, and even the light of the asuras cannot reach it. My palace, which was once perpetually dark, is now suddenly filled with great brightness.

Having awakened to this and become free from defilement, my body attains peace and stability; my heart leaps with joy and is free from all ailments. Cool and refreshing, it is free from feverish distress, the fruit of countless billions of eons of unwavering diligence.
"Go to the foot of the Bodhi tree! Excellent!

Let us together take flowers, incense, garments, precious necklaces, rare jewels, famous perfumes, powdered incense, lutes, and musical instruments; we shall go there to make offerings, for this will result in great merit."

Upon hearing this, the Dragon Queen was filled with joy and delight; she went forth to observe the four directions and saw from afar the Bodhisattva, majestic like Mount Sumeru, adorned with radiant splendor, and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of billions of devas. As Śakra and Brahmā paid him reverent homage, her heart leaped with joy as she beheld his path.
At that time, the Dragon Queen joyfully approached Du-shi (the World-Savior), prostrated herself in salutation, and stood before him with palms joined.
Greatly delighted, she made offerings of flowers, incense, various kinds of renowned perfumes, and music, and sighed in praise, saying: "Your merit is true and sublime;

it is wonderful to behold your honor. Like the full moon, you transform the multitudes and deliver them from the world. Beholding the auspicious responses seen by the former Sages, what we see now is likewise equal, without any difference."

Now, having surely subdued Māra and attained parinirvāṇa, he is like a merchant who has escaped peril; having practiced giving in former lives, he has obtained his wishes, attained patience, cultivated the diligence he sought, delighted in meditative contemplation, and kindled the lamp of wisdom. Having now fully perfected all his original practices and vows, he will certainly achieve supreme victory.
"It is like a tree with abundant flowers and fruit; until the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it will be like a thousand springs from which water can be drawn without end.
With a heart full of joy, he universally raised clouds that rained down throughout the entirety of space:
"He shall now surely attain the Way; his body, of purple-gold color, will radiate light that pervades the Buddha-lands, and all evil realms shall be brought to the great essentials [of liberation]."

The eminent and honored leaders of those three thousand lands shall command that the physicians of the three ages must surely go to the Buddha; he shall shine upon the world like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be shaken, and like a man of clear wisdom who perceives that even the four great oceans might be exhausted, yet one who has approached the foot of the King of Trees can never be obstructed or fail to achieve the Way of Buddhahood.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Thereupon, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
'In what kind of seat did all the Buddhas of the past sit when they attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment as a Perfectly Awakened One?'"
He further thought to himself:
"The Buddhas of the past sat upon mats of grass and attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
Then, hundreds of thousands of deities in the void, perceiving the Bodhisattva's thought, immediately replied:
“As the Great Sage’s intention was, it was thus in the past: they all sat upon mats of grass and attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

“At that time, the Bodhisattva saw on the right side of the road a man named Śrī, who was cutting fresh green grass that was soft, smooth, and lustrous, arranged in neat rows without disorder, as beautiful as celestial garments.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva saw him and immediately left the path to go to where Śrī was; with a heart of loving-kindness and harmony, he engaged him in conversation, saying to him:

"Expound the excellent teachings and encourage them; let your words be gentle and refined, free from coarseness; let your mind be peaceful and harmonious, devoid of malice; eliminate lust, anger, and delusion, and produce the mournful, melodious cry of a phoenix; let your voice possess the eight qualities of Brahmā and Indra, profound and difficult to surpass, like the roar of a lion or the thundering of a storm."
Sentient beings in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions receive his transformation and all attain peace and security.

Whatever he expounds, hundreds of thousands of Dharma-sounds cannot obstruct him; with a single Dharma-sound, he universally enters into all sounds, making them all harmonious and peaceful until they reach liberation.
He brought universal joy to the assembly; all that the Buddhas speak is timely and imbued with words of kindness and benevolence.
"I wish to obtain some grass; Śrīghoṣa, give it to me!
Today I shall subdue the power of the wicked and achieve unsurpassed enlightenment."
The power of self-restraint cultivated through giving over incalculable eons, the observance of the precepts by abandoning all conceptualizations—these shall now be attained.

The power of patience, diligence, and wisdom; the power of renown, intellectual strength, meditative concentration, and supernormal faculties; the doors of liberation and the powers of the Path—all these shall now be realized.

Thereupon, hearing the gentle and harmonious words spoken by the Guide, Śrī was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with body at ease and mind delighted, he offered soft grass, giving rise to great merit and blessings that lead to the infinite:
"When I attain the Ambrosia, may Śrī, who has provided this seat, likewise attain the Way of the Buddha."

Because of this offering of grass, I practiced diligent asceticism for countless billions of kalpas, performed various deeds, and cultivated wisdom, merit, and skillful means; with a firm and resolute mind, I have now attained Buddhahood and shall certainly achieve perfect enlightenment just as I do today.

If you reach the site of enlightenment, you should teach others; if you truly attain your aspiration, know that I have attained Buddhahood and distinguished the nectar of immortality, and you shall come to hear the Dharma and achieve the state of supreme sagehood.
As soon as he spread the grass seat, the earth shook violently.
The devas in the void all joined their palms together and praised him, saying:
"Today, having subdued Māra and his retinue by force, you have attained the ambrosia of the unsurpassed, right, and true [enlightenment]."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"When he approached the tree, the devas manifested eighty thousand Buddha-trees and lion thrones, thinking to themselves:
'We shall cause the Bodhisattva to sit upon these adorned and pure seats and attain supreme perfect enlightenment.'"

Furthermore, the flowers and fruits of the various Buddha-trees were lush and flourishing; some were trees of pure fragrance forty *li* high, while others were Buddha-trees made of the seven treasures, eight thousand *li* high, or four thousand *li*, or a hundred thousand *yojanas* high. All these Buddha-trees were fully endowed with eighty thousand [features].
Various celestial robes were spread upon them, or various kinds of lotus flowers were laid out to serve as seats.

Upon the Bodhisattva’s seat, there is a samādhi called the Samādhi of Pure Radiance (*Vimalaprabhā-samādhi*). As soon as he enters this samādhi of meditative absorption, all the Buddha-trees become seats upon which the Bodhisattva sits, his body adorned with the primary and secondary marks.
Each of the devaputras perceives and knows that the Bodhisattva is seated upon their own seat and not on any other.

By virtue of the majestic spiritual power of the Samādhi of Pure Radiance, those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals all find rest; and among the gods, humans, and all classes of sentient beings born within the five realms of existence, everyone beholds with their own eyes the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva seated beneath my Buddha-tree, and does not see him elsewhere.
Those of inferior disposition and great meager merit, seeing the Bodhisattva’s body seated upon a mat of grass, approached the Bodhisattva’s location and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upon a natural lion throne; his power and majesty were firm and robust, surpassing even dragons and elephants, noble, sovereign, and beyond compare.

His fame is heard everywhere; through his perfection in giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, he has attained sublime merit and is able to subdue the enmity of Māra; therefore, he now sits upon a bed of grass.
His body sat upright and his mind was fixed in right concentration.
This virtuous person saw the Bodhisattva seated upon the lion throne, like the full moon illuminating the ten directions.
The Bodhisattva made this vow:
"Even if my body were to perish, my flesh and bones wither and rot, and my frame were to crumble away entirely, I shall never rise again until I have attained the Way of the Buddha.
Having practiced asceticism with diligent effort for countless billions of *kalpas*, I have now finally achieved it; I shall never turn back."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

“At that time, when the Bodhisattva sat beneath the Bodhi tree, there was a great radiance called ‘Proclaiming the Way at the Site of Enlightenment. He emitted this light, which universally illumined the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions, pervading the limits of space and shining upon all the Buddha-lands.”

At that time, in the eastern world-realm called Vimala, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Vimalaprabha, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāvyūhaprabha. He went forth to offer exhortation and illumination, accompanied by a retinue of countless bodhisattvas, and proceeded to the site of enlightenment; having just arrived at the tree of awakening, he stood there.

In the Buddha-lands of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—the ten directions throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space—all Buddha-fields were seen to have Bodhisattvas sitting beneath the tree of the single path of enlightenment, such that everyone beheld them as if seeing them face-to-face nearby.
The sentient beings of the five realms of existence looked at one another and all saw the Bodhisattva as clearly as observing one's own fingers.
"How is it that the Great Sage is so subtle and wondrous?
those bodhisattvas, beholding his facial features, spoke this verse:
“Free from the defilements and blemishes, having uprooted all turbid impurities;
the light of his body illuminates the ten directions, surpassing all majestic radiances.”
"His merit, wisdom, and meditative concentration have been accumulated over incalculable eons;
that most supreme Śākyamuni pervades all directions.

At that time, from the southern Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Ratnārcis, in the world-system called Most Pure, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhūtaratnacchatrasaṃdarśana. His light went forth to offer encouragement and illumination, and together with an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas as his retinue, he proceeded to the Bodhi tree to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
Each held a single precious parasol that completely covered the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings addressed one another, saying:
"For whom have we obtained these adorned and pure parasols as an offering?
At that time, from within the precious parasols, this verse emerged:
“Having bestowed hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas upon those without equal,
and always harboring a heart of vast compassion— this is the mark of distinction.”
"Interlaced with hooks and gems, it radiates brilliant light; now it has reached the Buddha’s site of enlightenment.
Its power and majesty are difficult to equal; therefore, we have come to make offerings here.

At that time, from the western buddha-field of Sīmantikā, the world of Flower-Adorned Spiritual Powers (Puṣpavyūhābhijña) Tathāgata, there was a bodhisattva named Unattached Radiance (Asaṅgaprabha). His light shone forth as an exhortation, and together with countless bodhisattvas, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment, where there was a jeweled, interlaced canopy.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas of the ten directions said to one another:
"From where has this Pure Radiance come?
Then, from within the jeweled lattice canopy, these verses were spoken:
“The precious chariot and precious robes reach as high as the three realms;
with the precious renown, the precious joy, and the precious eye, they don the armor and exert themselves with diligence.”
"Now he shall attain the Way of the Buddha; all the bodhisattvas have arrived.
To provide this jeweled canopy, they come to make offerings to that Most Victorious One.

At that time, from the world-system called *Divākara-vartana* in the northern direction—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata *Candrasūryaprabhāsa*—a bodhisattva named *Vimalarāja*, having been exhorted by the radiance, went together with countless bodhisattvas to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
All the pure virtues of the worlds in the ten directions were manifested upon high seats, and at that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas all spoke these words:
"Who has now brought about such a magnificent purity as this?"
Then, Samantavyūha spoke these verses:
“Those whose bodies are pure possess immeasurable merit and wisdom;
Those whose speech and conduct are pure proclaim this gateway of the Dharma.”
"This mind is ever pure, having long since given rise to the heart of compassion;
now, beneath the King of Trees, he makes offerings to the Honored One of the Śākyas.

At that time, from the world-system of King of Virtue (Guṇarāja) in the southeast—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata King of Virtuous Radiance (Guṇaprabharāja)—there was a bodhisattva named Sound of Virtuous Radiance (Guṇasvaraprabha). His light shone forth with exhortation, and together with countless other bodhisattvas, he went to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
In the midst of the jeweled lattice pavilion was a high seat.
From that jeweled lattice pavilion, these verses were proclaimed:
“His meritorious virtues are universal; The asuras, gandharvas, and yakṣas;”
"That King of Virtue, Renowned for His Merit, has offered it to the site of enlightenment.

At that time, from the world-system called Joyful Accomplishment in the southwest, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Jewel Forest, a bodhisattva named Jewel Radiance—whose light shines with encouragement—arrived at the site of enlightenment together with countless bodhisattvas to make offerings to the Bodhisattva;
he brought a pavilion of immeasurable jewels and latticed canopies, within which was a high throne.
From that jeweled pavilion, he recited these verses:
"With a mind of good intention and reverence, he bestowed countless precious jewels;
He gave away lecture halls and balconied windows, as well as his own body and chariots."
“Adorned with a canopy of dewy blossoms, A subtle and exquisite garden pavilion;
By giving away my head, hands, and feet, I thereby sat at the site of enlightenment.

At that time, from the world-system of Varṣā in the northwest—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Gandharvarāja—there was a bodhisattva named Saṃgharṣitameghasvaraprabha. His light shone forth as an exhortation, and together with countless other bodhisattvas, he came to the site of enlightenment to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
They reached the Terrace of Interwoven Fragrances, where there was a high seat; a rain of various famous incenses fell, scattering over the high seat.
As the rain of incense fell, it proclaimed these verses:
"The rain of Dharma pervades the three realms, Endowed with the light of liberation."
He rains down the nectar of detachment, reaching the unconditioned state of nirvāṇa.
He eliminates all the dust of the world and completely severs the poison of fetters;
through the power of meditative concentration and supernormal faculties, he creates flowers and incense of the three grades.

"At that time, in the northeastern world-system called *Vaijayanta-vitāna*, within the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnacchattra-udgataprabha, there was a bodhisattva named Vyūhapaṭa-vitāna-prabha. His light radiated forth as an exhortation, and together with countless bodhisattvas, he came to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

Their *vitāna* canopies were made of jewels, and they manifested themselves in the form of bodhisattvas, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence. Each of these bodhisattvas held celestial flowers and incense, lowered their bodies, bowed their heads, and spoke these verses:
'Beholding this great assembly in reverence, We praise the Buddhas of billions of eons;'"
"Your speech is like that of Brahmā; we prostrate and approach the site of enlightenment.

Thereupon, from the world-system of Universal Radiance in the nadir, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Universal Manifestation, a bodhisattva named Jewel-Treasury Radiance—whose light shines forth with encouragement—arrived at the site of enlightenment together with countless other bodhisattvas to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

A high seat of blazing light and a purple-gold lotus appeared spontaneously; upon that lotus, a celestial image manifested by transformation, holding a precious necklace in his right hand and trailing silken banners and streamers, bowed his body and lowered his head, speaking these verses:
"With body ever reverent, he constantly pays homage to the disciples of the Buddha;
having abandoned arrogance by bowing to the Buddha, I now pay homage to his virtues and meritorious achievements."

"Then, from the world-system of Infinite-Eye-King Tathāgata in the space of the zenith, a bodhisattva named Ākāśagarbhaprabha, with his light illuminating all, arrived at the site of enlightenment together with countless bodhisattvas to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

From the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as vast as the realm of empty space, they gathered various flowers, renowned incenses, powdered perfumes, robes, flower-canopies, banners, and streamers, gold, silver, and myriad jewels, elephants, horses, and chariots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, men and women, young and old, gandharvas, kinnaras, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, who then sent down a great rain, causing all sentient beings to feel joy and delight; those who were afraid were made free from fear and distress."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Like a Bodhisattva fond of discourse, He attained the Way through compassionate pity;
Adorned, pure, and ready to deliver others, His virtue surpasses that of great majestic power."
Some shower from above in the void a hundred thousand jeweled necklaces;
some offer fragrant jewel garlands, manifesting hanging canopies of exquisite incense.
Some roar the lion’s roar upon the earth, expounding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Some raise great sounds in the void; such flowers have never been seen before.
Some, in the upper realms of space, manifest billions of jewels;
because they pervade all of space, they are auspicious, extolling the blessings and merits of the Bodhisattva.
He emits radiant light at that moment, obscuring the palaces of Māra;
Or he manifests the splendor of jeweled banners, as one of supreme merit approaches the Bodhi tree.
A bright pearl hovers in the void, its radiance surpassing the moon and the auspicious moon.
Some mentally transform *sumana* flowers, raining them down upon the Buddha-trees at the site of enlightenment;
some bow their heads in prostration, as the Son of Heaven contemplates the creation of reverence;
others, like Mount Sumeru, scatter flowers from hands reaching into the void.
Or they go to the marshes of the four quarters, burning various excellent incenses;
holding precious staffs in their hands, they behold the Bodhisattva from afar.
Or they manifest the form of a tranquil Brahmā, dwelling in profound stillness and serenity.
The hair that grows is soft and fragrant, equal to the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness,
compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Like Śakra, Lord of Devas, surrounded by billions of celestial beings,
they proceed to the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, join their palms, and scatter bright pearls.
Some reached the four quarters—the Gandharvas and Kinnaras—raining down light, fruits, and *sumana* flowers; these deities praised his valor.
Others took up flowers and incense, scattering tree leaves and floral fragrances.
The Son of the Buddha manifested his half-body; bowing low, he scattered flowers and incense.
Some received *pundarīka* lotuses and various blue lotuses;
abiding in the thirty-two marks, they praised the Honored One who is free from attachment.
With a body as vast as Mount Sumeru, he casts himself from the void;
with banners, streamers, flowers, and incense, he beholds the Buddha-fields of the three thousand worlds.
With his eyes he witnesses heaven and earth ablaze, seeing clearly all their unions and disintegrations.
Mindful of entering the practice of the Dharma-gate, they hear celestial sounds yet do not yield to desire.
Some emit the voices of gandharvas, their exquisite features perfectly complete;
adorned like jade maidens, the gods and humans gaze upon them without weariness.
The body is as firm as adamant and indestructible; the mind’s activities abandon self-importance.
Some come to proclaim the meaning through speech; bathing the body, its radiance removes all impurities.
Others, with jewel-palms upon jeweled grounds, prepare hundreds of thousands of banners and canopies.
Raining down precious flowers and sublime incense, they establish peace for sentient beings suffering in distress.
They bring forth great treasuries from the earth and, with their voices, expound upon billions of sutras;
through their eloquence, they awaken the minds of others and resolve the delusions of sentient beings.
“Maintaining fearlessness like a mountain, he transforms chaos into supreme peace;
throughout the billions of lands in the ten directions, today they awaken to the nectar of immortality.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The Bodhisattva’s adornment and purification is of such a nature that the lands are spontaneous; the Buddha-lands of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and the adornments created at the Bodhisattva’s site of enlightenment, are all universally manifested as pavilions with latticed curtains."

As the Bodhisattva sat upon this high seat, among all the devas of the desire realm, Māra Pāpīyān was reckoned the most powerful and honored. [The Bodhisattva thought: "Now, in accordance with the Dharma, I shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become the Most Perfectly Awakened One; I must cause Māra to be summoned here so that, by means of this, he may be subdued."

By means of this, he gathers and transforms the sons of the gods of the desire realm, causing them to fully attain their original nature; likewise, the gods of the Māra realm see him roar the lion’s roar, subduing all, and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, thereby inspiring the sentient beings of the three realms.
Chapter Seventeen: Summoning Māra. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva possessed a radiance named 'Dissolving the Palace of Māra. He emanated this radiance, which shone universally throughout the three thousandfold world-system, pervading everywhere without exception, and its brilliance eclipsed all the palaces of Māra."

By means of that radiance, Māra Pāpīyas was made to hear this teaching: "The Great Pure Being, having accumulated merit and virtue over incalculable kalpas, has renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship; out of compassion and seeking the ultimate truth, he desires to realize the Ambrosia."

Beneath the Bodhi tree, having already crossed over oneself, one shall cross over others; having transcended the three realms oneself, one shall liberate others; having attained peace for oneself, one shall bring peace to all; having attained the tranquility of nirvana for oneself, one shall lead others to extinction. Dwelling in seclusion, one protects against all evil destinies so that none remain, serving as the teacher and father to all gods and humans.
Having perfected the supernormal powers, he has forever left all evil realms behind without exception, becoming the teacher of gods and humans alike.
Having perfected the supernormal powers and attained eternal great peace, he brings peace to all through the nectar of immortality.
I shall empty your realm and bind your neck so that you are rendered powerless; you shall lose all your retinue, and with your heart stifled and choked, you will not know what stratagem to employ.
I shall then raise the rain of Dharma to moisten and nourish all beings.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān heard these verses of instruction, and while sleeping in a dream, he saw thirty-two omens:
first, he saw his palace become dark and obscured, lacking any light."
Second, they see the palaces fouled by mud and impurity;
third, they see the palaces destroyed, shattered, and overgrown with thorns;
fourth, overcome by terror, their hair stands on end as they flee in all directions.
Fifth, he saw that they had lost their way through delusion and entered upon evil paths filled with thorns, shards, and stones;
sixth, he saw that the trees growing in their rear gardens bore neither flowers nor fruit;
seventh, he saw that the ponds were parched and devoid of lotuses.
Eighth, he sees wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, mourning pheasants, and all manner of birds and beasts, all devoid of wings and feathers;
ninth, he sees large drums, *konghou* lutes, and other musical instruments broken, severed, and abandoned upon the ground;
tenth, he sees his beloved and respected wife, children, and kinsmen having abandoned him to sleep separately in another place.
11. He saw himself fall from his bed to the ground, his head and face wounded and bruised;
12. He saw the sons of Māra, possessing great and powerful majesty, all coming to prostrate themselves and take refuge in the Bodhisattva;
13. He saw the four daughters of Māra lose their sense of time and transform into old women.
14. He sees his own body covered in filth, mud, and dust;
15. He sees the walls, windows, balconies, pavilions, and gates of his residence becoming dilapidated and collapsing;
16. He sees all the hands and feet, as well as the bodies and heads, of his retinue of military hosts, ghosts, spirits, yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, devas, and nāgas falling to the ground.
Seventeenth, he saw that the various devas of the desire realm—the Śakras, Suyāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmita-vaśavartins—each departed on their own and did not follow his instructions;
eighteenth, he saw the hosts dwelling in the palace of Māra with their heads shrouded;
nineteenth, he saw that Mahābrahmā no longer acted according to his own will.
20. He saw that his own retinue did not submit to him;
21. He saw his crown, turban, pearls, and necklaces spontaneously consumed by fire;
22. He saw the palace of Māra spontaneously shaking and trembling.
Twenty-three: seeing all the trees being cut down and falling to the ground;
twenty-four: seeing that all pleasing activities no longer appear;
twenty-five: seeing the waters burst forth, submerging and destroying the palaces.
Twenty-sixth, he saw the riverbanks collapse and their waters inundate the houses of the inhabitants;
twenty-seventh, he saw all the celestial kings come to take refuge in the Bodhisattva and gaze upon his countenance;
twenty-eighth, he saw his own bed spontaneously move outside.
Twenty-nine: He saw his other attendants abandon him and depart to return to the Bodhisattva;
thirty: He saw that all his auspicious cauldrons and stoves were completely destroyed;
thirty-one: He saw various Brahma kings and the retinues of Māra proclaiming inauspiciousness.
32. "He beholds all sentient beings throughout the ten directions taking refuge in the Bodhisattva and receiving his teachings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When Māra saw these various transformations in a dream, he arose from sleep with terror in his heart and his hair standing on end. He summoned his ministers and military hosts and recounted to them what he had seen in the dream."
Māra had a wise minister named Siṃhasthita. The King questioned this great minister and those assembled:

"In a dream, I heard a voice spontaneously emerge from the air, saying: 'A son has been born to the Śākya clan, endowed with all the marks of excellence; after six years of practicing diligent asceticism, he shall go beneath the Bodhi tree and attain Perfect Enlightenment.'"
Having awakened from the dream, he thought to himself:
"Now this bodhisattva will deliver countless billions of people; he will surely empty my realm until nothing remains. I must restrain him."
When one possesses such virtue, they immediately attain the Way of the Buddha and are named a Dharma King; all turn toward him for refuge.
By what skillful means can their path be severed so that they do not achieve success?
"Lead a great host of troops and lie in wait to strike him down.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Leading a great host of troops, We shall go together to harm and eliminate him."
He then went beneath that tree and treacherously slew this śramaṇa.
Leading his fourfold army, he desired to show me love and respect;
yet they fought against me, so I quickly dispatched them.
Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats shall fill the world;
they will destroy my hosts and deprive them of all power and might.
Thus I shall become a Buddha, the Dharma King of heaven and earth.
"Our factions are exceedingly powerful and flourishing; for the sake of the Buddha, we shall never cease.
Thereupon, the son of Māra, the Instructor, spoke this verse to Māra Pāpīyas:
"Why has the face of the Great Man changed? His complexion is not as it usually is."
Like the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, whose bodies are no longer in harmony, what have you seen or heard?
Tell me quickly, for I wish to know;
by constantly observing the root and the branches, one may treat and cure their ailments.
"Having heard what the devas and humans say, he will see evil dreams while lying in sleep;
if these are all recounted among the assembly, those who hear them will cast themselves down.
Then the Māra-son, the Guide, went in person to address his father:

"Though I address the great assembly with vocal sounds, I shall cause them to be unsurpassed and free from anything non-virtuous. Whether the minds of the multitude give rise to something or do not give rise to anything, such a resonance will naturally arise beneath the tree. Now, this manifestation of an auspicious omen is a sign of good fortune; it is not to be viewed with contempt."
I observe that he is necessarily at peace, endowed with all auspiciousness; he skillfully reduces affairs so that offenses do not arise.
I see that he is serene and capable of guiding others; he does not employ illusory arts nor harbor a sense of self, but acts to accomplish auspiciousness as a truly authentic teacher.
The Guide spoke again:
"If one possesses power yet fails to exercise it, they will naturally become weak. A brave hero who practices compassion will achieve victory.

Even if fireflies were to fill the three thousandfold world-system, a single hair’s worth of light would surely be able to illuminate the ten directions of the world. Those whose minds harbor impurity and false ways, who are habituated to delusion, and who treat the wise with contempt—their illness is difficult to cure; not even billions of Buddhas could move them or heal them."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Thereupon, Pāpīyān did not heed the words of the Guide. He immediately summoned his thousand sons—five hundred of whom, like the Guide himself, had faith and delight in the Way and its Virtue and had taken refuge in the Bodhisattva, standing to the Bodhisattva’s right;
while the other five hundred sons, who followed the teachings of Māra, stood to the Bodhisattva’s left. Then Māra Pāpīyān addressed his sons, saying:”
"You all must unite with one mind to devise a plan; by what power or force can you surpass the Bodhisattva?
The son on his right, named Śāstṛ, replied to his father Pāpīyas with these verses:
"What good is it to incite strife among our sons? We must personally take up the legal case to sever the root."
"A tiny insect wishes to battle a lion; how could one who acts with such bravado ever surpass the Buddha?
The son on the left, named Evil Eye (Akṣamāla), replied in verse:
"Upon merely beholding my physical strength, [the enemy] is wounded, like a tree falling to the ground with its roots and branches torn out."
"Now this śramaṇa observes my dwelling; having barely regained his breath, he wishes to gasp for air again.
The son on the right, named Mṛdusvara, replied in verse:
"He seeks to rouse fear to dry up the great ocean, practicing perversely while seeking peace and harmony."
"Beholding the facial features of this Bodhisattva, I do not consider my father’s wonder to be strange.
The son on the left, named Impurity (Aśuci), replied with a verse:
"Seeing only himself as one who would prevail, you, O Śramaṇa, withdrew in silence."
"Behold my countless thousands of troops, all together fierce and valiant, who shall destroy your form.
Then the son on the right, named Subhāṣita, spoke this verse:
"The elephant’s great power of the hook and chain, and the courageous, secret, and robust man wielding the vajra;
"Having established the treasury of the power of patience and gentleness, he causes all who are fierce and stubborn to be forever rendered powerless.
The son on the left, named Powerful Majesty (Balavikrama), spoke again in verse:
"Though the light of the Bodhisattva’s body dispels disease, I shall enter it and utterly destroy it."
"The roots of goodness he upholds are like the conflagration at the end of an eon; my body shall bring harm to this Bodhisattva.
Then the son of Māra on the right, named Śubhahetu, replied in verse:
"Mountains may yet be moved, and the sky may fall; The waters of the great ocean may yet be exhausted;"
"Though one might walk upon the void as if it were the earth, One shall not leave this tree until the nectar of immortality is attained.
The son of Māra on the left, named Parivarta-praveśa, replied with a verse:
"The radiance of the sun and moon may be obscured, And the palaces of Māra can hide within the waters; But he who has reached the end of all conditioned things— How could he ever be led away?"
"How could one take a single drop to exhaust the rivers and seas? Lead the troops back and do not let them roar like thunder.
Then the son of Māra on the right side, named Guṇatīrtha, replied with a verse:
"The light of the sun and moon might be extinguished, and the Iron Ring Mountains might become impure;"
“The purity of the Bodhisattva—none can withstand it alone.
Then the son of Māra on the left, named *Anveṣin* (Seeking an Opportunity), immediately replied with a verse:
“Without troops and without allies, he is called pure; his countenance is exquisite, yet he bears no armor or weapons.”
"I have never seen one who wishes to fight without weapons; as I am today, I shall certainly cause you harm.
The son on the right, named Guṇavīrya, replied in verse:
"One must not speak solely according to one's own will; the mind should harbor the power of patience and be strong in diligence."
"Practicing the wealth of wisdom through the three gates of liberation, he shall subdue us with the power of his virtue as his weapon.
The son of Māra on the left, named Anivartin (Not-Returning), replied in verse:
"We shall surely strike him back like burning grass; even if one uses auspicious incantations, they cannot avoid the arrow."
"By means of this incantation, even if he were to shatter the mountains and return, it would not allow the Prince to remain but would cause him to gallop on.
Then the son on the right side, named Dharmarata, replied with a verse:
"The void could be made to have form, And the realms of sentient beings could be made one; But the power of the Prince’s merit is such that Not even the gods can obstruct his path."
"A gentle breeze and coolness may still be obtained, But the Bodhisattva beneath the tree cannot be moved.
The son on his left, named Tan-pa, replied with a verse:
"The realm of my father provides spontaneously; Whatever the multitude desires is all present there."
"All shall destroy and take his life; approach the foot of the tree, endanger him, and then depart.
The son on the right, named Sarvaśiva, replied in verse:
"Even if the three thousandfold world were filled with things, all becoming poison, they could not harm him."
"The great terrors of the poisons of lust, anger, and delusion—though all these sought to assail the Sage, they were ultimately unable to do so.
Then the son of Māra on the left, named Rati-rāga, replied in verse:
"A hundred thousand jade maidens, adorned in their finery, play the sounds of countless musical instruments; [yet he remains unmoved]."
"Experiencing joy and frequently experiencing delight and pleasure, from this one attains peace and all that is cherished.
The son of Māra on the right, named Dharmacārin, replied in verse:
"One finds amusement in what is delighted in by the Dharma; cherishing and honoring meditative concentration, one delights in the nectar of immortality."
"Delivering sentient beings and receiving them with compassion—who else would have a mind that delights in desire?
The son of Māra on the left, named Supratibhāna, replied in verse:
"The moon travels through the void wherever it goes; Because it dispels the darkness, it is bright and clear."
"Today we have become śramaṇas, having destroyed all the karmic activities of our former perceptions.
