Then the son on the right, named Siṃhanāda, replied with a verse:
"The cries of countless jackals are not equal to the roar of a single brave lion."
When the hundred beasts hear this sound, they are filled with fear; trembling and terrified, they flee in all directions.
Now you, O ministers, are likewise: having failed to hear the Honored One proclaim the Dharma, you have strenuously propagated far and wide what is but false speech.
Now that you hear the Holy Lion’s Roar, you shall be subdued.
The one on the left face, named *Pāpasmṛti*, replied in verse:
“The assembly that has gathered here now is of countless transformations; how can one contemplate these various leaders?”
"Fools who see this do not abandon it and flee; to say they have 'subdued' it is but a false claim.
Thus, to speak in brief, all the sons of Māra—both those of the Pure and White faction and those of the Dark and Obscure faction—each spoke a verse.
At that time, there was a general named Bhadradatta who spoke these verses for Māra Pāpīyas:
"What you know, O Lord, The Four Śakra Kings and the Cāturmahārājikas,
The Asuras and the Kālayas— Ten thousand times ten thousand prostrate in worship."
How much more so those who are not deluded— the Brahmā gods, the Ābhāsvara gods,
and the sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens— who all likewise take refuge in you.
All the sons now born here receive your instructions and commands.
These beings, revering the Bodhisattva, all prostrate themselves here.
Now this host of Māra’s army, three thousand two hundred li in extent,
gazes with respectful joy, their hearts filled with exultation.
Beholding him, his countenance was serene and joyful; hundreds of thousands of devas rained down flowers.
Innumerable spirits made offerings, and the various devas descended as honored guests.
Amidst all that the hosts of Māras could do to cause confusion, the drums failed to sound.
One who can retreat possesses wisdom; they will certainly not suffer defeat.
The Bodhi tree is auspicious, yet the wild ducks and geese revile the peacock;
though the peacock does not fear them, it cries out in sorrow. When one cannot prevail, it is better to retreat.
In the abodes where the hosts of Māra dwell, rain falls of ink and dust;
at the site of enlightenment, rain falls of various flowers—pray, listen and turn back!
In the abodes where the hosts of Māra dwell, ditches and pits are strewn with spikes.
The site of the Way is now perfumed with incense; wisdom beholds it and shall depart.
As for the auspicious signs previously seen in dreams, why does the eye not behold them now?
What can be done about this? The sacred precinct has already been destroyed.
That *laṅgha* transformed a person who was angry with an ordinary great seer;
through his supreme praise of diligence, rain and thunder failed to produce grass.
When the diligent seer returned, he was able to match the one of noble deportance as a consort.
Because he does not harm sentient beings, his head and crown attain mastery.
Great King, have you not heard? His physical marks emit light that shines afar;
when he leaves the world there is no difference, yet as a Buddha he subdues the afflictions.
His body being thus pure, the seers revere him;
one should go before the Most Honored One, for there are none who do not receive his teaching.
From the white tuft of hair between his brows, he radiates forth its brilliant light.
Covering billions of lands, it eclipses the palaces of Māra so they do not appear.
No one can see its crown; even with the utmost scrutiny, none can behold it.
None is able to gaze upon it, for he has accomplished perfect and true awakening.
Like Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, the sun, moon, Indra, and Brahmā;
the lands and all places of enlightenment, the trees and mountains bow their heads.
Through the power of merit and the power of wisdom, through the power of the sages and the power of diligence.
The power of patience and the power of meditative reflection render the power of Māra powerless to destroy.
Just as a vessel made of unbaked clay is certain to break quickly;
a lion compared to other beasts, or a firefly compared to the sun and moon.
"Seeking a peer, none is found to equal him; is he like a lion or a viper?
When compared with a Bodhisattva, no one of equal rank is seen.
— *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Five.

Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyān’s mind was in turmoil; his countenance changed with terror, yet he forced a smile and would not depart. Unwilling to retreat, he spoke deceitful words:

"What I have done is right. Tell your troops: 'Unite your hearts and act in harmony. All you gods and spirits who can see him must constrain the Bodhisattva and not allow him to be heedless; we shall subdue him together, and only then shall we depart.'"
At that time, Pāpīyān addressed his four daughters—first named Kāmāvatī, second named Rati, third named Darśanī, and fourth named Anuvartinī—and said:
"Go to the Bodhi tree to delude and confuse the Bodhisattva; extol the virtues of sensual desire and destroy his pure conduct."
Upon hearing Māra’s words, the woman went at once to the Bodhi tree and stood before the Bodhisattva, employing thirty-two seductive gestures and words:
"The first was to widen her eyes and play with her pupils."

“The Bodhisattva’s mind is pure, like a bright moon gem without flaw; like the sun first rising to illuminate the world; like a lotus flower in the mud and water that remains unstained; like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be moved; his virtue is lofty and far-reaching, his faculties are tranquil and settled, and his mind is serene, without increase or decrease.”
At that time, the demoness, having well-mastered the arts of feminine illusion and the practice of seduction, went forth with the intent to disturb his path, speaking again:
"Your virtue is most profound and you are revered by the devas; you ought to receive offerings, and for this reason the devas have sent me."

Since we are in the prime of our youth and vigor, and there are no celestial maidens as beautiful as the color of the *utpala* lotus who could compare to us, we wish to rise at dawn and sleep at night to serve you by your side.
The Bodhisattva replied:

“You possess merit from past lives and have obtained this celestial body, yet you do not contemplate impermanence and instead practice seductive charms. Though your physical form is beautiful, your mind is not upright; it is like a painted vase filled with foul poison, destined for its own destruction. What extraordinary fortune is there that cannot endure long?

Your lustful evil and unwholesome conduct will cause you to lose your very foundation. Upon death, you shall fall into the three evil realms and take the form of birds or beasts, making liberation exceedingly difficult.”
"You have come on purpose to disturb the good intentions of others; you are not of pure lineage. Why have you come, carrying this leather bag filled with stench?
Begone! I have no need of you.
Now that you, my mother and the others, are not at peace in the heavens, why have you come here so abruptly?"
The daughters of the Māra-king were transformed into old women; unable to restore themselves, they returned to the Māra’s abode and spoke these verses:
“His precepts are pure and not to be looked upon with ease; In whatever he beholds, he is respectful and free from resentment;
In his observations of dignified conduct, there is no delusion or darkness; His body is subtle and wondrous, composed and orderly.”
Speak quickly of the impurities of women; you have already departed from desire and have nothing to cling to.

Wherever she goes or stays, she appears in the form of a woman; fundamentally pure and prudent, she is wondrously sublime.

Observing his merit, majestic power, and great achievements, having observed the precepts through incalculable kalpas;

"You shall surely subdue my demonic armies and swiftly achieve the Way and its Virtue like the Buddhas of the past;

That which is observed is like a bright pearl-jewel in the void, to which billions of bodhisattvas have gone to pay homage;
its various forms are like exquisite flowers, such as those of the kinnaras, asuras, mountains, and trees.
Though he has thoughts, they are free from conceptualization; all come to make offerings to the One of Ten Powers.
From the mark of merit between his eyebrows, this light shines most brilliantly, illuminating everything far and wide.
In whatever place one dwells, there is no seeking for convenience; that which is fundamentally received is never lost.
Without anger, without defilement, and without possessiveness, one’s every movement and action is always characterized by few desires.

Thereupon, the tree spirit, beholding his majestic spiritual power, was immediately seized with awe. Sustained by the Buddha’s awesome power, they joined together in sincerity to praise the Bodhisattva with sixteen points:
"Now this pure person is most wondrous and sublime, like the moon on the fifteenth day when it is full;
its radiance shines everywhere, like the rising sun illuminating the world."
Like the lush flowering of a tree, there is nothing that does not emit fragrance; his extraordinary marks and various excellences are golden and composed.
His faculties are tranquil and settled, like a lotus flower situated in a bathing pool;
his discourse possesses majesty, being as unique and extraordinary as the roar of a lion.

I still remember the Bodhisattva, walking alone among the forest trees without fear; he who practices what he has cultivated is uniquely honored among men, like Mount Sumeru standing tall in the great ocean, surpassing all and manifesting alone;
as firm and stable as the Iron Ring Mountains rising above all other mountains;
the merit and fame of this Honored One are heard far and near, like water that fully sustains and upholds heaven and earth.
His intention is vast and expansive, yet uniquely distinguished; this mind is limitless, like empty space.
His mind dwells uprightly with a brilliance beyond compare, just as heaven and earth are that which all living beings look up to.
His mind is pure and free from defilement, bringing joy to the myriad people to the utmost degree.
His mind is clear and pure, such that none can perceive its depths; it is that which all sentient beings admire and delight in.
He brings about liberation and possesses transcendent excellence, having completely severed all conceptualizations and mental constructions.
His sovereign power is unsurpassed, like a hook or a chain, such that there is none who does not submit to it.
His practice of diligence is firm in its resolve and nature; he completely resolves all doubts and knots of the various skeptics.

He subdues the hosts of Māra and casts away their weapons, causing them to return to their palaces. This Honored One, through his excellent benefit, attains the ten powers, possessing peerless power and majesty.

The Bodhisattva replied:

"Just as Mount Sumeru cannot be shaken, even if all the multitudes gathered from the ten directions were to fall to the ground, and even if all things—plants and trees—were to become sentient beings and none could incline their hearts [to help], and even if with a single intent one were to exhaust the great ocean, it would not diminish my resolve. Until I have attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall never rise."
The Māra spoke again:

"I am born in the realm of desire; all the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra the Lord of Devas, the Asuras, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Mahoragas, and Garuḍas are my subjects under my authority without exception. You, too, are subject to me—do you now act according to your own will?"
The Bodhisattva replied:

"You, who are the honored one of the realm of desire, consider yourself possessed of majestic spiritual power; yet you are certainly not the truly honored one, for you are not the Honored One of the Dharma. Only he who honors the Way and the Dharma is called the Honored One."

It is not merely that you wish to be honored; even among those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, you are most venerable due to your heavy transgressions, yet you are not a true, upright, and unsurpassed holy sage.
You shall certainly attain Buddhahood and subdue the evil Māra.
The Māra replied again:

"Today this śramaṇa dwells alone amidst these rugged mountains; his desire for such a vow is exceedingly difficult to fulfill. If he wishes to establish what should be practiced, it will now be ruined and lost. By what cause could he attain the Way?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Since you have lost the correct principle, what need is there to ask where you come from?

Not violating the merit of meditative concentration and the bases of psychic power, not losing one's majestic power, and being able to practice with great diligence—this is called the power of vigor. One shall not rise until the Way of the Buddha is accomplished."
"Why does Māra stand before me in such resentment, uttering such coarse and evil words? [The Buddha replied:
"It may be said that he has ceased.

Previously, I was alone in the wilderness, like a single day extinguishing the darkness of the ten directions with the light of many torches; now, accompanied by a great multitude, he appears before me and reveals his countenance."
"I shall press you; rise quickly and depart! Otherwise, I will surely bring harm upon you, manifesting many transformations and causing you to encounter manifold sufferings and hardships.

The Bodhisattva replied:

"Empty space might yet be exhausted; the wind might yet be grasped; men, women, the large, and the small—indeed, even the stainless light of the moon that dispels all darkness might yet fall to the earth."

though they raise up their power, I shall not abandon my host nor give rise to a mind of coarse malice. I have always taken benevolence, compassion, gentleness, and harmony as my foundation.
