All the devas rejoiced and arrived to offer flowers: the unrighteous king was defeated, and the Dharma King prevailed.
Fundamentally derived from the power of equanimity and wisdom, this wisdom can immediately avert all inauspiciousness;
it can even cause enemies to become disciples—one should pay homage to the realization of the four immeasurables.
His face is like the full moon, his demeanor composed; his fame resounds through the ten directions, and his virtue is like a mountain.
It is difficult to find a likeness for the Buddha’s physical marks; one should prostrate before this World-Saving Immortal.

Chapter 19: On Practicing the Path and Meditative Contemplation. In the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance), Chapter Nineteen: On Practicing the Path and Meditative Contemplation, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Bodhisattva sat beneath the Bodhi tree and, having subdued the demonic adversaries, attained Perfect True Enlightenment."
He eradicates the roots of the three poisons—the source of thorns and brambles—so that there are no more seeds of the aggregates, obscurations, or decay arising from conditions.
He is forever free from even the slightest clouding; his manifold thoughts are settled and pure like space.
Possessing courageous vigor without hindrance, he raises the great banner to manifest all things, summoning those from the ten directions to deliver them from the three realms.
Sitting silently beneath a tree, he manifested the four dhyānas to reveal the path of the Way for future learners;

by binding all notions of self with subtle and wondrous supernatural powers, he cast off desires and unwholesome dharmas so that the five hindrances no longer existed; not receiving the five desires, his manifold evils were extinguished of their own accord, and his mindfulness and discernment became clear;
contemplating and observing the unconditioned, like a strong man who has defeated his enemies, his mind was purified as he accomplished the practice of the first dhyāna.

The mind naturally opens and understands, thereby dispelling the impulses of desire; with no evil to attack, one no longer engages in discursive observation. Serene and tranquil, like the conduct of a sage, one extinguishes thoughts through mindfulness and reflection. Just as a spring at the summit of a mountain flows freely from within and overflows outward, such that streams, rain, and floods have no way to enter, one remains still, guarding the One with undistracted focus, thus accomplishing the practice of the Second Dhyāna.

Furthermore, having abandoned thoughts of joy and perceived only desirelessness, neither external likes nor dislikes can enter, nor do they arise within; the mind is upright and the body is at ease. It is like a lotus whose roots remain in the soil while its petals are closed and have not yet opened, with its roots, stems, flowers, and leaves saturated in water; through pure vision of the truth, one accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna.

Having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and being free from the perceptions of sorrow and joy, the mind neither relies on the wholesome nor clings to the unwholesome; with no inclination toward suffering or pleasure, one dwells precisely within that state. Like a person who has bathed until clean and is covered with a fresh, fine white silk cloth—pure both inside and out, without defilement on the surface or within—the breath ceases of its own accord, becoming tranquil and unchanging, thus accomplishing the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
"It is like a potter who, having mixed clay that is well-kneaded and soft, free from grit and pebbles, can fashion any vessel he desires.

So too, one who develops diligence is capable of all things; having attained concentration of mind, they establish great loving-kindness and do not abandon great compassion, while their wisdom and skillful means thoroughly master the essential subtleties."
He thoroughly mastered the practices of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, namely:

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path, beginning again from the end.
Having realized the three liberations and attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), they encounter no obstruction regarding matters of the past, future, or present.
Their transformations and manifestations of dharmas accord with their wishes; without further deliberation, their bodies can fly through the air.
They can divide a single body into a hundred, a thousand, up to hundreds of millions or countless forms, and then cause them to become one again.

He is able to penetrate the earth and pass through stone walls as if they were open space, appearing from one side and then submerging or emerging from another like moving in and out of water. He can emit water and fire from his body; he walks upon water and traverses the void without sinking.

Sitting or lying in mid-air, he is like a bird in flight; while seated, he can reach the heavens and touch the sun and moon with his hand. Standing upright, his body can extend to the Brahma Heaven, appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease.

His eyes can see through all things, and his ears can hear clearly across all distances; he possesses foreknowledge of the physical actions, speech, and thoughts of all devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and even the smallest crawling and wriggling creatures.

Regarding all that is to be recollected, he perceives, hears, and knows them all: those who possess lust and those who are free from lust; those who possess anger and those who are free from anger; those who possess delusion and those who are free from delusion; those who possess craving and those who are free from craving; those who possess great resolve and those who lack great resolve; those who possess internal and external conduct and those who lack such conduct; those who possess mindfulness of the wholesome and those who lack it; those who possess one-pointedness of mind and those who lack it; and those who possess the intention for liberation and those who lack it—he knows them all completely.

"The Bodhisattva contemplates the five realms—gods, humans, hells, animals, and spirits—and clearly distinguishes each one, including the names and surnames of their parents, brothers, wives, children, and relatives from previous lives."

Regarding the affairs of one lifetime, ten lifetimes, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a billion, and countless lifetimes—up to the times when heaven and earth are formed and destroyed, and the time when they become desolate and empty, until they are formed once again—he is able to know, within one eon, ten eons, up to a thousand billion eons and countless eons, the internal and external names, clothing, food, suffering and joy, and the length of life;

where one dies here and is born there, transmigrating through successive destinies; from the very beginning of all bodies experienced throughout successive lives, including their growth, aging, and death, as well as their physical forms, beauty or ugliness, virtue or folly, and suffering or joy—he discerns and knows all this throughout the three realms.

He saw that the spirits of people each follow their own karma to be born within the five destinies: some fall among the hungry ghosts, some among the animals, some become spirits or deities, some are born in the heavens, and some enter human form; some are born into families of noble rank, wealth, and pleasure, while others are born into families of low status, poverty, and meanness.

He knew that sentient beings are deluded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which obscure for them form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they all indulge in the five desires—the forms of the eyes, the sounds of the ears, the fragrances of the nose, the flavors of the tongue, and the sensations of the body—and their mental states are dragged along by craving and desire, deluded by wealth and beauty, longing only for peace and happiness.
"From this arise the roots of all evils, and from evil comes suffering.
One who can sever the habituation to craving and does not follow even a hair’s breadth of lustful thought, and who practices the Eightfold Path, shall extinguish all suffering."
What are the eight?
Right view, right mindfulness, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right intention, and right concentration.
For example, where there is no fuel, there is no fire; it neither burns nor is extinguished. This is called the unconditioned path that transcends the world.

"The Bodhisattva knows for himself that he has abandoned the root of evil and is free from lust, anger, and delusion. Birth and death have been eliminated, the seeds and roots [of existence] have been severed, all calamities and afflictions are gone, what was to be done has been accomplished, and through wisdom, all is fully realized."
When the morning star appeared, he attained great enlightenment and realized the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
At that time, he obtained the ten kinds of supernatural powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas.
The ten powers of a Buddha are as follows:
"The Buddha perceives and knows all things—whether profound, subtle, hidden, or distant; whether possible or impossible, limited or unlimited—with clear and thorough discernment, exactly as they are.
This is the first power."
“The Buddha fully and clearly knows the stages of conduct performed in the past, present, and future, as well as the places where the resulting retributions are received.
This is the second power.
“The Buddha is able to manifest transformations through dhyāna, samādhi, vimokṣa, and samāpatti.”
This is the third power.
"The Buddha discerns each and every distinct thought of devas, humans, and sentient beings.
This is the fourth power."
“The Buddha knows the various kinds of speech of sentient beings as well as the speech that transcends the world;
this is the fifth power.
The Buddha fully and thoroughly understands the immeasurable and diverse dispositions of the world.”
This is the sixth power.
"The Buddha knows the bondage of desire and knows the essential requirements for the practice that leads to liberation from that bondage.
This is the seventh power."
“The Buddha’s wisdom is like the ocean; his eloquent words are immeasurable, and he recollects all that has been experienced throughout past lives.
This is the eighth power.

“The Buddha’s divine eye is pure; he sees people at the moment of death and their subsequent rebirth, and how they receive retribution according to their deeds—whether good or evil, calamity or fortune.”
This is the ninth power.

"The Buddha’s outflows are exhausted and he is no longer bound by attachments; through his divine, true, and sagely wisdom, he has personally realized and witnessed [the truth], thoroughly mastering the practice of the Path and what is to be done. His wisdom is clear and discerning regarding the end of all further birth and death."
These are the ten powers of a Buddha.
As for the four fearlessnesses of a Buddha:
the Buddha’s divine wisdom is perfectly such that there is nothing he does not know or see.
Fools are deluded by words and do not fully understand the Buddha;
even the Brahmās, Māras, and various sages are unable to discourse upon the Buddha’s wisdom. Therefore, he walks alone without fear.
This is the first fearlessness:
"The Buddha possesses the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) and knows it all.
Yet, deluded and confused people say that the Buddha's outflows are not yet exhausted."
As for the Brahmās, Māras, and the assembly of sages, none are able to discuss the Buddha’s wisdom; thus he walks alone without fear.
This is the second fearlessness.
"The Buddha has preached the sutras and precepts, which are recited and practiced throughout the world."
The deluded and confused say among themselves that the Buddha’s scriptures can be exhausted;
yet, as for the Brahmās, Māras, and the assembly of sages, none are able to debate or disparage the Buddha’s true scriptures—therefore, he walks alone without fear.
This is the third fearlessness.
The Buddha manifests the meaning of the Path, declaring it true and essential, capable of delivering one from suffering and calamity.
Those who are deluded and confused say that it cannot deliver one from suffering; [the Buddha's fearlessness lies in his ability to overcome such challenges].
As for the Brahmās, Māras, and the assembly of sages, none are able to debate the Buddha’s true reality; thus, he wanders everywhere without fear—this is the fourth fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
"The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*):"
From the attainment of Buddhahood until entering Nirvana, he possesses three qualities: first, no loss of the Way;
second, no empty words;
third, no forgetting of his resolve.
4. There is no lack of tranquility of mind.
5. There is no diversity of perceptions.
6. There is no lack of introspection.
7. No impairment in the attainment of one’s resolve;
8. No impairment in diligence;
9. No impairment in meditative concentration.
10. Wisdom is undiminished.
11. Liberation is undiminished.
12. The knowledge and vision of liberation is undiminished.
13. He fully knows and sees the events of past ages.
14. He fully knows and sees the events of future ages.
15. He fully knows and sees the events of the present age.
16. To gather the various bodily activities and transform them through the primordial limit.
17. To gather the various verbal activities and transform them through the primordial limit.
18. To gather the various mental activities and transform them through the primordial limit.
These are the eighteen unique qualities.
When the Buddha attained the mind of the Way and possessed all-knowing vision, he sat and reflected to himself:
"This reality is truly subtle, difficult to know, difficult to clarify, and exceedingly hard to attain."
It is lofty and unsurpassed, vast and limitless; it is profound and bottomless, deep and unfathomable.
It encompasses heaven and earth in its greatness, yet enters the infinitesimal gaps in its subtlety.
Long ago, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he prophesied that I would become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni.
Now that I have finally attained this fruit, which was sought through diligent toil over incalculable kalpas, it is only now that it has been realized.

Reflecting upon my past lives and all that I practiced—virtue, the Way, compassion, filial piety, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and trustworthiness; loyalty, rectitude, and the preservation of truth; learning from the sages with a vacant mind; practicing gentleness and purity of intent through the six perfections of giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; exercising the four immeasurable minds of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; responding appropriately to the four thoughts; nurturing all sentient beings as if loving an only child; serving the Buddhas and accumulating immeasurable merit—I see that the diligent toil and labors of many kalpas have not been in vain, for I have now obtained them all.
Nanda sighed to himself and said:
"Now I realize that the Buddha is most supreme; having abandoned lust, he is pure and without outflows.
He is able to lead all beings, and those who follow him will surely be joyful."
"The reward for heavenly merit is swift; all sublime vows have been fulfilled.
Having attained the supreme tranquility with agility, I shall now pass into *nirvāṇa*. Chapter 20:

The Devas Celebrate the Buddha’s Attainment of Enlightenment *The Sūtra of Universal Radiance* At that time, the daughter of the Heavenly King of the Realm of Desire saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath the tree. By means of his supernormal powers, he had reached the fulfillment of his vows; he had subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies, raised the great banners and pennants, and as the Great Benevolent One, acted as a Great Physician-King to heal the ailments of all beings.

The Boundless Lion does not experience the bristling of body hair even amidst fear; he harmonizes the mind, extinguishes the three impurities, and achieves the three types of supernormal knowledge to transcend the four torrents.
Grasping the canopy of the One Path, he rescues and protects the triple world. As a pure brahmin, he abandons all evils; as a bhikṣu, he eliminates all ignorance and darkness.
What is meant by a śramaṇa?
One who transcends the six paths, whose extensive learning is boundless—this is called "vast erudition.
Through virtue, one eliminates worldly toil and becomes courageous, crossing over to the other shore.
As for what is called "power," it refers to the complete possession of the Dharma-treasure consisting of the ten powers.
Seeing the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree,
he praised him with these verses:
"Now beneath the Bodhi tree, he has subdued the hosts of Māra;
as immovable as Mount Sumeru, he is fearless and has nothing to relinquish."
For countless billions of kalpas, they practiced giving, precepts, and wisdom;
for countless billions of kalpas, they gathered and applied themselves to the meaning of the Path.
Their conduct eclipsed that of Śakra and Brahmā, for they originally set out to seek the Buddha-way.
Having practiced patience for incalculable eons, He was able to endure all manner of suffering and affliction.
Therefore his radiance is the color of purple gold;
Through practicing diligence for incalculable eons, He transcended the perils of birth and death, And thereby subdued Māra.
For countless billions of kalpas, he practiced dhyāna, supernatural powers, and wisdom;
he served countless Buddhas, and for this reason, he receives manifold offerings.
For countless billions of kalpas, he has maintained sincerity and cultivated vast wisdom.
Protecting billions of sentient beings, he therefore swiftly attains Buddhahood;
having subdued the demon of the body and likewise departed from the demon of death;
having removed the demon of the dust of desire, he thus attains freedom from sorrow and affliction.
He is the God among Gods, served and honored by all the devas;
revered and sustained by the three realms, he is an immeasurable field of merit.
He completely transcends all sounds and voices; meeting the Buddha, he becomes a source of manifold blessings.
None are able to look upon him, even as he sits at the site of enlightenment.
The mark between his eyebrows shines radiantly across countless billions of Buddha-lands;
it completely eclipses the light of the sun and moon, causing all beings to attain the illumination of the Way.
Most exquisite among the upright, with a complexion foremost of all;
endowed with the marks and signs, he compassionately regards the multitudes, and is honored by those in the three realms.
His eyes are exceedingly pure, beholding countless Buddhas.
The bodies of sentient beings throughout the lands, and all that is conceived within their minds—
his mind is exceedingly pure, and he hears countless sounds:
the words of devas and humans, and the resonance of the Buddha’s teachings.
Now having obtained a broad and long tongue, he speaks with gentle words at the proper time;
you should listen to this True Dharma and reach the nectar of the unconditioned.
Having beheld the hosts of Māra’s army, his mind rejoices and is not terrified.
Furthermore, he saw all the devas and humans, who were as joyless as Mount Sumeru;
beholding the hosts of Māra’s armies, he remained unmoved and unshaken;
though they harbored harmful intentions, he subdued them through his heroic power.
Seated without shifting, his body did not sway;
neither joyful nor angry, he faced the moment without difficulty.
For all the devas and the people of the world, this was the attainment of a sublime benefit.
Having heard the True Dharma, he immediately practiced it with utmost sincerity.
Always established in meritorious deeds, he received the most supreme blessings;
whatever he undertook was swiftly accomplished, as he stood in silent tranquility as a hero among men.
The Honored One among Men, the Guide, having attained Perfect Enlightenment,
shook billions of lands and subdued the hosts of Māra.
His voice was like that of Brahmā and also like the cry of a sorrowful phoenix.
Fame and fragrance are foremost; thus has Gautama spoken.
The retribution of merit is the most secure, removing all afflictions and distress.
Whatever one aspires to will surely be accomplished; such a person possesses merit.
Swiftly attaining the Way of the Buddha, one then subdues the hosts of Māra;
immediately returning to the state of coolness, one enters parinirvāṇa through tranquility.
Therefore, what person of merit would ever grow weary of establishing such practice?
Having heard the Dharma of the Deathless, who would ever grow weary?
Dwelling amidst the forest thickets, who would harbor thoughts of retreat?
To bring benefit to the myriad people, one should practice with diligent perseverance.
Following the conduct of a Bodhisattva, they take refuge in humanity;
through the offerings they perform, each establishes their own land.
Level as the palm of a hand or a clear mirror, they dwell constantly upon that ground.
A hundred thousand lotus flowers with a hundred petals each spontaneously emerge in brilliant splendor;
hundreds of billions of devas come to behold the Buddha’s place of enlightenment;
all this arises from their own meritorious deeds, as boundless as the great ocean.
Having subdued the power of Māra and attained the gateway to the nectar of the Dharma,
they all prostrate in worship and take refuge in the Tathāgata;
with various pure offerings, each holding incense and canopies.
Having beheld the Lion, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual transformations,
they then give rise to the bodhisattva mind; that which they abide in cannot be shaken,
and their renown is such that it is as immeasurable as the ocean.
As firm as Mount Sumeru, the king among all mountains;
With ten fingers joined in salutation, a Brahma-voice issues from the void.
The Sage among men is likewise so: seated upon the lion throne, he remains steadfast.
Hundreds of thousands of trees bowed their branches toward the site of enlightenment;
hundreds of thousands of rays of light shook billions of lands,
extinguishing all evil realms and bringing peace to every hardship.
None can surpass him; all who are ill receive healing.
This one is the Ultimate Truth among men, seated upon the lion throne.
The Buddha’s majestic spiritual transformations are like the radiance of a bright pearl.
Naturally there was a radiant splendor, like the brilliance of the sun and moon.
From between his eyebrows, he emitted a great light, a radiance manifested at that moment;
it shone universally throughout the three realms, yet none were able to see the crown of the Buddha’s head.
The Hero among Men, thus seated upon the lion throne,
manifested miraculous transformations such that all who came beheld them.
As they reverently honored the Buddha with serene minds, the earth shook in six ways.
Even if one does not lay down their weapons, skillful means can move many;
yet if one does not lay down their arms, they shall encounter manifold poisonous afflictions.
The Honored One, like a lion, while seated, manifests such responsive transformations.

Thereupon, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, the Brahmakāyika devas, the Subrahma devas, and the son of Māra named Kāmapathin went to where the Buddha was. Holding a great precious parasol, they offered it to the Buddha and, with palms joined, praised him in verse:
“The Benevolent Honored One appears before our eyes; By the power of his diligence, meditation, and wisdom, While in the midst of Māra he displayed great eloquence, And the Sage has now subdued him.”
Though countless billions of Māras came to seek the destruction of Sarvārthasiddha, he did not rise from his seat nor stir;
I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Universal Pervasiveness.
Even as many as the sands of the Ganges cannot equal the Supreme Honored One.
Nothing can shake him, even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He has performed hundreds of thousands of millions of sacrifices for the sake of the Way;
no one dares to disparage this capable man, whose conduct is unattainable.
There were those who once gave away their wives and children, Their sons, daughters, and servants;
Gardens, parks, kingdoms, and cities, Kingship and all manner of adornments.
They gave their hands, feet, and even their heads, As well as everything within their bodies.
Because he practices the Way, his benevolence and compassion are never deluded.
Just as he speaks with his mouth, his words never change;
the Buddha, free from attachment and of great capacity, shall deliver countless multitudes.
For billions of eons, you have crossed the surging currents through the power of meditative concentration and spiritual feet;
having subdued all with the pure and correct Dharma, may you vow to fully deliver all sentient beings.
Bestowing eyes upon the world’s blindness and darkness, may you cause all to be universally harmonious.
With single-minded resolve, he aspired for universal wisdom, Gathering all merits to take refuge in the Honored Guide.
His aspiration was boundless, such that none failed to offer praise;
Thus he subdued the hosts of Māra and awakened to all-encompassing wisdom.
"Having thus praised the Buddha, the son of Māra withdrew to stand to one side.

Thereupon, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Yāma, and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, as well as the Four Great Kings, the gods of the celestial vault, and the earth-deity gods, all made offerings to the World-Honored One, adorning him everywhere."
Throughout the entire world, flowers were scattered and incense was burned; banners and canopies were raised as they took refuge in the Supreme Honored One, praising him with these verses:
“The gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations, The gods of the Heaven of Delight and Tuṣita;
The Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, and Cāturmahārājika gods— All have come to make offerings to the Buddha.”
Firm as a diamond, dwelling within the three thousandfold world;
his will is so strong it cannot be destroyed, as he abides correctly in the Buddha’s place of enlightenment.
Even if his flesh and skin should waste away, and his marrow be exhausted until nothing remains;
If I do not achieve the Way of the Buddha, I shall never rise from this seat.
You, O Lion of Benevolence, speak with righteousness;
throughout all the three thousand worlds, I vow to manifest my majestic spiritual power so that even the grasses and trees shall become my army.
Arousing great, boundless compassion, they come to where the Bodhisattva is;
I govern billions of lands, level and free from all difficulties.
We gods of the various grounds have all come together to obtain this excellent benefit.
And even were he to command the Most Honored One to lift his foot and tread upon me;
that one who is valiant in the world, whose light illuminates all things—
how much more so would he protect the three thousandfold world system, let alone a single body?
Below, hundreds of thousands of koṭis, all of a single class;
universally delivering all sentient beings, this shall be the foundation of what is to be done.
We shall protect this ground, extending throughout the three thousandfold world-system.
May all attain their supreme aspirations, obtaining whatever food and drink they desire.
If there are those who transgress the boundaries, may they find peace and security wherever they are;
so too for the sons of the Buddhas and the śrāvakas of Gautama.
"When the Way and the Dharma are proclaimed, if there are those who hear them,
they shall all encourage and assist in the Buddha-way— the root of all virtues.

Having thus made offerings to and praised the Buddha, the Brahmā gods, the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), the gods of the Heaven of No More Strife (Yāmā), the Tuṣita gods, the Yama gods, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Four Heavenly Kings, the gods of the space-dwelling heavens, and the earth-dwelling gods each withdrew to stand to one side.
*Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 21: Contemplating the Tree.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Having attained perfect enlightenment, all the devas came and offered praise to the Buddha."

The Tathāgata sat upright with a single mind, gazing at the tree without blinking his eyes; taking the joy of dhyāna as food and liberating wisdom as drink, he remained eternally peaceful and free from calamity.
For seven nights and days, he contemplated the Bodhi tree of the site of enlightenment to repay its kindness.

After seven days had passed, the gods of the desire realm each brought ten thousand jars of scented water; the gods of the form realm did likewise. They went to where the Buddha was and washed him with the scented water, bathing the Buddha for the first time with various kinds of incense.

The devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas used perfumed water to bathe the body of the Tathāgata; the overflowing scented water sprinkled upon all these beings, and by the grace of this fragrance, they all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that time, all sentient beings were suffused with the fragrance, which did not leave their bodies; meanwhile, the sons of the gods returned to their palaces and could no longer perceive any other scent.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There was a son of heaven named Puhua (Viśva-nirmāṇa), who prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, rose to his feet with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'During the seven days that the Buddha sat beneath the tree, you remained in samādhi; what is the name of that concentration?'"
The World-Honored One replied:
"This concentration is called 'the food of joy. By means of this concentration of the mind on the food of joy, the Tathāgata gazed at the tree day and night for seven days without blinking."
Then the Devaputra Puhua praised the Buddha with a verse:
“Constantly practicing all deeds, Through the majestic power of the words of joy and tranquility,
He causes Māra to lose his path, And casts himself down, bowing his head to the Buddha.”
Taking refuge at the Buddha’s feet with a joyful heart,
the sons of the gods then spoke these words on the dispersal of all mental constructs.
Those gods and humans who are established in tranquil concentration— if they know this lineage;
Thus, having exhausted lust, anger, and delusion, his wisdom is bottomless.
He eliminates the doubts of devas and humans: for what reason does he possess the ten powers?
Thoroughly understanding the ten directions, he has reached the perfection of all dharmas.
Out of compassion, he remained for seven days, his resolve as vast as space;
sitting firm and unmoving, he gazed at the tree with unblinking eyes.
Why did that Honored One among lions sit thus for seven days?
And observing this tree, why is it so silent and traceless?
It is because of the original vow he established: "I shall be a lion for all beings.
Due to the fulfillment of that original vow, he sits beneath the tree and does not rise.
Bestowing with the mind of the World-Honored One, dwelling in peace in the present;
thus the Honored One of Ten Powers follows and practices all the teachings.
He knows the beginning and end of devas and humans, as well as the vows made in previous lives.
Having heard the teachings of the sūtras, he constantly practiced their instructions.
Such were his ten powers and his fearlessnesses, fully perfected;
therefore, he sat for seven days without rising from his seat.
The courageous one is able to contemplate them all and subdue everything;
sitting equanimously at the site of enlightenment, he extinguishes all worldly defilements.
Being pure and reaching the furthest distance, he thereby brings peace to all sentient beings.
Therefore, one should leave the household life and practice the true and correct Dharma.
Having attained freedom from all defilements, one will forever be without fear;
thus becoming a member of the Noble Assembly, one does not commit unrighteous deeds.
One who can endure the existence of affectionate ties, as well as all ignorance and formations;
who cuts off the root of all fetters and regards them as mere dust;
who perceives through the perspective of long duration, thereby conceiving of a self—[such a one is truly wise].
The universal bases dwell amidst the hindrances; I know how to sever and eliminate them entirely.
Having long accumulated this practice, I have mastered the discipline for delusion;
having brought all hindrances to their ultimate end, I have removed the notion of self through wisdom.
Having severed desire, ill-will, and resentment, for sentient beings dwelling in ignorance and darkness—like the moon reflected in water—I have subdued them so that nothing remains.
This practice is free from confusion; it is simply liberation within the mind itself.
From antiquity until now, all [suffering] has been utterly severed and extinguished.
You who are present here, fallen into the fire-pit through evil delusion—
may the Buddha pull you out so that nothing remains, and you shall never again pass through this.
By removing all hindrances and obscurations, one bestows the root of their extinction;
by eliminating the four inversions, one cures and removes them without remainder.
These various marks of mindfulness are defilements; he who knows them understands the root of the sūtras and the Dharma.
The Master commands their total extinction, Turning them back so that none remain.
There are sixty-five bodily sufferings, And thirty impurities among the past;
There are forty in the present— At the site of enlightenment, all these are severed.
There are sixteen births, eighteen teachings currently manifest;
these constitute twenty-five, which are severed at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
There are twelve treasures of the noble ones (ārya) and twenty-eight fears of men.
I have transcended these karmas, crossing over by the power of diligence.
Through awakening, I am a non-returner, having discerned five hundred matters;
I have fully mastered the hundreds of thousands of dharmas of the past.
These fetters are forever exhausted—the ninety-eight roots and sources;
all possible bases of existence upon which sentient beings rely and receive [rebirth];
the doubts regarding habitual tendencies, and the net of ignorance and false views.
"Exhaust the four rivers of defilement, so that they may no longer hold one in their power.
"The World-Honored One has preached the Dharma and proclaimed his teachings; one should abandon flattery, the notion of self, and greed."

Vast and expansive in his resolve, he takes pity on the weariness of worldly toil; through the correct teaching of the Vinaya, he uproots all greed, and with his feet, he eliminates all deviant conduct.
He practices the true and right, removing all clamor and noise; through diligence, he attains the limit of Nirvana.

Now, being free from the notion of self, he brings forth the merit of dhyāna and a concentrated mind; crossing over the four torrents, he extinguishes the karma of sorrow, fetters, arrogance, and heedlessness, subduing these matters so that they are forever exhausted.
Because it is true and authentic, one brings forth a concentrated mind to restrain all defilements, eliminating all false imaginings as if uprooting a tree by its roots.

The mind transcends to the other shore, severing all traces of their abode so that nothing remains; thus one utters the lion’s roar with immense power, attaining sovereignty over the three realms without a master.
All objective realms are extinguished, and with the wisdom of dhyāna, one cuts away enmity and hardship, just as the Lord of Devas causes his net of manifold sins to be utterly exhausted.
By means of the thirty-six practices of diligence, one abides within the stages; with the military force of wisdom, one cuts off and severs all craving.

These various roots—the attachments of worldly toil—are investigated as the source of bitter poison; by the power of the light of wisdom, one seeks to bring them to eternal extinction, and with this eye of wisdom, one skillfully treats the fundamental purity.

Those who are truly human clarify the power of medicine to treat their ignorance; they cause the vast and far-reaching tree of delusion to have no root, and thus they practice with sincerity within this realm.

With focused mind, destroy the dead snake of hatred; when the mind and its thoughts differ, they become enemies and thieves. I have dried up the twelve seas and extinguished the smoke and fire of objective conceptualization to manifest the brilliance of the three types of supernormal knowledge.
It extinguishes the blazing flames of all defilements and delights in the gates of liberation to eliminate all blemishes; such is its instruction.

It consoles all beings by removing the perception of thorns and brambles; it is empty and soundless, yet it understands through diligence the pursuit of purity, like fire produced by rubbing wood together, and like a spring source, its mind is profoundly still.

Using the power of wisdom to plunder the dust and defilements of the mind, and harboring a concentrated intent—this is called "holding the banner. Upholding the instructions, one is able to understand them for oneself.
Subduing contentious matters and harboring a compassionate heart, one recognizes true nobility and wealth through these five desires.
Abiding in all practices, one abandons flattery and deceit; that which arises from the root as dust constitutes the hindrance of the various fetters.
When there is strife and discord, I thoroughly investigate and master them to bring about samādhi-concentration.
Fully knowing internal matters, one establishes a sense of shame and remorse; whether in states of perception or non-perception, from this one attains and fully acquires these practices.
Thoroughly investigating all that exists, one casts off all conceptualizations and every fetter; such a practitioner abandons them without remainder, subduing them through the power of diligence.

Possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge and the gates of liberation, for this reason, one does not harbor thoughts of inferiority toward those without such conditions; nor does one falsely conceive of suffering, pleasure, and impermanence as "self," thereby creating conceptualizations that seek the root of the six sense-decays.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he completely severed all these impermanent, vast, desolate, and turbid matters. Through holy wisdom and penetration, he extinguished all cravings and desires;
surpassing the sun and moon in his transcendence of such passions, he dwelt in the void and attained mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge.
His countenance was immeasurable as he crossed over birth and death, rescuing and severing the great ocean of existence; by the power of his diligence, he transcended lust, anger, and delusion.

By means of subtle and wondrous conduct, they sever the notion of self; through the six perfections, they eliminate billions of afflictions. Regarding the direct suffering of birth and death, they take pity on beings and bring their mental activity to rest.

Thus, they aspire to sever both past and future, remaining free from the two pitfalls, and attain the equality of the infinite perfections. Having reached the nectar of immortality, they leave nothing behind as they exhaust the very roots of birth and death.

Therein, there are neither the four great elements nor the various sense bases; seeking the jewels of wisdom, one attains them in incalculable numbers. Through the radiance of the jewel of the Way, one reaches fearlessness; these immeasurable Buddhas attain peace within, having few desires and discerning the fundamental source as being like an illusion.

"What was practiced in previous lives I have fully understood; because for billions of kalpas I have sincerely bestowed countless jewels and ambrosia, I have mastered this learning. I delight in gentle conduct and have heard the teachings of billions of nayutas of dharmas throughout the world; furthermore, I have analyzed dependent origination as being both entirely arising and entirely empty."

In the mere instant that the mind arises, it is understood to be like a wild horse; this is my purity, and my eyes are clear and excellent, surpassing all sentient beings of the ten directions. I observe things as clearly as one’s own palm, just like the fruits produced on a tree from seeds planted in the past; thus I have attained understanding through what was experienced in previous lives.

Throughout billions of kalpas of the various *pāramitās*, he has fully understood the manifold awakenings from the dream-like thoughts [of sentient beings]; regarding the inverted karmas that past devas have contested and contemplated, those were thus, and these are likewise so.

At that time, I went forth to the practice of the medicine of immortality; the reason I practiced the power of compassion through the ten powers was out of pity for sentient beings, thus exercising the power of compassion.

Now my father dwells in the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*); the reason he exercises the power of pity and compassion through the ten powers to convert and transform all beings is to cause me to dwell within the midst of this nectar.
By constantly practicing the power of protection, one subdues all [adversaries] and, through this transformation, leads them into the deathless realm (*amṛta-pada*).

Because one practices sympathetic joy (*muditā*) universally to bring delight to all, one subdues all by means of this power of joy; therefore, one establishes oneself within the state of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Recalling ten directions’ worth of eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I beheld past Buddhas and made offerings to them; for this reason, I abide within the realm of ambrosia.

Regarding my original vow and what I have spoken with both mind and mouth: until I have subdued Māra, transformed those with false views, and reached the other shore without rising from my seat, remaining free from negligence;

until I have destroyed the net of delusion, dwelt in the wisdom-vajra for countless eons, attained the ten powers and reached non-attachment, and subdued all outflows so that none remain—until then, I shall not relinquish this power nor rise from my seat.

Fully endowed with the purification of turbid defilements through bathing, at that time the World-Protector, possessing the ten powers and sovereign mastery, traversed the infinite trichiliocosm. Like a diamond, he constantly cultivated equanimous conduct; billions of koṭis of devas made immeasurable offerings, as did innumerable celestial maidens beyond all reckoning.

O Son of the Buddha, all these have their causes and conditions: they occupy the seats of the worthy and holy, receive great sovereignty, and wash the world-protectors with thousands of precious jars filled with various fragrant waters; by this means, they attain mastery over the three thousandfold world system.
O Son of the Buddha, all such things have their causes and conditions. This is why he did not rise from his seat for seven days and nights, but constantly observed the tree.
During those seven days and nights of gazing upon the Bodhi tree, he transformed seven thousand *koṭis* of people, causing them to resolve upon the Way and contemplate in profound stillness.

The earth shook in six ways; at that time, the Buddha rose from his lion throne, his mind peaceful and composed and his body supple. Knowing the proper time for his conduct, he was at the site of the Buddha’s enlightenment; he gazed upon the Bodhi tree as if it were a lion, free from all fear, contemplating the gates of dhyāna and the noble practices of the sages.

Chapter 22: The Merchants Presenting the Gruel; according to some versions, this is titled "The Four Heavenly Kings Offering the Alms Bowl. At that time, Trapuṣa, Bhallika, and their companions, five hundred merchants in all, were traveling together. At that moment, the trees were lush with flowers and fruit, and they emitted the voice of the Buddha, remaining unmoved and unshaken for seven days.

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Śikhin who, dwelling in the Brahma-heaven, saw that the Buddha had newly attained the Way and had sat joyfully for seven days without anyone yet having offered him food.
"I shall seek out people and have them provide food for the Buddha.
He then caused five hundred merchants to all stumble and be unable to proceed.
This was because Śikhandin recognized these merchants as his acquaintances from five hundred previous lives; desiring to deliver them, he acted in this manner.
When Trapusa and Bhallika were returning in fear, they deliberated together with the crowd.
At that very moment, a deity praised them in verse, saying:
"The Tathāgata has realized the Way of the Buddha; All his vows have been fully fulfilled."
"You have offered this food; by this cause, the Wheel of Dharma shall be turned.
At that time, the five hundred men went to the place of the tree deity. Brahmā manifested as the tree, appearing with a brilliant and distinct radiance, and said:

"In this world, there is a Buddha currently in the realm of Kuru, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River. No one has yet brought him food. It would be fortunate for you all to first be able to give with a benevolent heart; you will surely obtain great merit."
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the merchants were all greatly delighted and said,
"The Buddha must surely be uniquely and most venerable, revered by the heavenly deities, and not of ordinary caliber.
They then mixed parched grain with honey and together prostrated themselves beneath the tree to offer it to the Buddha.
The Buddha thought:

"The Buddhas of antiquity took pity on those who offered alms; their law was to always carry an alms-bowl. It is not fitting that I should receive food directly in my hands like the practitioners of other paths.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, upon Mount Pāṇa, obtained four alms-bowls made of blue stone, intending to eat from them.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Jyotirviśuddha who said to the Heavenly King:
"There is now a Buddha named Śākyamuni; he should use this bowl, for it is not a vessel for you. He is about to receive food, so you should go and offer it to him."

Thereupon, the Four Kings, together with the deva-sons, carrying flowers, incense, music, banners, canopies, and the alms-bowl, descended to the Buddha’s presence as quickly as one extends or contracts their arm. Each of the Four Heavenly Kings took the bowl they held and offered it collectively to the Buddha.
The Buddha thought:
"If I accept one, it will displease the others; therefore, I shall accept them all.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra offered his first, and the Buddha accepted it, then spoke this verse for him:
“Now I present this vessel to the World-Honored One; may I obtain the vessel of the Honored Dharma.
Having attained the bowl of tranquility myself, may my mind never forget it.”
Then King Virūḍhaka next offered a bowl; the Buddha accepted it immediately and spoke this verse:
“If one offers a vessel to the Tathāgata, The mind shall never again be deluded;
The Four Heavenly Kings will protect and guard them, Until they attain the cool awakening.”
Then King Virūḍhaka next offered a bowl. The Buddha accepted it and spoke this verse:
"Because he has given a pure vessel, And with a pure mind bestowed it upon the Tathāgata;
His body and mind shall always be light and agile, Praised by devas, nāgas, and spirits."
Then King Vaiśravaṇa followed by offering a bowl. The Buddha accepted it and spoke this verse:
“The Buddha’s precepts are without flaw; I accept this vessel of perfect integrity.
The faithful donor is free from distracted mind, So that virtue may never diminish.”

After the Buddha had accepted the bowls, he stacked them in his left hand and pressed down upon them with his right hand; they immediately merged into one, yet the four rims remained visible. He then uttered this verse of praise:
"In my previous lives, I gave alms-bowls, And thus there is this karmic fruit;
Now I have obtained these four vessels, Brought forth by the supernormal power of the Four Kings."
After the Buddha had finished reciting these verses of praise, he took the merchant’s bowl of parched grain and honey.
He then offered a blessing for the merchant, saying:

“May this present offering cause those who eat it to obtain full physical strength; may it cause the donor’s family to fulfill their wishes in every lifetime, obtaining longevity, beauty, power, vision, and joy; may they be peaceful, healthy, and free from illness; may they obtain eloquence and wisdom; and may they preserve their years of life until the end, such that no malevolent spirits or demons can harass or approach them, because they have harbored kind intentions and established the roots of virtue.”
All benevolent spirits shall constantly protect them, revealing the stages of the Path so that they may obtain benefit and favorable conditions, and never suffer setbacks or distress.
Free from further hardships and afflictions, those who perceive the truth shall regard it with faith, joy, and reverence, remaining pure and free of regret.

For one who bestows upon those of moral virtue, their merit shall cover the heavens; whatever they achieve will be increasingly superior, auspicious, and free from all adversity. The sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, celestial deities, and kings of ghosts shall constantly follow, protect, and assist them.

The Four Great Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Kuvera in the north—will bestow special favor upon virtuous people; they shall protect you all so that you do not encounter untimely calamities.

If one possesses a wise mind to investigate and refine their learning, reveres the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, abandons all evils, and does not indulge in self-indulgence, they will ultimately receive auspiciousness.

By planting merit one obtains merit; by practicing the Path one attains the Path. Having already seen the Buddha first and having single-mindedly received and honored him, one shall thereby bring about the foremost merit.
"May you obtain blessings in this present life, swiftly realize the vision of the Truth, constantly enjoy wealth and joy, and personally attain Nirvana.
Having heard these words of benediction, they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

When the Buddha had finished eating, he cast his bowl into the air. A devaputra named Subrahma immediately caught it; this bowl was unimpeded, and he carried it up to the Brahma Heaven, where billions of Brahmas all made offerings to it together, circumambulating it to the right in reverent service.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, whose virtues are peerless, praised their meritorious achievements, declaring that by virtue of these roots of merit, in a future age, these merchants shall attain Buddhahood, being named Mṛdvīkābhisambhava Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, the Guide bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon them without limit; thereafter, he transformed countless bodhisattvas, and those who received the prediction became non-retrogressive on the path to Buddhahood.

Upon hearing that the Buddha had granted them their prediction of enlightenment, they leaped for joy; at that time, the brothers joined their palms in self-surrender and together offered up their very lives to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Tathāgata had fully attained perfect enlightenment, he used his supernormal powers to move his seat to the stone chamber."

Reflecting upon my original vow to deliver sentient beings, I contemplate that birth and death fundamentally arise from the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). When conditions arise from phenomena (*dharma*), there is birth and death; when phenomena cease, birth and death are exhausted. Because one acts thus oneself, one experiences this result; if one does not act thus, it comes to rest.

The minds of all sentient beings constitute their spirits; these spirits are profound and dark, vague and indistinct, and formless. From them arise perceptions and thoughts, which follow along as they receive physical bodies.

The body has no permanent master, and the spirit has no permanent form. The spirit-mind undergoes transformations that are agitated and turbid, difficult to clarify; it arises and ceases of its own accord, never resting.
One thought departs and another arrives, like grass and trees swept by a current, or like bubbles upon the water; as one perishes, another immediately arises.

As for the three realms—the desire, form, and formless realms—and the nine abodes where spirits dwell, they are all bound to consciousness; one cannot escape suffering. In a state of dull obscurity and darkness, one remains unaware of it oneself; therefore, this is called delusion (*moha*), wherein one knows nothing of the essential path.
The Way is supremely subtle, empty, still, and free from thought; it cannot be known by the ordinary worldly mind.

There are ninety-six kinds of worldly paths and arts, each adhering to their own objects of worship—who knows how deluded they are? All of them delight in life, seek security, crave desires, relish flavors, and take pleasure in sounds and forms; therefore, they are unable to find joy in the Buddha-way.

The Buddha-way is pure and devoid of anything substantial; when one calculates the body and all things, they cannot be found to exist eternally. Even if one were to preach that heaven and earth are impermanent, that the world is entirely suffering, and that the body is not "mine," who could believe this teaching of emptiness and non-existence?
The Buddha intended to remain silent and not preach the Dharma to the world, and he entered a state of meditative concentration.

A light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows shone upward upon Śakra, Lord of Devas. Knowing that the Buddha did not wish to preach the sutra, Śakra felt sorrowful, thinking that the three realms were all destined for long-term decline; since they could not know the path to transcend the world, they would fall into the three evil paths upon death—when would they ever be liberated?

It has been a long time since the world last had a Buddha; a Buddha is as difficult to encounter as the *uḍumbara* flower. Now, I shall plead for the lives of all people in the world, entreating the Buddha with compassion to preach the Dharma.
He was about to lead Pañcaśikha down to the stone chamber.
The Buddha, entering this state of meditative concentration, instructed Pañcaśikha to play the lute and sing of the virtues of the Buddha’s original vows, extolling them with these verses:
“Listen to my song of the Ten Powers, Who has cast off hindrances and dwells in tranquil dhyāna;”
His light shines through the seven heavens, and the fragrance of his virtue is like sandalwood.
The Supreme Deity arrives in divine majesty, praising and yearning to behold the Honored One;
Brahmā and Śakra, bearing respectful hearts, bow their heads, desiring to receive and hear [his teaching].
The fundamental practices and vows of the Buddha were cultivated with diligence through a hundred kalpas;
through the four immeasurables and great giving, the ten directions received his vast grace.
His observance of the precepts was pure and stainless, and he protected all sentient beings with kindness and gentleness.
With courageous wisdom, he entered the meditative knowledge; with great compassion, he spread the sutras of deliverance.
Having accumulated ascetic practices for countless eons, his meritorious achievements were perfected this day;
through the power of precepts, patience, concentration, and wisdom, he shook the earth and subdued Māra.
His virtue encompasses heaven and earth; his divine wisdom surpasses that of the Celestial Sovereign.
His marks and signs are uniquely peerless; his eightfold voice resounds through the ten directions.
His resolve is loftier than Mount Sumeru; his purity and subtlety are beyond compare.
Forever free from lust, anger, and delusion, No longer subject to the afflictions of old age and death.
We pray that you arise from meditative concentration out of compassion, Taking pity on all devas and humans;
Bestow upon us the treasure of the Dharma-treasury, And spread the precious nectar of wisdom.
May they be liberated from sorrow and fear, finding peace amidst peril and distress;
may those who are deluded see the true path, and those with false doubts behold the sublime words.
May all desire and delight in them, listening and receiving them without ever wearying.
"I shall now open the Dharma of Immortality, extending its transformation to infinity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, conforming to worldly customs, thought to himself:

"This Dharma is exceedingly profound; that which it enters is limitless. Having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, it is tranquil, subtle, and wondrous—difficult to reach and difficult to know. It is not what the mind can conceive, nor what speech can fully express; it is beyond the reach of either ordinary beings or sages."
All instructions cannot be practiced; by abiding in their fundamental source, one reaches extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding all that is encountered, there is ultimately no attachment, even unto the coolness of the ultimate non-arising.
No locus can be found, for all is non-existent; thus one transcends the six realms.

Without ideation, without aspiration, without acquisition, and without speech; without sound, without instruction, and without the accumulation of anything; with all conditioned phenomena stilled, one arrives at the karma of non-interruption and the unconditioned.

I have now set forth this teaching from its beginning to its end: that all things are impermanent and that having a body is suffering; that the body is not truly a self, being empty and devoid of anything real;

yet people do not understand this and suffer in vain toil. All one's kinsmen and household members are ultimately not one's own; when the truth is spoken thus, it seems like a contradiction—who would be willing to believe it?
"Would it not be better to remain silent?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Profound and serene, radiant and stainless;
I have attained this, the ambrosial state of non-action.
Now that I speak of it, the multitude does not understand."
As I am today, it would be better to remain silent.
Cast away words; there is neither thought nor attainment.
Thus, it is spontaneous, just like empty space.
Contemplating the mind and its mental objects, the consciousness is liberated;
non-conceptualization is supreme, for it can know others.
This cannot be expressed through written words.
By entering into the meaning of the Way, one does not enter into mere single-minded diligence.
All Buddhas of the past acted for the sake of sentient beings;
such is the nature of spiritual knowledge, which arises from its causes and conditions.
When one calculates these karmas, they are entirely devoid of any dharma;
therein neither existence nor non-existence exists.
All arise from causes and conditions, giving rise to birth and old age.
He likewise does not conceive of existence or non-existence;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it is beyond measure or limit.
In my previous lives, following all the Buddhas,
Never before had they attained such a dharma-patience;
there is no self, no person, and likewise no life-span.
Should they ever attain it, they would obtain this dharma-patience.
There is also no arising, and sentient beings have no life-force.
This is called primordial purity, the dharma of no-self;
at that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed this wisdom upon me.
At that time, I felt compassion for infinite sentient beings;
I did not require sentient beings to come and entreat me.
Now, for the sake of sentient beings, I have moved Brahmā.
Because he exhorted me, I have now turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Now that I am thus established in the pure and true Dharma,
Brahmā has descended from above to offer his support and encouragement.
"Turning the subtle and sublime True Dharma away from defilement, sentient beings, through awakening, shall then understand the divine consciousness.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Brahmā Encourages the Preaching of the Dharma. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

At that time, the Tathāgata manifested the majestic spiritual power of the light from the mark between his eyebrows; furthermore, that light was named "Illuminating Birth," which caused a million Brahmā kings to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, and this radiance pervaded the trichiliocosm Buddha-field.

At that time, the Brahma King Śikhin, receiving the Sage’s intention just as the Buddha had thought in his mind— that the World-Honored One remained silent and was unwilling to preach the Dharma— thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place where the Buddha is and entreat the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of the true Dharma."

At that time, the Brahma King Śikhin, surrounded by a retinue of sixty-eight thousand Brahmās, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
Heaven and earth offer no protection now that they are about to be destroyed. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, has already attained the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One.

"Remaining in silent meditative concentration, you are unwilling to preach the Dharma; while the masses of suffering remain stagnant and submerged within the triple world, we pray that you turn the wheel of the Dharma to instruct all sentient beings.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"I pray that the wealth of the noble ones May purify all sentient beings;"
Who shall exhort and bring peace to the millions of subjects?
Bestowing wisdom through giving, they cause the lotus of hearing and awakening to bloom;
proclaiming right contemplation, they eliminate the many rebellious thieves.
Striking at the appropriate times, it is the drum of the immeasurable Dharma;
by blowing upon this, it is the conch of the infinite Dharma.
One should establish this, the lofty and manifest banner of the Dharma.
Who shall arise to cause the great Dharma to shine forth?
Surely they shall raise the clouds and let fall the rain of the Great Dharma;
may it be perpetually disseminated, and may the assembly of Great Sages sit together.
One should treat this, the locus of great pain;
merely extinguish the dust and toil, the heat of the many fires.
For their sake, manifest the path of profound stillness.
In Anfeng there is no heat; it is a realm free from the karma of sorrow.
Through the Way of non-action, one guides and transforms others toward the Truth;
constantly giving rise to compassion, one harmonizes the masses and settles their disputes.
One must surely open the gate of liberation;
expounding the meaning of ultimate sincerity, which is free from the root of resentment.
For those who are blind and ignorant, one opens their eyes so they may see.
He heals and purifies them, causing them to attain the supreme Dharma-eye.
This is not the world of devas, nor the palaces of Brahmā;
it is not the realm of ghosts, gandharvas, or asura subjects.
There is no one able to cure and extinguish the disease of manifold fevers;
only the Holy Honored One, the sun and moon among men.
Therefore, I now entreat the Dharma King:
Now, establishing this supreme creation, all the devas,
by means of these merits, exhort the Tathāgata themselves:
"You must surely turn and preach the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, silently consented.
Śikhin Brahmā, seeing that the Buddha was silent, felt compassion for the devas, the people of the world, the asuras, nāgas, and spirits, wishing to bring them across to liberation.
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, seeing that the Buddha had approved, scattered various fragrant sandalwood incenses over the Buddha and suddenly vanished.
Then the tree deity of the Buddha’s bodhi tree—named Dharmaprabhāsa, also named Dharmarati, also named Dharmacitta, and also named Dharmadhara—approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“In which country shall the World-Honored One now turn the wheel of Dharma?”
Then the Buddha told him:
"It is at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages in Vārāṇasī.
The tree deity addressed the Buddha:
"In the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the population is so sparse that it is not possible to preach the Dharma there.
The Buddha told the tree deity:
"Do not speak such words."

Why is this? In a former life, I established a Dharma shrine therein; for sixty trillion years, I made offerings there to sixty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as various kinds of seers, who studied and dwelt within it.

The devas, nāgas, and spirits of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī all join in praising him; they bow their heads and take refuge in this unsurpassed Great Dharma. Ten billion buddhas all keep him in mind from beginning to end, knowing that he must turn the wheel of the Dharma here amidst these divine trees and groves.
Tranquil and serene, he beholds no faction of ignorant darkness; for this reason, he turns the wheel of Dharma amidst these divine trees of the immortals.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, the World-Honored One had accomplished all that was to be done and was free from further affliction; he had severed all hindrances and purified all defilements. With all stains exhausted, he had subdued the enmity of Māra and attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

With the extinction of ignorance, volitional formations are extinguished; with the extinction of volitional formations, consciousness is extinguished; with the extinction of consciousness, name-and-form is extinguished; with the extinction of name-and-form, the six sense bases are extinguished; with the extinction of the six sense bases, contact is extinguished; with the extinction of contact, feeling is extinguished; with the extinction of feeling, craving is extinguished; with the extinction of craving, clinging is extinguished; with the extinction of clinging, existence is extinguished; with the extinction of existence, birth is extinguished; with the extinction of birth, old age, sickness, death, and all [suffering] are extinguished.
