The Buddha then thought of his native land and desired to see his kinsmen.
Now I listen to King Śuddhodana’s words, which are most piteous.
There is a bhikṣu named Udāyin, whose appearance and nature are pleasing to others;
the Buddha has dispatched him as a messenger to bring back news.
Returning to his father the king’s kingdom, he entered it to proclaim the Buddha’s intent;
now the King’s Crown Prince has turned his gaze back, desiring to return to the palace.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, Udāyin immediately accepted it and set out to practice it.
At that time, before the Buddha, his manifestations followed the contours of the terrain.
His body suddenly vanished, and by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), he entered the city;
eventually arriving at the Great King’s palace, he stood before where the father-king sat.
The bhikṣu Udāyin appeared before Śuddhodana;
manifesting various transformations, he leaped forth from his father the king’s palace.
Pure as a lotus flower, not a speck of mud or dust could cling to him.
The Father King, seeing this terror, immediately asked: "What spirit is this?
Is it perhaps a deity? Why does the earth manifest such a marvel?
Who are you, and what is your clan?"
From where have you originally come?
I pray that you will open my understanding and untie the knots of doubt in my mind;
from birth until now, I have never witnessed such a transformation.
"The Prince originally renounced his kingdom to seek the Way and deliver sentient beings;
after diligent practice for incalculable eons, he has now finally attained success."
"Now, O King, do not fear; for now, relax your mind and be joyful.
I have destroyed all evils and come as a messenger from the Crown Prince.
When the King heard the Prince's message, tears fell from him like falling stars.
“For twelve years now, I have heard the name Siddhārtha.
Today, from this auspicious arrival, my thoughts awaken as if born anew.
When the Prince renounced his royal station and attained the Way, what was his name?”
Having left the country and sat for six years, through diligent effort he manifested the attainment of Buddhahood;
he is named the God among Gods, the foremost Honored One of the three realms.
"In former times, while in my own kingdom, you constructed for me a palace of many jewels;
it was carved and adorned with all manner of exquisite decorations—how does your current dwelling compare?"
Udaya replied: "The Buddha is truly sublime;
he always sits beneath the trees as the devas come to take refuge in him."
"When my son was in the palace, his quilts and mats were spread with fine brocades;
all were made of embroidered silk, soft and lustrous."
“The dragon’s wife offered a jeweled couch, and the Lord of Devas presented a kāṣāya;
yet he took no pleasure in fine garments, for his mind was neither increased nor diminished.”
"In the kingdom you enjoyed fine foods, with sweet delicacies that enriched their flavors;
what kind of sustenance do you now consume to maintain your body?"
“Holding the alms-bowl to go on the rounds for food, may the merit be shared among all, whether coarse or fine;
may I offer prayers for the families who give, so that they may be secure and at peace in every lifetime.”
"When Siddhārtha was lying down to sleep, we did not dare to call him awake recklessly;
only when we played the lute and raised the sound of song did we cause him to wake and rise."
“The Tathāgata remains in samādhi, Sleepless and awake day and night;
When Śakra and Brahmā come to offer encouragement, He manifests before them all and receives their prostrations.”
"Laypeople bathe with blended incense, With many kinds of various fragrances;
The scent of each perfume pervades the room— What kind of fragrance do you use now?"
Through the eight liberations and the three gates of deliverance, they bathe and wash away the impurities of the mind;
their minds are as pure as space, universally peaceful and free from affliction or sorrow.
"When Siddhārtha was at home, he pounded various blended incenses;
his robes were perfumed by them, pure and free from the obscuration of defilement."
“Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—these constitute the fragrance of the Way and its Virtue;
It perfumes even the eight difficult states of existence, delivering beings throughout the ten directions in every lifetime.”
"Four kinds of excellent couches and seats, fashioned from various jewels;
with many implements spread in layers, one lies and rises upon them."
"The four dhyānas serve as his bed and seat; his mind is concentrated and free from agitation.
Pure like a lotus flower, he is not defiled by the mud or the water."
Within the palace, countless soldiers and various ministers stand guard;
constantly surrounded by attendants on all sides, his eyes never behold anything foul or impure.
“The assembly of disciples together numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty;
bodhisattvas beyond measure all came to pay homage and practice.”
“Originally, while still at home and not yet having gone forth, I possessed four kinds of fine chariots—
drawn by elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and men— to travel about and observe the four directions.”
"The five supernormal powers serve as his side-horses; with penetrating vision and clairaudience, he soars through the air.
Perceiving the source and beholding the minds of all beings, he wanders and observes, crossing over birth and death."
"When the son goes out or returns, he is adorned with banners, standards, feathers, and eagles;
his various attendants before and behind each carry their respective weapons."
"The four immeasurables—compassion, kindness, protection, and equanimity; grace, wisdom, benevolence, and joy;
universally covering all calamities and hardships, thereby adorning all sentient beings."
"At the time of his departure, various musical instruments resounded, with bells being struck and drums beaten;
spectators filled the roads entirely, such that those in front and behind could not accommodate one another."
"Under a tree in Vārāṇasī, he beat the drum of the deathless;
Kauṇḍinya and others attained the Path, as did eighty-four thousand devas."
"Subduing the ninety-six paths, his voice is heard throughout the three thousandfold world;
there are no sentient beings who do not rejoice, and as they open their hearts to receive it, all become clear-minded.
"What lands does he govern?"
How many are the people? How many have been converted?
Have they all submitted and come to take refuge?
"Governed over the three thousand great realms, he instructs and transforms all sentient beings;
throughout the ten directions, they are beyond reckoning—there are none who do not receive his salvation."
"While in the kingdom, he contemplates the True Dharma, assisting me in governing the myriad people;
his movements accord with ritual and instruction, and there are none who do not receive and hear his teaching."
“The Buddha understands that emptiness is fundamentally non-existent, And has abandoned the four inversions;
There is none who does not submit and take refuge, For his spirit is tranquil and his activity is non-action.”
The Buddha has no enmity with the world; his vast knowledge is all-encompassing and thorough.
Why do you not turn back from your words? All things return to their own source.
If the whole world were filled with people, each person would have as many heads as there are [in the world].
Even with a single head and many tongues, each tongue could explain countless meanings.
Should all people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges join together to praise the Buddha’s virtues, they would not exhaust them even in eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
how much less so my own light, which is but like that of a firefly?
Upon hearing this, the king was moved even more by grief and joy, and he sighed in admiration, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Āyuṣmān said, "Your words are not spoken in vain.
Will the Buddha come?
On what day will he arrive?"
Udāyin replied,
"It will arrive in seven days.
The King leaped for joy and immediately issued an edict to his ministers and the myriad people of the kingdom:
"I shall go forth to welcome the Buddha.

With a retinue and majestic deportment like those of a Wheel-Turning King, he leveled the roads and swept them clean, sprinkling the ground with fragrant liquids and hanging silk banners and colored streamers. He erected victory banners and parasols throughout the entire kingdom; his preparations and adornments were all perfectly suited. With a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry, he traveled forty *li* to go and respectfully welcome the Buddha, bowing his head in homage and taking refuge.
Udayin came forward and reported to the King:

"I originally received the Buddha's instruction to come see Your Majesty and convey his intent; now I have returned to deliver that command and speak Your Majesty’s purpose. He is immeasurably hungry and thirsty for the Dharma and wishes to see the Most Honored One, prostrate himself, and receive the teachings, so as to transform the myriad people so that they all may receive blessings and joy."
The King said, "You should know that this is the time; do not delay any further.
At that moment, Udāyī returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and conveyed the King’s intent.
The World-Honored One and his disciples had pledged that they would return to their own country within seven days.

The king, his ministers, and the common people were all filled with joy; having been parted for many years, they had thought of them day and night, finding no pleasure in food or drink and unable to sleep, counting the days and passing the time as they grew increasingly hungry and weary.
Now that the seven days had concluded, the World-Honored One had arrived.
At that time, the Great Sage addressed his disciples:
"Tomorrow we shall set out for Kapilavastu to see our father, the King; all of you must properly adjust your robes and take up your alms bowls."

When Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings heard that the Buddha was returning to his kingdom, they all came to attend upon and escort him. Heaven rained down fragrant juices, flowers were scattered, and incense was burned; various banners and canopies were erected. The Four Kings and the devas all led the way in front, with Brahmā attending on the right and Śakra attending on the left, while the assembly of bhikṣus followed behind the Buddha.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits followed from above, offering flowers, incense, and music as they attended him.

Just as the Buddha set out on his journey, auspicious omens first appeared: the three thousandfold world-system shook in six ways, withered trees a hundred years old all bore flowers and fruit, and springs spontaneously gushed forth from parched ravines and streams.

When the King beheld these auspicious omens and knew that the Buddha had already arrived, he immediately commanded all the Śākya ministers and officials to proceed to the Buddha to scatter flowers and burn incense; they erected various banners and streamers, played a multitude of musical instruments, and all went forth to welcome the Buddha.

From afar, the king saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly, like the moon among the stars; like the sun first rising to illuminate the dawn; like a tree in full bloom with fragrant flowers in profusion; his massive body sixteen feet tall, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, shining like a mountain of gold.
The King, moved by both grief and joy, stepped forward and prostrated at his feet, saying, "We have been parted for a long time; only now do we meet again.
The ministers and all the officials likewise bowed their heads in salutation.

As he immediately returned to the city, the earth shook violently as his feet stepped upon the threshold. Heavenly flowers rained down, musical instruments resounded of their own accord, the blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the lame regained the ability to walk, the sick were healed, the mute regained the power of speech, the insane became sane, the hunchbacked straightened their spines, and those who had been poisoned found the venom neutralized. A hundred birds and beasts sang together in harmony, and the pearl bracelets of the women jingled as they struck one another.

At that time, all who witnessed these transformations were filled with joy; the precious treasuries within their homes spontaneously opened, becoming filled with rare and wondrous jewels. Those who harbored divergent thoughts all became harmonious and, with minds of equanimity, joined their palms in reverence and took refuge in the Buddha.
All classes of animals, having been moistened by its light, were reborn in the heavens;

pregnant women, touched by this radiance, experienced only slight pain during childbirth and gave birth to children who were upright and beautiful. Their lust, anger, and delusion were extinguished, and they were no longer subject to worldly afflictions; looking at one another, they regarded each other as fathers, mothers, elder brothers, younger brothers, sons, or even as their own selves.
Those in the hells found relief, and the hungry ghosts were satiated; following the light, they came to take refuge in the World-Honored One and all resolved to attain the Way.

The King beheld the Buddha’s immense body, sixteen feet in height, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and radiant with light; his body was the color of purple gold, his faculties were tranquil and composed like the moon among the stars, and he shone like a mountain of gold, honored by the Lord of Devas, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings.

He observed the various brahmins who had long dwelt in the mountains, their bodies exposed to the elements, scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind until they were dark and emaciated, standing in attendance beside the Buddha like black elephants unable to outshine a mountain of purple gold.

To manifest the Buddha’s great virtue and cause all to rejoice, he commanded the prominent clans of the kingdom to select five hundred men of upright and exquisite appearance, whose countenances were extraordinary, to go forth as śramaṇas to attend upon the Buddha’s left and right; they were like phoenixes atop Mount Sumeru, or like mani jewels set within crystal vessels.
At that time, the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda had also become a śramaṇa and was having his beard and hair shaved.
Nanda had a supervisor who served as his barber; he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“A human body is difficult to obtain, and an encounter with a Buddha’s world is rare; such a bright era is hard to meet. Now, this man and these venerable ones possess a supreme and immeasurable realization of the Way. They have no longing for worldly glory and have renounced their noble positions to practice as śramaṇas.”
"Now I am of lowly character and inferior capacity, unable to reach [the goal]; what is there to crave or delight in that would not lead me to leave the world for the Way?
Only may the Buddha take pity on me and rescue me from the three miserable realms; having been submerged in the dust of the mundane, may he pull me out and ordain me as a śramaṇa."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! and at that moment, he called out:
"Come, Bhikṣu!
As soon as he was addressed, his hair fell away and the saṃghāṭī robe appeared upon his body; he immediately became a śramaṇa.

He paid homage to the other śramaṇas and sat down according to seniority. Nanda followed behind, performing the prostrations in order, but when he reached this particular śramaṇa, he stopped and did not prostrate, thinking to himself:
"This is my household servant; he cannot perform the rites.
Knowing this, the Buddha told Nanda:

"In the Great Pervasion of the Buddha-dharma, whether one studies early or late is not determined by status of high or low. It is like the great ocean, which receives all ten thousand rivers and four currents without avoiding mud and filth; it holds fast with a mind like the earth, wherein the four great elements are equal."

Earth, water, fire, and wind are no different internally or externally; their spirit is empty and pure. That which is clung to is merely a name; one should discard self-importance and guide oneself by the Dharma, thereby responding to the boundless teachings of the ancient sages.

At that time, seeing that the Buddha’s exhortation was so earnest and thorough that the matter could not be halted, Nanda understood that all things are fundamentally non-existent; he cast aside his arrogance, lowered his mind, and paid homage.
Heaven and earth shook greatly, and the entire assembly sighed in admiration: "Excellent!
To practice the Way with an impartial mind, to eliminate self-conceit and adopt a humble heart—this has moved heaven and earth, causing them to shake so violently."

"From this time forth, the law was established that those who study first are senior and those who study later are junior; such is the constant propriety of the Dharma, wherein each has no limit and no cause for dispute.

At that time, the Buddha entered the palace and sat upon the throne hall. The king, his ministers, and the common people daily provided him with a hundred kinds of sweet delicacies. The Buddha preached the sutras and the Dharma, delivering immeasurable numbers of beings.
Gopī brought Rāhula and, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, gazed upon him and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"It has been a long time since we last attended upon you, and our offerings have been neglected for so long.
At that time, the king’s retinue were all filled with deep doubt, wondering: "The Prince abandoned the kingdom twelve years ago; from where did she conceive and give birth to this son, Rāhula?"
The Buddha said to the King, his father:
"Inform your ministers:
'Gopī maintains her vows with integrity, purity, and cleanliness; she is without blemish.'"
"If Your Majesty does not believe me, I shall now provide direct proof.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One transformed all the members of the monastic community so that they all appeared like Buddhas, their marks and signs and their radiance being identical and without distinction.
At that time, Rāhula was seven years old; Gopī then took her signet ring and gave it to him, saying:
"Give this to whoever is your father."
Rāhula immediately went straight before the Buddha and presented the seal-ring to the World-Honored One.
The king and his ministers were all filled with joy and exclaimed,
"Excellent!"
"What you have seen is immeasurable; he is truly a son of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the King, his father, and the various ministers:
"From this day forward, do not harbor any further doubts. This is my true son, born through my transformative power (*pariṇāmanā*); do not blame Gopī."

The King attained the realization of the Way, and Jiuci received the precepts and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring. All the palace attendants, both great and small, likewise received the dharma of the precepts; they observed the six monthly fasts and the three annual fasts, upholding them without slackening.

Within the realm, all is tranquil and peaceful; wind and rain come in due season, and time does not overstep its proper order. The five grains ripen in abundance and remain cheap; the people dwell in security within their homes, and the commoners of the myriad states all come to offer congratulations. Virtue and morality flourish like the waxing moon at its beginning.

Chapter 29: Praising the Buddha Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the eight deities of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—namely, Divaukasa, Mahādivaukasa, Prīta, Mahāprīta, Candana, Mahāpramudita, Śānta, and Śāntavihārin—and their retinues:

"The Buddha has turned the Wheel of Dharma through this great assembly for the sake of all beings, to rescue and deliver those throughout the ten directions. Do not allow it to be interrupted; open the minds of the multitude with the sutras and spread them throughout the world; only then will you have repaid the Buddha’s kindness."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Great Sublime Son of Heaven:

"This present sutra is named the *Puyao Dafangdeng Dian* (The Universal Radiance Great Vaipulya Scripture). It is that which all Bodhisattvas delight in; it shall cause it to be heard throughout all Buddha-worlds. Wherever this scripture enters, there shall be no lack of brilliant illumination. The Buddha proclaims it from his own mouth; you should quickly receive, uphold, recite, and read it, so that this eye of the Buddha-dharma may be widely disseminated."
If a bodhisattva studies and hears this sutra-dharma, their mind shall be firm and strong; by diligently practicing the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, they achieve the most authentic study.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the subtle and wondrous, they should abide in the mind of the Mahāyāna Dharma with no doubt, subduing the nets of Māra. Having fully recited it, they will certainly attain the Great Sage; heterodox practitioners of other schools shall find no opportunity against them. They shall encourage and assist those studying the subtle to establish the root of great virtue, reaching the Mahāyāna.

"If there are worthy persons who, upon hearing this *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance), join their palms in self-refuge, they will immediately abandon the eight matters that are the root of indolence and achieve the eight meritorious virtues."
What are the eight?
First, obtaining an upright and handsome appearance.
Second, obtaining powerful and flourishing strength.
Third, one’s retinue will flourish and prosper.
Fourth, one will attain immeasurable eloquence.
Fifth, one will swiftly succeed in the training for renunciation.
Sixth, the purity of conduct;
seventh, the attainment of samādhi concentration;
eighth, the attainment of the light of wisdom that illuminates all things without exception.
These are the eight merits.
"If there is anyone who prepares a seat for a Dharma teacher and recites this sutra, they shall obtain the merit of eight seats.
What are these eight? They are as follows:"
First, one obtains the seat of a householder;
second, one obtains the seat of a wheel-turning monarch;
third, one obtains the seat of a celestial lord.
4. Attaining the seat of the Sovereign Deva (Īśvara).
5. Attaining the seat of Mahābrahmā.
6. Attaining the seat of the Bodhisattva.
Seventh, attaining the Tathāgata’s seat.
Eighth, attaining the seat for turning the wheel of Dharma to deliver all beings.
These are the eight seats.
"If there is a Dharma master who proclaims this Dharma, and someone should praise them, saying 'Excellent!', they shall attain eight pure practices.
What are these eight?
First, their words and deeds correspond, with no contradiction or failure."
Second, their speech is utterly sincere and free from falsehood.
Third, when among assemblies, they speak the truth without deception.
Fourth, what they say is trusted by others and not abandoned or rejected.
Fifth, his speech is gentle and supple, never coarse or harsh.
Sixth, his voice is mournful and harmonious, like that of a sorrowful phoenix.
Seventh, his body and mind accord with the occasion, and his voice is like that of Brahmā; among those gathered, there are none who do not receive it with reverence and accept it.
The eighth is that his voice and resonance accord with the minds of sentient beings like those of a Buddha.
These are the eight.

"If there are those who transcribe this *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) onto bamboo slips or silk, not begrudging their hearts nor harboring envy toward the scripture, such people will be praised for thirty-four qualities, and their fame and virtue will spread abroad."
If one attains the study of this sutra, one shall attain the eight great treasuries.
What are these eight?
First, the treasury of the intended meaning, which is never forgotten or abandoned.
The second is the attainment of the treasury of mind, through which there is nothing regarding the sutras and dharmas that cannot be understood and discerned.
The third is the attainment of the treasury of coming and going, through which one universally understands all the sutras and dharmas of the Buddhas.
Fourth, they attain the treasury of dhāraṇī, whereby they are able to recognize and remember everything they have heard.
Fifth, they attain the treasury of eloquence, whereby they proclaim the scriptures for all sentient beings, who receive them with joy.
Sixth, attaining the treasury of the Dharma and upholding the True Dharma.
Seventh, attaining the treasury of the Dharma according to one's will, never severing the teachings of the Triple Gem.
The eighth is: by attaining the practice of the Dharma-treasury, one immediately achieves the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
These are the eight great Dharma-treasuries.
"If there are those who receive, uphold, recite, and master this *Samantaprabhāsa-sūtra*, they shall attain these eight karmas."
What are the eight?
First is the practice of giving, which is free from stinginess and envy.
Second is the practice of precepts, which fulfills all vows.
The third is the karma of hearing, which consists of gathering wisdom up to the stage of *anābhoga* (the stage of non-effort).
The fourth is the karma of tranquility, which consists of diligent application toward all meditative concentrations and right attainments (*samāpatti*).
The fifth is the karma of vision, by which one is able to fully perceive the wisdom of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
The sixth is the karma of merit, by which one is endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and instructs beings within the Buddha-land.
Seventh is the karma of wisdom: preaching the Dharma for the multitude, administering medicine according to their ailments.
Eighth is the karma of great compassion: planting the roots of all virtues throughout the ten directions without weariness.
"By upholding this *Lalitavistara* (*Puyao fa*), one thinks to oneself:
'May all sentient beings attain this Dharma.
By virtue of this root of merit, one further attains the eight great blessings."
What are the eight?
First, a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieves great merit and virtue; beholding the Infinite, he establishes firm faith.
Second, he attains the status of a Four Heavenly King.
Third, one shall become Śakra;
fourth, one shall become the Heavenly King Yama;
fifth, one shall become a son of the Tuṣita Heaven.
Sixth, one shall become a deva of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
seventh, one shall become a deva of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven;
eighth, one shall become a Tathāgata, severing all unwholesome dharmas and becoming fully endowed with all roots of goodness.
These are the eight.
"If there are those who receive this *Puyao jing*, and if they listen with a sincere heart, their ears attuned and their minds focused, they shall attain the eight pure minds."
What are the eight?
First, constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness to eliminate anger and resentment.
Second, constantly practicing compassion to remove all suffering and harm.
Third, constantly practicing joy to eliminate all forms of dissatisfaction.
Fourth, constantly practicing protection to eliminate all fetters and attachments.
Fifth, cultivating the practice of the four dhyānas to attain mastery while remaining within the desire realm.
Sixth, to practice the four formless concentrations and attain mastery over them.
Seventh, to obtain the five supernormal powers to travel through all Buddha-lands, eliminating the afflictions of all hindrances and obscurations.
The eighth is: attaining the meditative state of courageous subduing, walking alone through the three realms.
These are the eight. Chapter 30:
Entrustment At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda, and Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"I have followed and practiced this Dharma for incalculable kalpas, and thereby attained the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
I entrust it to you, handing it over with my own hands; you must receive, uphold, recite, and widely expound it for others."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause this Dharma to be universally disseminated throughout the ten directions, spoke these verses:
“May all classes of sentient beings beheld by the Buddha’s eye Attain arhatship like Śāriputra;
If one were to make offerings for billions of kalpas, One would still advance further, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”

Furthermore, if one were to make offerings to pratyekabuddhas for a single day by honoring this sutra, the merit calculated from this would surpass that [former merit]; the arhats are not even sufficient to stand comparison.
If all sentient beings were to become pratyekabuddhas, and someone were to make offerings to them for billions of kalpas—
with food and drink, clothing and bedding, powdered incense, blended incenses, and famous flowers—
If one with single-minded focus joins the ten fingers together, with an impartial mind takes refuge in the One Tathāgata,
and personally utters the words "Namo Buddha," this merit and virtue shall be supreme.
All sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood, even those who for a hundred kalpas provide offerings of clothing,
food and drink, bedding and seating, powdered incense, blended incense, and famous flowers.
If the True Dharma is about to collapse, one should cast away one’s body and sacrifice one’s life;
if one protects this Dharma for even a single day and night, one will surely transcend that [suffering].
If there are those who serve the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas;
if there are those who firmly uphold this bodhicitta, they shall receive this essential scripture from the Kings of Dharma.

All these scriptural volumes are the Truth of the Path; even if there were Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and one were to honor and serve all those Tathāgatas, it would be better for one to have this scriptural volume in hand.
His great eloquence is peerless, analyzing a single phrase for as many as a hundred million eons;
his wisdom and righteous principle never diminish as he expounds this sutra for others.
The wisdom of all these guides is boundless and bottomless; there is no one who can be said to be their equal.
Just as the rivers and oceans can never be exhausted, so too are those who hear this Dharma like this.
The Buddha addressed the venerable Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Maitreya, entrusting them with repeated earnestness:

“Receive this, uphold it, recite it, and study it; cause it to spread far and wide, showing it to your fellow students and to the people of the ten directions, so that all may receive its saving grace.”
Ensure that [the lineage] is not severed, that it is transmitted from one to another through mutual instruction and mutual accomplishment, and that there is no delay.
To ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted is to repay the Buddha’s kindness.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Great and Wondrous Son of Heaven, the Sons of Heaven of the Pure Abodes, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, Mahākāśyapa, and the great disciples, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, all rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Universal Radiance Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
